regions.name: Bordeaux
regions.tagline: Three rivers, two banks and a merchant city that taught the world what a château, a classification and a futures campaign could be.
regions.summary:
Bordeaux is the reference point for most of the world's red wine. Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot were planted from Napa to Coonawarra because of what they do on the gravel of the Médoc and the clay of Pomerol, and the vocabulary of fine wine (château, grand vin, second wine, classed growth, en primeur) was invented on the quays of the Chartrons. The vineyard covers the Gironde department, around the estuary that the Garonne and the Dordogne form when they meet at the Bec d'Ambès just north of the city.

The region is also a lesson in scale and in its risks. Around 2005 Gironde carried roughly 120,000 ha of vines; by 2010 it was still close to 118,000. Then demand for everyday red Bordeaux collapsed in France and in China, prices for bulk wine fell below the cost of production, and a state and interprofession funded grubbing-up plan began in 2023. By the official count about 21,000 ha were pulled up between August 2023 and May 2026, and the vineyard in production fell to 91,543 ha in 2025 (86,600 ha of it AOP), down 9% in a single year, with another 8,000 ha expected to go in 2026 and 2027. The 2025 harvest was 3.2 million hl. The famous names sit on a small fraction of this land: the 61 classed growths of the 1855 Médoc list farm only a few thousand hectares between them.

That split explains Bordeaux. On one side is a luxury trade in a few hundred estates, sold through the négociants of the Place de Bordeaux each spring as futures; on the other, thousands of family growers and cooperatives making honest claret, rosé and dry white that compete on price with the whole world. The appellation map, some 60 AOCs, tries to sort the land in between.
regions.history:
Romans planted vines around Burdigala in the first century AD, probably with the *Biturica* vine that Pliny describes, and the poet Ausonius (fourth century) wrote fondly of his estate near the Garonne. The modern trade began in 1152, when Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet, soon Henry II of England. For three centuries Bordeaux was English, and its light red *clairet* (the origin of the English word claret) filled the wine fleets that sailed each autumn. The city protected its own wines with the *privilège des vins de Bordeaux*, which held back wines from the upriver 'Haut-Pays' (Bergerac, Cahors, Gaillac) until the Bordeaux harvest was sold. The English era ended with the defeat of John Talbot at Castillon in 1453.

In the seventeenth century the Dutch became the key customers. Their engineers, led by Humphrey Bradley under an edict of Henri IV in 1599, drained the marshes of the Médoc, exposing the gravel ridges where the great châteaux now stand. Dutch merchants also wanted white wine, sweet wine and brandy, which shaped the Sauternais and the Entre-Deux-Mers. In the 1660s Arnaud III de Pontac began selling the wine of Haut-Brion under its own name in London, the first branded estate wine; Samuel Pepys drank 'Ho Bryan' in 1663. The new style of 'New French Claret', darker and aged longer, spread to Lafite, Latour and Margaux in the early eighteenth century.

Irish, English, German and Dutch families (Barton, Johnston, Lawton, Schröder, Schÿler) settled in the Chartrons and built the négoce. Their courtiers drew up the 1855 classification for the Paris Exposition Universelle. Oidium in the 1850s and phylloxera from the 1870s were followed by downy mildew, which Alexis Millardet and Ulysse Gayon fought with the copper and lime *bouillie bordelaise* in the 1880s. AOC law arrived in 1936. The killer frost of February 1956 replaced much Cabernet with Merlot on the right bank. Compulsory château bottling for classed growths (1972), the promotion of Mouton Rothschild (1973), the 1982 vintage and Robert Parker's influence, the Asian boom of the 2000s and the 2020s crisis complete the arc.
regions.terroir:
Bordeaux has a maritime climate: mild, wet winters, warm summers and roughly 900 mm of rain a year. The pine forest of the Landes shelters the vineyards from Atlantic gales, and the estuary and rivers temper frost and heat. Vintage variation is real because autumn rain and spring frost can strike at any point; that is why the region blends several grapes that flower and ripen at different times.

Soils follow the rivers. On the left bank of the Garonne and the Gironde (Médoc, Graves, Sauternais) the rivers left terraces of Quaternary gravel washed down from the Pyrenees and the Massif Central. The best sites are low hummocks of gravel called *croupes*, often within sight of the estuary. Gravel drains fast, warms early and forces deep roots, which is what Cabernet Sauvignon needs to ripen this far north. On the right bank (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac, Castillon, Bourg, Blaye) the bedrock is Oligocene limestone, the *calcaire à astéries* packed with fossil starfish, with clay and the sandy-clay *molasse du Fronsadais* on the slopes. Cool, water-holding clay suits Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Pomerol adds gravel and clay over an iron-rich hardpan called *crasse de fer*. Between the two rivers, the rolling clay-limestone plateau of the Entre-Deux-Mers carries the volume vineyards and most of the white grapes.

Climate change is already moving the targets: harvests now start weeks earlier than in the 1980s, alcohol levels rose, and in 2021 the INAO (after a growers' vote in 2019) let Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur use a few heat-tolerant 'varieties of interest for climate adaptation' (among them Touriga Nacional, Marselan, Castets, Arinarnoa, Alvarinho and Liliorila), capped at a small share of plantings and blends.
regions.grapes: Merlot is the most planted grape by far, around two thirds of red plantings, followed by Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and small amounts of Petit Verdot, Malbec (Côt) and Carmenère. The left bank leans on Cabernet Sauvignon for structure and cassis; the right bank on Merlot for flesh and Cabernet Franc for perfume. Whites are Sémillon (the backbone of Sauternes), Sauvignon Blanc and Sauvignon Gris for dry wines, and Muscadelle for floral lift. Colombard and Ugni Blanc survive in the cheaper whites.
regions.styles: Red wine makes up roughly 85% of the output, from cheap and cheerful Bordeaux AOC to the long-lived grand vins of the classed growths, usually aged 15 to 20 months in French oak. Dry whites range from crisp Entre-Deux-Mers Sauvignon to barrel-fermented Pessac-Léognan that can age for decades. Sweet whites from noble rot (Sauternes, Barsac, Loupiac, Cadillac, Sainte-Croix-du-Mont, Cérons) are among the longest-lived wines on earth. There is also rosé, the darker *clairet*, and Crémant de Bordeaux.
regions.classification: Bordeaux runs several unrelated classifications, each tied to a place and a moment. The 1855 classification ranked 61 red wines (60 from the Médoc plus Haut-Brion in the Graves) in five tiers and 27 sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac; its rankings have changed only once, with Mouton Rothschild's promotion in 1973 (Cantemerle was added to the list soon after publication). The Graves classification (1953, confirmed 1959) names 16 estates, now 14, for red and/or white, all within Pessac-Léognan. Saint-Émilion's classification, created in 1955, is the only one designed to be revised, roughly every ten years; the 2022 edition named 85 estates and was boycotted by Cheval Blanc, Ausone and Angélus. The Crus Bourgeois of the Médoc, first listed in 1932, were reborn as a three-tier classification in 2020 and revised in 2025 (170 estates, 14 Exceptionnels). Pomerol has never had a classification. Separately, the appellation pyramid runs from regional Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, through district AOCs (Médoc, Haut-Médoc, Graves, Entre-Deux-Mers, Côtes de Bordeaux), to communal AOCs such as Pauillac and Pomerol.

regions.name: Médoc
regions.tagline: A low gravel peninsula between forest and estuary, home to four of the five first growths.
regions.summary: The Médoc is the tongue of land north of Bordeaux between the Atlantic pine forest and the Gironde estuary. Its wine strip is narrow, rarely more than 10 to 12 km wide, and runs about 80 km from Blanquefort to the Pointe de Grave. The southern two thirds is the Haut-Médoc, with six communal appellations (Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, Listrac-Médoc and Moulis); the flatter, clay-rich north is the Médoc AOC, once called the Bas-Médoc. Sixty of the 61 classed growths of 1855 are here.
regions.history: Before the seventeenth century the Médoc was marsh, heath and isolated priories, reachable more easily by boat than by road. Dutch drainage engineers opened it up after 1599, and in the late 1600s and early 1700s parliamentary families of Bordeaux (Pontac, Ségur, Brane, Rauzan) planted the gravel ridges near the river. The Marquis Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur owned Lafite, Latour and Calon at once and was nicknamed the 'prince of the vines'. The estuary was the highway: wines left from small ports such as Pauillac and the *esteys* (tidal creeks) that cut the vineyards.
regions.terroir: The secret is gravel and water. The best gravel croupes face the estuary, which moderates temperature and reduces frost; the jalles (small streams) between them drain the land and mark appellation borders. Vineyards a few kilometres inland, behind the croupes, sit on heavier soils and ripen later. In the north and in Saint-Estèphe, clay under the gravel retains water and favours Merlot.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates the great estates, often 60 to 90% of a grand vin, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot in support. Merlot leads in the Médoc AOC and in Listrac.
regions.styles: Dry red only under the Médoc appellations; Médoc white wines (Pavillon Blanc de Château Margaux, Blanc de Lynch-Bages) are sold as Bordeaux.
regions.classification: The 1855 classification (five tiers of crus classés) and the Crus Bourgeois du Médoc (Cru Bourgeois, Supérieur, Exceptionnel; 2025 list valid five years) are the two hierarchies.

regions.name: Graves
regions.tagline: The only French wine region named after its soil, where Bordeaux's fame began in the city's own suburbs.
regions.summary: The Graves runs south-east from the city of Bordeaux along the left bank of the Garonne to beyond Langon, a 50 km band of gravel, sand and clay with the Landes forest at its back. The northern section, around Pessac, Talence and Léognan, has had its own appellation, Pessac-Léognan, since 1987 and holds all the classified estates. The south wraps around the sweet-wine enclaves of Cérons, Barsac and Sauternes.
regions.history: This was Bordeaux's first fine-wine district. Pope Clement V planted what became Pape Clément in the early fourteenth century, and Haut-Brion was the first estate wine sold under its own name in London in the 1660s. Urban growth in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries swallowed most of the vineyards around the city; Haut-Brion and La Mission Haut-Brion now sit among houses, tram lines and a university campus.
regions.terroir: Gravel terraces are deep and mixed with sand and clay, warmer than the Médoc because the vineyards are closer to the city and further from the estuary. Forest clearings in Léognan and Martillac, surrounded by pines, give cooler nights and fresher whites.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot for reds, often in near-equal parts; Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon for whites, sometimes with Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle.
regions.styles: Red and dry white (both often barrel-aged), plus the sweet Graves Supérieures.
regions.classification: The Graves classification was drawn up in 1953 and confirmed in 1959: 16 estates, classified for red, white or both, with Haut-Brion also a 1855 first growth. Mergers have reduced the list to 14. There is no hierarchy within it.

regions.name: Sauternais
regions.tagline: Five villages where a cold stream, warm river and autumn mist turn rotten grapes into gold.
regions.summary: The Sauternais is a small area about 40 km south-east of Bordeaux, where the Ciron stream joins the Garonne. Its five communes (Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac and Barsac) make lusciously sweet white wine from grapes attacked by noble rot, *Botrytis cinerea*. Barsac, on the north side of the Ciron, has its own appellation but may also use the Sauternes name. Across the Garonne, Loupiac, Cadillac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont make similar wines from clay-limestone slopes.
regions.history: Sweet wine made sense here because Dutch merchants wanted it in the seventeenth century, and because the Garonne carried it cheaply to the sea. Noble rot probably came into deliberate use in the late seventeenth or eighteenth century; by the time Thomas Jefferson ordered Yquem in 1787 the style was famous. The 1855 classification gave Sauternes its own list, with Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur. The later twentieth century brought heroic vintages (1921, 1929, 1937, 1945, 1967, 1975, 1988 to 1990, 2001) but also falling demand, and many estates now make dry white wines as well.
regions.terroir: The Ciron rises from springs in the Landes forest and runs under a shady canopy of trees, so its water stays cold. In September and October it meets the warmer Garonne, and on clear nights the temperature difference makes dense morning fog. Fog lets the spores of botrytis germinate on ripe grapes; afternoon sunshine then dries the berries, so the fungus feeds without turning into grey rot. The fungus pierces the skins, water evaporates, and sugar, acidity and glycerol concentrate while the fungus adds its own aromatic compounds. Gravel and sand over clay and limestone dominate Sauternes; Barsac has thin red sand and clay over a limestone plateau.
regions.grapes: Sémillon, with its thin skin and rich texture, is about 80% of plantings; Sauvignon Blanc adds acidity and aroma, and a little Muscadelle brings florals.
regions.styles: Sweet white (*liquoreux*), plus dry whites sold as Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur (Y d'Yquem, R de Rieussec, G de Guiraud, S de Suduiraut).
regions.classification: The 1855 Sauternes-Barsac list ranks 27 châteaux today: Yquem as Premier Cru Supérieur, 11 Premiers Crus and 15 Deuxièmes Crus.

regions.name: Libournais
regions.tagline: Merlot's homeland on limestone and clay, run from the old river port of Libourne.
regions.summary: The Libournais is the area around Libourne, on the right bank of the Dordogne: Saint-Émilion and its satellites, Pomerol, Lalande-de-Pomerol, Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac, with Castillon and Francs to the east. Estates are much smaller than in the Médoc, often family farms of a few hectares, and the wines are softer, plusher and earlier-drinking, built on Merlot and Cabernet Franc.
regions.history: Libourne was founded as an English bastide in 1270 and its quays shipped right-bank wine to northern Europe, mainly through Breton and Dutch traders, while the Chartrons négociants focused on the Médoc. In the twentieth century Libourne houses such as Jean-Pierre Moueix built Pomerol's international reputation. The February 1956 frost killed many vines and led to wide replanting with Merlot.
regions.terroir: Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau and slopes (*côtes*), Pomerol's gravel and clay terrace, and Fronsac's limestone hills give cool, water-retaining soils that suit early-ripening Merlot, with Cabernet Franc on the warmest gravel and limestone sites.
regions.grapes: Merlot (often 70 to 100%), Cabernet Franc, and some Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Red only under the main appellations.
regions.classification: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé (2022: 2 Premiers Grands Crus Classés A, 12 B, 71 Grands Crus Classés); no classification in Pomerol or Fronsac.

regions.name: Entre-Deux-Mers
regions.tagline: Rolling farmland between two tidal rivers that grows much of Bordeaux's everyday wine.
regions.summary: 'Between two seas' is the triangle between the Garonne and the Dordogne, where both rivers are still tidal. It is a landscape of clay-limestone hills, bastide towns and Romanesque churches, and its vineyards supply much of the Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur volume. The Entre-deux-Mers AOC itself was white-only from 1937; reds were added from the 2023 vintage. Its Garonne-facing edge forms Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux and the sweet-wine appellations of Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont.
regions.history: The great Benedictine abbey of La Sauve-Majeure, founded in 1079, organised much early viticulture. The area was hit hardest by the 2020s crisis and the grubbing-up programme.
regions.terroir: Clay-limestone plateaus with patches of gravel and boulbènes (silty clay).
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon and Muscadelle for whites; Merlot and the Cabernets for reds.
regions.styles: Dry white; red since 2023; sweet whites on the Garonne slopes.
regions.classification: No estate classification; district and regional AOCs.

sources.title: Jane Anson: Entre-deux-Mers introduces red as well as white wines under the AOC

regions.name: Blaye and Bourg
regions.tagline: Steep riverside slopes opposite the Médoc, older in vineyard history than their famous neighbour.
regions.summary: Blaye and Bourg face the Médoc across the Gironde estuary. Bourg, on the slopes above the confluence of the Dordogne and Garonne, is sometimes called the 'Switzerland of the Gironde' for its hills; Blaye stretches north around the Vauban citadel. Both make mostly Merlot-based reds that offer some of the best value in Bordeaux.
regions.history: These slopes were planted before the Médoc was drained, and Roman villas stood on them. The citadel of Blaye, built by Vauban in the 1680s to defend the estuary, is part of the UNESCO-listed Fortifications of Vauban.
regions.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes and plateaus, with gravel and sand patches near the water.
regions.grapes: Merlot dominates, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Malbec; Sauvignon Blanc for whites.
regions.styles: Red and some dry white.
regions.classification: District AOCs only: Blaye, Côtes de Blaye, Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, Côtes de Bourg.

regions.name: Champagne
regions.tagline: A cold, chalky edge of the wine world where blending, patience and a single brilliant brand built the world's most famous sparkling wine.
regions.summary:
Champagne is the northernmost of France's great wine regions, about 150 km east of Paris, and its 34,200 ha of vines are spread over 319 villages (*crus*), mostly in the Marne but also in the Aube, the Aisne, the Haute-Marne and the Seine-et-Marne. Just three grapes do almost all the work: Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay. The vineyard is farmed by about 16,200 growers, who own around 90% of the vines, while some 370 houses (*maisons*) ship more than two thirds of the wine. That division of labour, growers who sell grapes and houses who blend and market, is the economic engine of the region and is managed jointly through the Comité Champagne.

The region is defined by scarcity and control. Each summer growers and houses set a maximum marketable yield for the coming harvest, in kilograms of grapes per hectare, to match supply to demand. It was 12,000 kg/ha for 2022, 11,400 for 2023, 10,000 for 2024 and 9,000 for 2025. With shipments down to about 266 million bottles in 2025 (from 271.4 million in 2024 and a record of nearly 326 million in 2022), the 2026 limit was cut to 8,800 kg/ha, enough for roughly 250 million bottles, one of the lowest levels of the modern era. Underneath, a reserve system lets houses hold back wine from good years to blend into poor ones.

Champagne's status is protected relentlessly: the name may only be used for wine from the delimited zone, and the Comité has fought cases from Spain to Russia. In 2015 UNESCO listed the 'Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars' as World Heritage: the historic vineyards of Hautvillers, Aÿ and Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, the Avenue de Champagne in Épernay, and the Saint-Nicaise hill in Reims with its Roman chalk quarries.
regions.history:
Romans planted the first vines around Reims (Durocortorum), and the region's medieval wine was a pale, still red, rival to Burgundy at the courts of Paris. Kings of France were crowned in Reims cathedral, which gave the wine prestige. Bubbles were at first a fault: the cold winters stopped fermentation, and it restarted in spring, sometimes bursting barrels and bottles. The English, who imported Champagne in barrel and bottled it in strong coal-fired glass, were the first to enjoy it fizzy. In 1662 Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society in London describing how adding sugar to wine made it sparkle, decades before the French deliberately made sparkling wine.

Dom Pierre Pérignon (1638 to 1715), cellarmaster at the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers, did not invent sparkling Champagne. He spent much of his life trying to prevent the bubbles that burst bottles, but he did pioneer blending of grapes from different villages, gentle pressing to make white wine from black grapes, and careful vineyard work. The legend of him crying 'Come quickly, I am drinking the stars!' was created by the houses in the nineteenth century.

The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries built the houses: Ruinart (1729, the oldest), Taittinger's predecessor Forest-Fourneaux (1734), Moët (1743), Veuve Clicquot (1772), and German-founded houses such as Krug, Bollinger, Mumm and Heidsieck. Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin, widowed in 1805, took over her husband's company; her team developed the *table de remuage* (riddling rack) around 1816 to clear sediment, and she shipped the 1811 'comet vintage' to Russia. Pharmacist Jean-Baptiste François's work on sugar and pressure in 1836 made bottle fermentation predictable.

The phylloxera epidemic and fraud with grapes from outside the region led to the Champagne riots of 1910 and 1911. Growers in the Marne, angry at houses buying cheap wine from the Loire and Midi, attacked cellars in Aÿ and Damery in April 1911; troops occupied the region. The Aube growers, excluded from the 1908 delimitation, revolted too, and were finally admitted in 1927. Both world wars were fought across the vineyards; during the First World War the chalk cellars of Reims sheltered schools and hospitals under bombardment. The Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne (CIVC) was created in 1941.
regions.terroir:
Champagne is cold for wine: an average annual temperature of about 11°C, a mix of oceanic and continental influences, spring frosts and frequent hail. That marginal climate gives grapes with high acidity and low sugar, perfect for a base wine that will be refermented and aged. Climate change has pushed the average harvest date forward by around two weeks since the 1980s and made ripeness easier; it also brings more extreme heat, drought and disease pressure. The 2023 harvest, picked in a heatwave, was overshadowed by the deaths of several pickers and by a scandal over harvest labour: in July 2025 a court in Châlons-en-Champagne jailed the head of a labour contractor for human trafficking of about fifty workers lodged in squalid conditions at Nesle-le-Repons.

The key to the region is chalk. The Côte des Blancs, the Montagne de Reims and the Reims area sit on Belemnite chalk, a soft, porous Cretaceous limestone that drains well but stores water like a sponge and releases it to roots in dry summers. It also reflects light and heat. Its other gift is cellars: the chalk can be quarried into cool, stable galleries, and Reims and Épernay hold hundreds of kilometres of them. The Vallée de la Marne has more clay, marl and sand, which suits Meunier. The Côte des Bar in the Aube is on Kimmeridgian marl and limestone, the same rock as Chablis, which suits Pinot Noir.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir (about 38% of plantings) gives body, red fruit and structure; it dominates the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Bar. Meunier (about 32%) is fruity and supple, hardy against frost, and dominates the Vallée de la Marne. Chardonnay (about 30%) gives finesse, citrus and longevity and is king of the Côte des Blancs. Four other old varieties are allowed: Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris (Fromenteau), together under 0.3% of plantings. In 2022 the INAO authorised the disease-resistant hybrid Voltis on a trial basis, up to 5% of plantings and 10% of blends.
regions.styles: Champagne is made by the *méthode champenoise* (called the traditional method elsewhere): a still base wine is blended, sweetened with the *liqueur de tirage* (sugar and yeast) and bottled under crown cap; a second fermentation in bottle creates about 6 atmospheres of pressure. The wine then ages in the cellar (at least 15 months for non-vintage, 12 of them on the lees, and three years for vintage, often much longer), is riddled so the sediment collects in the neck, disgorged, and topped up with a *dosage* of sugar that determines the style: brut nature (0 to 3 g/l, no added sugar), extra brut (0 to 6), brut (under 12), extra dry, sec, demi-sec and doux. Most Champagne is non-vintage (sans année), a blend across years using reserve wine. There are also vintage Champagnes, *blanc de blancs* (only Chardonnay), *blanc de noirs* (from black grapes), rosé (usually made by blending red and white wine, a practice banned for other EU rosés), and prestige cuvées such as Dom Pérignon, Krug Grande Cuvée, Cristal and Salon. Still wines are made under Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys.
regions.classification: There is one AOC for sparkling wine, Champagne, with no hierarchy of sub-appellations. The échelle des crus, a scale created in 1911 and agreed between growers and houses in 1919, set the price paid for grapes by village: grand cru villages received 100% of the reference price, premier cru villages 90 to 99%, and the others down to 80%. The price system ended in 1990, and the scale was abandoned in the 2000s, but the terms 'Grand Cru' and 'Premier Cru' remain allowed on labels for the 17 grand cru and 42 premier cru villages. Labels also carry a code that tells the buyer who made the wine: NM (négociant-manipulant, a house), RM (récoltant-manipulant, a grower who makes his own wine), CM (coopérative de manipulation), RC (récoltant-coopérateur), SR, ND and MA (buyer's own brand). The project, launched in 2003, to revise the appellation area and add 40 villages was abandoned in October 2026.

regions.name: Montagne de Reims
regions.tagline: A wooded plateau ringed by Pinot Noir villages, with nine of the seventeen grand crus.
regions.summary: The Montagne de Reims is a low, forested plateau between Reims and Épernay, never more than 288 m high, around whose slopes the vineyards form a horseshoe. Its north-facing slopes, unusual for great wine, give Pinot Noir with structure and acidity at Verzenay, Verzy and Mailly; its south-facing slopes at Bouzy and Ambonnay give riper, richer Pinot. Nine grand crus are here, more than anywhere else.
regions.history: The forest on top is a regional park famous for its *faux*, twisted dwarf beeches. During the First World War the front line ran just north of Reims, and the Verzenay lighthouse, built in 1909 as an advertisement, served as an observation post.
regions.terroir: Chalk beneath a cap of clay and sand; the grand cru slopes have thin soils over chalk.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir dominates; Chardonnay at Villers-Marmery and Trépail; some Meunier on the lower slopes.
regions.styles: Structured blanc de noirs and the backbone of many house blends; still red Bouzy.
regions.classification: Grand crus: Ambonnay, Beaumont-sur-Vesle, Bouzy, Louvois, Mailly-Champagne, Puisieulx, Sillery, Verzenay, Verzy.

regions.name: Côte des Blancs
regions.tagline: An east-facing chalk slope south of Épernay that grows the world's most valuable Chardonnay.
regions.summary: The Côte des Blancs runs about 20 km south from Épernay, an east-facing escarpment covered almost entirely with Chardonnay. Six grand crus (Chouilly, Oiry, Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger) and premier crus such as Cuis, Vertus and Grauves give the precise, mineral blanc de blancs that are the backbone of prestige blends.
regions.history: Many top grower-producers are here, in Avize and Le Mesnil, and the Lycée Viticole de la Champagne trains winemakers in Avize.
regions.terroir: Belemnite chalk lies near the surface, under only a few centimetres of topsoil in places.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay (about 95%).
regions.styles: Blanc de blancs: taut, saline, long-lived.
regions.classification: Grand crus: Avize, Chouilly, Cramant, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Oger, Oiry.

sources.title: BKWine: Grand cru and premier cru in Champagne, the échelle des crus

regions.name: Vallée de la Marne
regions.tagline: River slopes from Tours-sur-Marne to Château-Thierry, Meunier country.
regions.summary: The Vallée de la Marne follows the river west from Tours-sur-Marne past Aÿ and Épernay to Château-Thierry and beyond, into the Aisne. Its eastern end, the Grande Vallée around Aÿ, Mareuil-sur-Aÿ and Hautvillers, is classic Pinot Noir country with two grand crus (Aÿ and Tours-sur-Marne). Further west, on clay and sand, Meunier takes over and gives fruity, supple wines, increasingly bottled as single-variety cuvées by growers.
regions.history: Hautvillers is the home of Dom Pérignon's abbey; Aÿ and Damery were the scenes of the riots of 1911.
regions.terroir: Chalk in the east, more clay, marl and sand to the west.
regions.grapes: Meunier, with Pinot Noir in the Grande Vallée and some Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Fruity Meunier, rich Aÿ Pinot Noir, still red Aÿ Rouge.
regions.classification: Grand crus: Aÿ and Tours-sur-Marne.

sources.title: BKWine: Grand cru and premier cru in Champagne, the échelle des crus

regions.name: Côte des Bar
regions.tagline: The Aube's Pinot Noir hills, closer to Chablis than to Reims, and the source of some of the region's most exciting grower Champagne.
regions.summary: The Côte des Bar in the Aube department, about 110 km south-east of Épernay around Bar-sur-Aube and Bar-sur-Seine, covers nearly a quarter of the Champagne vineyard. For decades it sold Pinot Noir to the houses of the Marne. Since the 1990s, growers such as Cédric Bouchard, Vouette et Sorbée, Jacques Lassaigne (Montgueux) and Drappier have shown what its ripe, structured Pinot can do. Les Riceys, the largest wine commune in Champagne, is the only village with three appellations.
regions.history: Excluded from the 1908 delimitation, the Aube growers rioted in 1911 and were admitted only in 1927 as a 'second zone'.
regions.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone, as in Chablis.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir (over 80%), Chardonnay, a little Pinot Blanc.
regions.styles: Ripe blanc de noirs, still Rosé des Riceys.
regions.classification: No grand or premier crus.

sources.title: BKWine: Grand cru and premier cru in Champagne, the échelle des crus

regions.name: Côte de Sézanne
regions.tagline: A southern continuation of the Côte des Blancs, softer and riper.
regions.summary: South of the Côte des Blancs and the Saint-Gond marshes, the Côte de Sézanne gives ripe, round Chardonnay that houses use for blends. Its east-facing slopes are on chalk mixed with clay and silt.
regions.history: The marshes of Saint-Gond were the scene of fighting during the First Battle of the Marne in 1914.
regions.terroir: Chalk under clay and silt.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Round blanc de blancs, blending material.
regions.classification: No grand or premier crus.

sources.title: BKWine: Grand cru and premier cru in Champagne, the échelle des crus

regions.name: Languedoc-Roussillon
regions.tagline: The world's largest vineyard area under one name, reborn from the bulk-wine 'wine lake' into a frontier of hill-grown reds, Picpoul and centuries-old fortified wines.
regions.summary:
Languedoc-Roussillon is the great Mediterranean arc of French wine, from the Rhône delta near Nîmes to the Spanish border at Banyuls. For most of the twentieth century it was the land of *gros rouge*, cheap high-yielding Aramon and Carignan that filled France's workers' glasses and the European 'wine lake'. Since the 1980s it has been transformed: vast areas were grubbed up with EU subsidies, the plains were replanted or abandoned, and the hillsides became home to ambitious growers who make some of France's most exciting reds and whites.

The CIVL's appellations cover nearly 46,000 ha, within a much larger total area under vine whose output is mostly IGP Pays d'Oc, France's biggest varietal-wine label. The CIVL counts about 2,000 private estates, 150 cooperatives and 500 négociants. Roussillon, the Catalan corner around Perpignan, is much smaller and shrinking, and it has long made the bulk of France's vins doux naturels (VDN), the fortified sweet wines of Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes, along with dry reds from old Grenache and Carignan in the schist hills.

The structure has been rebuilt in three tiers since 2007: the regional AOC Languedoc at the base; sub-regional AOCs (Corbières, Minervois, Saint-Chinian, Faugères, Fitou); and 'crus' such as La Clape, Pic Saint-Loup, Terrasses du Larzac, Corbières-Boutenac, Minervois-La Livinière and, since 2026, Montpeyroux, with more (Cabrières, Saint-Saturnin) in progress.
regions.history:
Greeks from Massalia founded Agde (Agathe) around the fifth century BC, and the Romans founded Narbonne (Colonia Narbo Martius) in 118 BC, the first Roman colony in Gaul, on the Via Domitia. Monasteries (Saint-Hilaire, Fontfroide, Valmagne, Aniane, Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert) kept vines through the Middle Ages. Arnau de Vilanova, a physician at the University of Montpellier, described the mutage technique behind the vins doux naturels around 1285, and Roussillon was Catalan and then Spanish until the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659.

The railway (Paris to Sète, 1850s) and phylloxera (from 1863 near the Rhône) turned the Languedoc into France's bulk-wine factory: high-yielding Aramon on the plains, shipped north to the industrial cities. Overproduction, fraud with sugared wines and imports from Algeria led in 1907 to the Revolt of the Midi: Marcellin Albert, a café owner from Argeliers, led mass protests that culminated in some 500,000 to 800,000 people in Montpellier on 9 June 1907; troops killed demonstrators in Narbonne, and the 17th Infantry Regiment mutinied at Béziers in sympathy. The law of 29 June 1907 against fraud and the creation of cooperatives followed. From 1970 to 2000, EU-funded grubbing-up and the arrival of pioneers (Aimé Guibert at Mas de Daumas Gassac, 1978; Olivier Jullien; the Grange des Pères) changed the region's image.
regions.terroir:
A hot, dry Mediterranean climate with 2,500 or more hours of sun, under 600 mm of rain in parts, and strong winds: the cold, dry *tramontane* and *cers* from the north-west, and the humid *marin* from the sea. Drought is the main constraint and growing worse; the dry years from 2022 onward cut yields sharply in parts of Roussillon.

Geology is remarkably varied: schist in Faugères, northern Saint-Chinian, Maury, Banyuls-Collioure and parts of Corbières; limestone in Pic Saint-Loup, La Clape and the Corbières massifs; *galets roulés* (rounded pebbles) on the Costières and the Grès de Montpellier terraces; volcanic basalt around Agde; red sandstone and marl in the Terrasses du Larzac; and black schist and black marl in Maury. Altitude matters: the Larzac foothills and Limoux are much cooler than the coastal plain.
regions.grapes: Reds are blends of Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Cinsault (the 'GSM plus' family). Old-vine Carignan, despised for decades, is now prized for its depth. Whites use Grenache Blanc and Gris, Roussanne, Marsanne, Vermentino (Rolle), Bourboulenc, Clairette, Picpoul, Macabeu and Mauzac (in Limoux). Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria make sweet Muscats.
regions.styles: Mostly red; rosé is booming; whites are improving fast; Limoux sparkling (Blanquette, Crémant); and the vins doux naturels: Muscats (Frontignan, Lunel, Mireval, Saint-Jean-de-Minervois, Rivesaltes), Grenache-based Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes, in oxidative and fresh styles.
regions.classification: AOC Languedoc (since 2007) covers the whole region and sits beneath sub-regional AOCs and crus. Dénominations géographiques (such as Pézenas, Grès de Montpellier, Sommières, Cabrières, Saint-Saturnin, Montpeyroux until 2026, Quatourze, La Méjanelle, Saint-Christol, Saint-Drézéry, Saint-Georges-d'Orques) can follow the Languedoc name. In Roussillon: Côtes du Roussillon, Côtes du Roussillon Villages (with five named villages), Collioure, and the VDN appellations.

regions.name: Roussillon
regions.tagline: French Catalonia: old Grenache on black schist, and the fortified wines that Arnau de Vilanova described in the thirteenth century.
regions.summary:
Roussillon is the department of the Pyrénées-Orientales, French Catalonia, an amphitheatre of mountains (Corbières to the north, the Pyrenees and the Albères to the south, the Canigou massif to the west) opening onto the sea at Perpignan. It is one of the sunniest and driest corners of France.

The vins doux naturels are its signature. Their method, mutage, is to add neutral grape spirit (at about 96% alcohol, typically 5 to 10% of the volume) to fermenting must once a few degrees of alcohol have formed. The yeast dies, natural sugar is kept, and the wine reaches about 15 to 18% alcohol. Arnau de Vilanova described it in Montpellier around 1285, and the category gained a special tax status under the 'loi Pams' of 1898, championed by Jules Pams, a politician from Port-Vendres. The must must be very ripe (at least 252 g/l of sugar). Ageing then splits the styles: reductive wines bottled young (grenat, rimage, Muscat), and oxidative wines aged in old casks or in glass bonbonnes left outdoors to bake in the sun and chill at night, which develop the walnut, curry and dried-fruit notes called *rancio*. Some estates keep perpetual reserves, topping up old casks with younger wine as a solera does. Its specialities are the vins doux naturels (Banyuls, Maury, Rivesaltes, Muscat de Rivesaltes) and, increasingly, dry wines from old Grenache, Carignan and white Grenache, Macabeu and Grenache Gris. Since the 1990s, growers such as Gérard and Lionel Gauby, Hervé Bizeul (Clos des Fées) and Jean-Philippe Padié have made the Agly valley one of France's most exciting wine areas.
regions.history: Roussillon was part of the Crown of Aragon and of Catalonia until it was annexed to France by the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659, and the Catalan language and identity remain strong. The Knights Templar had vineyards and cellars here, notably at Mas Déu and at Banyuls.
regions.terroir: Black and grey schist (Maury, Agly valley, Banyuls, Collioure), granite and gneiss (Lesquerde, Caramany), limestone and marl (Tautavel, Vingrau), and the alluvial terraces of the Têt and Tech. The tramontane wind blows on about one day in three, drying vines and preventing disease.
regions.grapes: Grenache Noir, Gris and Blanc; Carignan; Syrah; Mourvèdre; Lledoner Pelut; Macabeu; Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria; Malvoisie du Roussillon (Tourbat).
regions.styles: Fortified sweet wines (VDN), dry reds, dry whites, rosés.
regions.classification: Côtes du Roussillon Villages has five named villages: Caramany, Latour-de-France, Lesquerde, Tautavel and Les Aspres. Banyuls Grand Cru requires 30 months in wood.

regions.name: Loire Valley
regions.tagline: France's longest river strings together Muscadet, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc across a thousand kilometres of châteaux and chalk.
regions.summary:
The Loire is France's longest river, 1,012 km from the Massif Central to the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire, and its wine regions follow it for most of that distance. They are not one region but four or five, linked by the river and by a shared northern freshness: the Pays Nantais near the ocean (Muscadet), Anjou and Saumur (Chenin Blanc and Cabernet Franc on schist and chalk), Touraine (Chenin, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon, Côt and Gamay around Tours), the Centre-Loire (Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé and their neighbours on Sauvignon Blanc), and scattered upstream outposts in the Auvergne and Forez.

The vineyard managed by InterLoire covers about 42,000 ha across 14 departments, with roughly 2 million hl harvested in an average year (1.75 million in frost-hit 2024). InterLoire describes it as France's second sparkling-wine region after Champagne, and its output in 2024 was about 36% white, 28% rosé (largely Rosé d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou), 19% red and 17% sparkling. The wider Loire basin counts more than 50 AOCs, more than any other French region.

The Loire is also where the 'natural wine' movement found its most fertile ground, from Anjou's schist to the Touraine of Thierry Puzelat and Clos du Tue-Boeuf, and where Chenin Blanc reaches heights that show it to be one of the world's great white grapes: dry, sweet or sparkling, from Savennières, Vouvray and the Layon.
regions.history:
Vines spread up the Loire in the Gallo-Roman period, and the river carried wine to Nantes and the sea, then to England and the Low Countries. Monasteries shaped the vineyards: Marmoutier near Tours, founded by Saint Martin in 372; Bourgueil, founded in 990; Fontevraud, burial place of the Plantagenets. The Dutch drove the sweet-wine trade of Anjou and the Layon in the seventeenth century and bought cheap white for distilling, which encouraged the planting of Melon de Bourgogne in the Pays Nantais after the great frost of 1709.

The Valley's role as the playground of French kings in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries left the châteaux of Chambord, Chenonceau, Amboise and Blois, and in 2000 UNESCO listed the Loire Valley between Sully-sur-Loire and Chalonnes as a World Heritage cultural landscape. Phylloxera hit hard in the 1880s, and the Centre-Loire replanted largely with Sauvignon Blanc instead of Chasselas and Pinot Noir, laying the base for Sancerre's twentieth-century fame. In the 1970s and 1980s rosé and Muscadet boomed and then slumped; from the 1990s a generation of quality growers revived the Loire's reputation.
regions.terroir:
The Atlantic influence fades eastward. Near Nantes the climate is mild and wet, with maritime winds; by Sancerre, 400 km inland, it is semi-continental, with colder winters and warmer summers. Everywhere the Loire is northern for wine (around 47°N), and frost is the great threat: spring frosts in 2016, 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024 devastated crops.

The geology changes dramatically. In the west the vineyards sit on the Armorican Massif: granite, gneiss, gabbro and schist around Nantes, and the dark schists and volcanic rocks of the 'Anjou Noir'. East of Angers the land changes to the Paris Basin: the soft, pale chalk called *tuffeau* (a Turonian limestone) of the 'Anjou Blanc', Saumur and Touraine, quarried to build the châteaux, which leaves kilometres of cellars and troglodyte homes. Above the tuffeau lie flinty clays (*perruches* and *argiles à silex*) and sands. In the Centre-Loire, Kimmeridgian marl (*terres blanches*), Oxfordian limestone (*caillottes*) and flint (*silex*) give Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé their three classic terroirs.
regions.grapes: Melon de Bourgogne (Muscadet) in the west; Chenin Blanc in Anjou, Saumur and Touraine; Cabernet Franc (Breton locally) for reds in Saumur, Chinon and Bourgueil; Sauvignon Blanc in Touraine and the Centre-Loire; Gamay, Côt (Malbec), Pineau d'Aunis and Grolleau for reds and rosés; Pinot Noir in Sancerre and Menetou-Salon; Romorantin at Cour-Cheverny; Chardonnay in Crémant de Loire and Haut-Poitou; Folle Blanche in Gros Plant.
regions.styles: Bone-dry, lees-aged Muscadet; dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling Chenin Blanc; crisp Sauvignon; light to medium Cabernet Franc reds; rosés from off-dry Rosé d'Anjou to dry Rosé de Loire; and a large output of traditional-method sparkling wines in Saumur, Vouvray, Montlouis and Crémant de Loire.
regions.classification: A mosaic of AOCs without estate classification. One appellation carries the words Grand Cru: Quarts de Chaume (2011). Savennières has two separate sub-appellations, Roche aux Moines and Coulée de Serrant, and Coteaux du Layon has a Premier Cru, Chaume. Since 2011 Muscadet Sèvre et Maine has added 'crus communaux' (seven recognised; three more under INAO review). Many AOCs have 'dénominations géographiques complémentaires', such as the Coteaux du Layon villages and Touraine's Amboise, Azay-le-Rideau, Chenonceaux, Mesland and Oisly.

regions.name: Pays Nantais
regions.tagline: Melon de Bourgogne on ancient rock near the ocean, made for oysters and, increasingly, for the cellar.
regions.summary: The Pays Nantais around Nantes is Muscadet country: about 8,000 ha, most of it in Sèvre et Maine south-east of the city. The grape is Melon de Bourgogne, and the classic style is light, dry, saline white aged on its lees (*sur lie*). Since 2011 the crus communaux have shown that Muscadet from specific rocks, aged two years or more on the lees, can rival great whites.
regions.history: Melon de Bourgogne replaced the old red vineyards after the brutal winter of 1709, partly because Dutch traders wanted white wine for distillation. The Muscadet appellations date from 1936 (Sèvre et Maine, Coteaux de la Loire) and 1937 (Muscadet).
regions.terroir: Maritime climate. The bedrock is the Armorican Massif: granite (Clisson), gabbro (Gorges, Château-Thébaud), gneiss (Le Pallet), orthogneiss, schist and amphibolite, each now linked to a cru.
regions.grapes: Melon de Bourgogne; Folle Blanche (Gros Plant); some Gamay, Cabernet and Chenin in the Coteaux d'Ancenis and Fiefs Vendéens.
regions.styles: Dry white, sur lie; long lees-aged cru wines.
regions.classification: Muscadet regional and three sub-regional AOCs; crus communaux (DGC) within Muscadet Sèvre et Maine.

regions.name: Anjou-Saumur
regions.tagline: Black schist and white tuffeau, sweet Chenin, dry Chenin and the Loire's best Cabernet Franc.
regions.summary: Anjou-Saumur is the Loire's most varied stretch. West of Angers on the dark schists of the 'Anjou Noir' come Savennières and the sweet wines of the Layon and Aubance; to the east, on the white tuffeau of the 'Anjou Blanc' and the Saumurois, come Saumur, Saumur-Champigny and the sparkling Saumur houses. Rosé d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou are the region's bestsellers.
regions.history: Angers was the capital of the Plantagenet counts of Anjou. Dutch merchants built the sweet-wine trade of the Layon in the seventeenth century. Saumur's sparkling wine industry began in 1811, when Jean Ackerman, who had worked in Champagne, applied the Champagne method to Saumur Chenin.
regions.terroir: The geological boundary between the Armorican Massif and the Paris Basin passes through the region near Brissac and Doué. Schist, sandstone and volcanic rock to the west; tuffeau chalk and sand to the east.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grolleau, Gamay, Pineau d'Aunis.
regions.styles: Dry, sweet and sparkling Chenin; Cabernet Franc reds; rosés.
regions.classification: Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru; Coteaux du Layon village names and Premier Cru Chaume; Savennières subzones.

sources.title: EU geospatial inventory of wine PDOs (Candiago et al. 2022)

regions.name: Touraine
regions.tagline: The garden of France, where Chenin from tuffeau cliffs and Cabernet Franc from gravel terraces grew up beside royal châteaux.
regions.summary: Touraine centres on Tours and stretches from Bourgueil and Chinon in the west to Cheverny and Valençay in the east. Its most famous wines are Vouvray and Montlouis (Chenin Blanc on either side of the Loire), and Chinon and Bourgueil (Cabernet Franc). The regional Touraine AOC covers a huge area of Sauvignon Blanc, Gamay and Côt along the Cher.
regions.history: François Rabelais, born near Chinon around 1494, celebrated its wines. Abbeys such as Marmoutier spread Chenin (Pineau de la Loire) here; the royal court of the Valois built its châteaux in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
regions.terroir: Tuffeau chalk underlies the slopes, with clay-flint (*perruches*) and sand on top; river terraces of gravel and sand carry the lighter Cabernet Franc.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Gamay, Côt, Pineau d'Aunis, Romorantin, Grolleau, Menu Pineau (Orbois).
regions.styles: Dry to sweet and sparkling Chenin, Cabernet Franc reds, Sauvignon, light reds and rosés.
regions.classification: Touraine has five 'dénominations géographiques' (Amboise, Azay-le-Rideau, Chenonceaux, Mesland, Oisly) plus Touraine Noble Joué.

sources.title: EU geospatial inventory of wine PDOs (Candiago et al. 2022)

regions.name: Centre-Loire
regions.tagline: The Sauvignon Blanc benchmark: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé face each other across the river on Kimmeridgian marl, limestone and flint.
regions.summary: Centre-Loire is the group of appellations in the geographic heart of France, around Bourges and the upper Loire: Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Pouilly-sur-Loire, Menetou-Salon, Quincy, Reuilly, Coteaux du Giennois and Châteaumeillant. They are closer to Chablis than to Nantes, and their wines (mainly Sauvignon Blanc, plus Pinot Noir and Gamay) share a continental crispness. Further upstream lie the volcanic outposts of the Auvergne and Forez.
regions.history: Before phylloxera, Sancerre and Pouilly grew mainly Chasselas and Pinot Noir for the Paris market. Replanting with Sauvignon Blanc, and the Paris bistro fashion for Sancerre after the Second World War, made the region's name.
regions.terroir: The same Kimmeridgian marl that underlies Chablis surfaces here, along with Portlandian and Oxfordian limestone and flint (silex) on clay.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Gris.
regions.styles: Dry Sauvignon; light Pinot Noir reds and rosés.
regions.classification: No crus; Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé distinguish soil types informally.

sources.title: EU geospatial inventory of wine PDOs (Candiago et al. 2022)

regions.name: Loire Auvergne and Forez
regions.tagline: Volcanic outposts at the river's source: Gamay on basalt and granite.
regions.summary: Upstream, the Loire and its tributary the Allier rise in the Massif Central, and small vineyards cling to volcanic and granitic hills: Saint-Pourçain, Côtes d'Auvergne, Côte Roannaise and Côtes du Forez. Gamay dominates, giving bright, mineral reds closer to Beaujolais than to Touraine.
regions.history: Saint-Pourçain was a royal favourite in the Middle Ages; the area's vineyards shrank dramatically after phylloxera and urbanisation.
regions.terroir: Basalt, granite, and Allier limestone and sand.
regions.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Tressallier.
regions.styles: Light reds, rosés and dry whites.
regions.classification: Small AOCs created between 1994 and 2011.

sources.title: EU geospatial inventory of wine PDOs (Candiago et al. 2022)

regions.name: Provence
regions.tagline: France's oldest vineyard and the capital of pale rosé, with a few fiercely individual red and white appellations hidden among the pines.
regions.summary:
Provence, between the Rhône and the Italian border, is where French wine began: Greek settlers from Phocaea founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BC and planted vines. Today it is the world capital of pale, dry rosé. The three main appellations (Côtes de Provence, Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence and Coteaux Varois en Provence) covered 27,428 ha in 2025 and produced about 1.24 million hl, of which roughly 89% was rosé. Provence makes 40 to 45% of France's AOP rosé and about 5% of the world's rosé. More than 550 producers share the three AOPs; exports take 42% of the volume, and the United States is the biggest foreign market.

The rosé boom since the 2000s, driven by Château d'Esclans's Whispering Angel (Sacha Lichine, from 2006; majority-owned by LVMH since 2019), Miraval (Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie, from 2008) and the image of the Riviera, made Provence one of France's most profitable wine regions and drew luxury and drinks investors such as LVMH and Pernod Ricard. It also created a standardised style, pale salmon, dry, light, which the smaller appellations deliberately avoid. Bandol (Mourvèdre reds), Cassis (whites), Palette (Château Simone), Bellet (above Nice) and Les Baux-de-Provence are the region's specialists.
regions.history: The Phocaeans brought vines to Massalia around 600 BC, and the Romans made Provincia (hence Provence) their first province beyond the Alps in the second century BC. Monasteries such as the Cistercian Le Thoronet and the abbey of Saint-Victor in Marseille kept vineyards. Bandol shipped its sturdy Mourvèdre reds from its port in barrels marked with a 'B', since Mourvèdre stood up to sea voyages. In 1955 the Côtes de Provence (then a VDQS, created in 1951) classified 23 estates as crus classés, a unique and now frozen list; 18 still use the title. Côtes de Provence became an AOC in 1977. Since 2000 the rosé boom has transformed the economy of the Var.
regions.terroir: A Mediterranean climate with 2,700 to 3,000 hours of sun, hot dry summers and mild winters; the mistral wind from the north-west dries and cleans the vineyards. Geology splits Provence in two: a limestone Provence in the north and west (Sainte-Victoire, Coteaux d'Aix, Coteaux Varois, Bandol, Cassis) and a crystalline Provence in the south-east, the Maures and Esterel massifs, with schist, granite, gneiss and red volcanic rhyolite (La Londe, Fréjus, Notre-Dame des Anges).
regions.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Tibouren and Carignan for rosés and reds, with Cabernet Sauvignon in Aix and Les Baux. Whites: Vermentino (Rolle), Clairette, Ugni Blanc, Sémillon, Marsanne, Bourboulenc. Bellet keeps Braquet and Folle Noire.
regions.styles: Pale, dry rosé dominates; some powerful reds (Bandol, Les Baux) and characterful whites (Cassis, Palette, Bellet).
regions.classification: Côtes de Provence has five 'dénominations de terroir' (Sainte-Victoire and Fréjus from 2005, La Londe from 2008, Pierrefeu from 2013, Notre-Dame des Anges from 2019) and 18 surviving crus classés from 1955.

regions.name: Corsica
regions.tagline: A granite mountain in the sea, with Italian grapes, French law and its own language of wine.
regions.summary: Corsica, 180 km from the French coast and 80 km from Tuscany, is a mountain in the Mediterranean, and its wines are closer to Italy than to France: the main grapes are Nielluccio (Sangiovese), Sciaccarellu (a Tuscan grape, Mammolo) and Vermentinu. The island has roughly 5,750 to 6,000 ha of vines, of which about 2,800 to 2,900 ha are in nine AOPs: Patrimonio, Ajaccio, the regional Corse (Vin de Corse) with five named sub-areas (Calvi, Coteaux du Cap Corse, Figari, Porto-Vecchio and Sartène), and Muscat du Cap Corse. Rosé is the largest share of AOP production, as in Provence; reds make up about 17% and whites about 13%.
regions.history: Greeks from Phocaea founded Alalia (Aléria) on the east coast around 565 BC and planted vines. The island was Genoese from the thirteenth century until it was sold to France in 1768, a year before Napoleon was born in Ajaccio. In the 1960s and 1970s, French settlers ('pieds-noirs') from Algeria planted large vineyards of high-yielding grapes on the eastern plain, and fraud scandals over sugared wine led to the Aléria affair of August 1975, when Corsican nationalists led by Edmond Simeoni occupied a settler's wine cellar, a founding moment of modern Corsican nationalism. Since the 1980s Corsica has turned to quality and its own grapes.
regions.terroir: Granite dominates the west and south (Ajaccio, Sartène, Figari, Porto-Vecchio), schist the north-east (Cap Corse), and limestone and clay the north around Patrimonio. Mountains, sea breezes and altitude temper the heat.
regions.grapes: Nielluccio (Sangiovese), Sciaccarellu, Vermentinu, Grenache, Carcajolu Neru, Minustellu, Biancu Gentile, Muscat à Petits Grains, Aleatico.
regions.styles: Rosé, red, white and the vin doux naturel Muscat du Cap Corse.
regions.classification: Nine AOPs. Vin de Corse sub-areas (Calvi, Coteaux du Cap Corse, Figari, Porto-Vecchio, Sartène) are 'dénominations géographiques complémentaires'.

regions.name: Southwest France
regions.tagline: A patchwork of rivers, hills and Pyrenean foothills where France keeps its oldest and oddest grapes: Tannat, Manseng, Négrette, Mauzac, Fer Servadou.
regions.summary:
The Sud-Ouest is not one wine region but a loose federation of small ones, scattered across the basins of the Garonne, the Dordogne, the Lot, the Tarn and the Adour, from Bergerac in the north to the Basque foothills in the south and the Aveyron in the east. What unites them is history and grapes. For centuries these were the 'Haut-Pays' wines, which had to travel down the rivers past Bordeaux and were kept back by Bordeaux's merchants until their own wine was sold. That rivalry shaped everything: the Haut-Pays developed dark, tannic reds (the 'black wines' of Cahors) and sweet whites that could survive the wait and the voyage.

Today the region is France's greatest reservoir of indigenous grape varieties: Tannat in Madiran, Malbec (Côt) in Cahors, Négrette in Fronton, Fer Servadou in Marcillac and Gaillac, Duras and Prunelard in Gaillac, Mauzac and Len de l'El for Gaillac whites, Petit and Gros Manseng in Jurançon and Pacherenc, Abouriou in the Marmandais, Courbu, Arrufiac and Baroque in Gascony. Cooperatives such as Plaimont in Saint-Mont and the Vignerons de Buzet dominate many areas, alongside a lively scene of small growers. The huge IGP Côtes de Gascogne, built on former Armagnac vineyards, makes crisp Colombard and Gros Manseng whites in volume.
regions.history:
Gaillac claims to be one of the oldest vineyards in Gaul, planted along the Tarn by the first century AD; Roman-era amphora workshops have been excavated at nearby Montans. Medieval monasteries (Saint-Michel de Gaillac, Conques for Marcillac, Roncesvalles for Irouléguy) kept vines going. From the thirteenth century Bordeaux's privilège held back the 'wines of the High Country' until Martinmas or Christmas, so they had to be dark, strong and long-lived to compete. Cahors 'black wine' was prized in England and in Russia, where the Orthodox Church used it.

In 1553 the future Henri IV was born in the castle of Pau and, as legend has it, had his lips rubbed with garlic and Jurançon wine at his baptism. Phylloxera in the 1870s and 1880s, the 1956 frost and the rural exodus shrank the vineyards drastically. Their revival from the 1970s, through cooperatives and through a few determined estates (Alain Brumont at Montus, Robert Plageoles at Gaillac, the Jurançon growers), is one of the success stories of French wine.
regions.terroir: Climates are mostly Atlantic-influenced, warmer than Bordeaux, with the 'vent d'autan' from the south-east drying the Gaillac and Fronton vineyards and the Pyrenees bringing foehn winds and long, dry autumns to Jurançon and Madiran. Soils vary: river terraces of gravel and pebbles, clay-limestone causses (Cahors), the iron-rich *rougier* of Marcillac, and the clay and *poudingue* (conglomerate) of the Pyrenean foothills.
regions.grapes: Reds: Malbec (Côt), Tannat, Négrette, Fer Servadou (Braucol, Mansois, Pinenc), Duras, Prunelard, Abouriou, and Bordeaux varieties around Bergerac, Buzet and Duras. Whites: Petit and Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Arrufiac, Mauzac, Len de l'El, Ondenc, Baroque, Colombard, and Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle in the Bergerac area.
regions.styles: Tannic, dark reds; dry and sweet whites (Monbazillac, Saussignac, Jurançon, Pacherenc); traditional ancestral-method sparkling (Gaillac); rosés; and liqueur wines (Floc de Gascogne, Pineau des Charentes).
regions.classification: AOCs with no estate classifications. Several former VDQS became AOCs in 2011 (Saint-Mont, Tursan, Brulhois, Coteaux du Quercy, Saint-Sardos, Entraygues - Le Fel, Estaing, Côtes de Millau). Large IGPs (Côtes de Gascogne, Comté Tolosan) cover much of the region's volume.

regions.name: Bergerac and Dordogne
regions.tagline: Bordeaux's eastern neighbour on the Dordogne, with the botrytis sweet wines of Monbazillac and Saussignac.
regions.summary: The Bergerac vineyards continue the Bordeaux vineyard eastward along the Dordogne into the Périgord, with the same grapes and similar soils. The town of Bergerac (and its fictional son Cyrano) sits on the river; Monbazillac faces it from the south bank with sweet botrytised wines, Pécharmant makes the best reds north of the town, and Montravel in the west makes dry and sweet whites.
regions.history: Dutch merchants made Bergerac's sweet whites famous in the seventeenth century, especially after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685) sent Protestant growers into exile in Holland, where they kept buying their home wines.
regions.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes along the Dordogne, river gravels, and the iron-rich 'tran' subsoil of Pécharmant.
regions.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle.
regions.styles: Reds, dry whites, sweet whites, rosé.
regions.classification: Regional Bergerac and Côtes de Bergerac; sweet-wine AOCs Monbazillac, Saussignac, Côtes de Montravel, Haut-Montravel and Rosette.

regions.name: Cahors and the Lot
regions.tagline: The meandering Lot valley, homeland of Malbec and of the black wine of Cahors.
regions.summary: The vineyards of Cahors follow the Lot river's loops west of the city of Cahors, from river terraces up to the limestone *causse* plateau. Malbec, called Côt or Auxerrois here, is the grape, and it is from here that it travelled to Bordeaux and then to Argentina.
regions.history: The Pont Valentré, a fourteenth-century fortified bridge in Cahors, is the emblem of the region, which shipped wine downriver to Bordeaux and on to England.
regions.terroir: Alluvial gravel and clay terraces along the Lot; Kimmeridgian and Portlandian limestone on the causse, with red clay (*terres rouges*).
regions.grapes: Malbec (min 70% in Cahors), Merlot, Tannat.
regions.styles: Dark, structured reds.
regions.classification: Cahors AOC; Coteaux du Quercy AOC.

regions.name: Gascony and the Pyrenees
regions.tagline: Tannat, Manseng and the Pyrenean foothills, from Madiran's tannic reds to Jurançon's late-harvest whites.
regions.summary: South of the Garonne the foothills of the Pyrenees hold some of France's most distinctive wines: the dark, tannic Tannat of Madiran; the sweet and dry Mansengs of Jurançon and Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh; the cooperative-led Saint-Mont; the Basque wines of Irouléguy; and the small appellations of Béarn and Tursan. Armagnac and the IGP Côtes de Gascogne cover the rolling hills of the Gers.
regions.history: Henri IV's baptism with Jurançon in 1553 and the rise of Alain Brumont's Madiran estates in the 1980s bracket a long history of local trade and decline.
regions.terroir: Clay and limestone, pebble-studded *boulbènes*, siliceous clays, and Pyrenean *poudingue* (conglomerate) and flysch; foehn winds give dry, sunny autumns.
regions.grapes: Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Fer Servadou, Pinenc; Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Arrufiac, Baroque.
regions.styles: Tannic reds, dry and late-harvest whites.
regions.classification: AOCs only.

regions.name: Gaillac, Fronton and the Tarn
regions.tagline: Old Gallo-Roman vineyards along the Tarn and Garonne north of Toulouse, rich in rare local grapes.
regions.summary: North and north-east of Toulouse, Gaillac on the Tarn and Fronton between the Tarn and the Garonne are the vineyards of the Toulouse hinterland. Gaillac keeps the widest palette of local grapes in France, and Fronton champions Négrette.
regions.history: Gaillac's Benedictine abbey of Saint-Michel, founded in 972, organised medieval viticulture along the Tarn.
regions.terroir: Gravel terraces on the left bank of the Tarn, limestone plateau on the right bank, and the warm, drying autan wind.
regions.grapes: Mauzac, Len de l'El, Ondenc, Loin de l'Œil, Muscadelle, Sauvignon; Duras, Braucol (Fer Servadou), Prunelard, Négrette, Syrah.
regions.styles: Reds, dry and sweet whites, ancestral-method sparkling.
regions.classification: AOCs only.

regions.name: Aveyron
regions.tagline: Small, steep mountain vineyards in the gorges of the Lot, Dourdou and Tarn.
regions.summary: The Aveyron, at the south-western edge of the Massif Central, has four tiny appellations: Marcillac, Entraygues - Le Fel, Estaing and Côtes de Millau. Their wines, mostly from Fer Servadou (Mansois), served the miners of Decazeville and the pilgrims of Conques.
regions.history: Monks of Conques planted Marcillac's vineyards in the Middle Ages; nineteenth-century mining towns kept them alive until the mines closed.
regions.terroir: Red, iron-rich *rougier* (Marcillac), schist and granite (Entraygues, Estaing), limestone (Millau).
regions.grapes: Fer Servadou (Mansois), Gamay, Cabernet, Chenin Blanc, Mauzac, Syrah.
regions.styles: Light, peppery reds, rosés, dry whites.
regions.classification: AOCs only.

appellations.name: Médoc
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
appellations.summary:
The Médoc AOC covers the northern third of the peninsula, the old Bas-Médoc, around Bégadan, Saint-Yzans, Blaignan, Valeyrac and Lesparre. It has no classed growths but it is the heartland of the Crus Bourgeois, and three of the fourteen 2025 Exceptionnels (La Cardonne, Castéra and Laujac) are here. The wines are firm, fresh and often more Merlot-driven than further south, with dark fruit, graphite and a savoury, slightly rustic edge in youth. They are the Médoc's best value: well-made bottles from Château Potensac, La Tour de By or Goulée age a decade or more at a fraction of Pauillac prices.

The appellation also legally covers the Haut-Médoc area, so any Médoc red can use the name, but in practice it is used by estates north of Saint-Estèphe.
appellations.terroir: Flatter land with more clay and limestone and less gravel than the Haut-Médoc. The best sites are the gravel islands near the estuary at Bégadan, Valeyrac and Saint-Christoly. Clay holds water in drought years and ripens later in cool ones, which is why Merlot is often half the blend.
appellations.nerd_note: The northern Médoc's best sites are gravel 'islands' rising out of former marsh at Bégadan, Valeyrac and Saint-Christoly; between them lie reclaimed *palus* meadows, still drained by channels first dug under the Dutch engineers of the seventeenth century.

appellations.name: Haut-Médoc
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
appellations.summary:
The Haut-Médoc appellation covers the 29 communes of the southern Médoc that are not entitled to, or choose not to use, one of the six communal names. It is a patchwork that runs from the suburbs of Bordeaux at Blanquefort and Le Taillan to Saint-Seurin-de-Cadourne north of Saint-Estèphe, and from the river to the forest edge. Five 1855 classed growths use it: La Lagune (third) and Cantemerle (fifth) on the southern sands and gravel near Ludon and Macau; La Tour Carnet, Belgrave and Camensac (fourth and fifth) inland at Saint-Laurent.

Quality varies with distance from the estuary. The best non-classified estates, such as Sociando-Mallet at Saint-Seurin and Lanessan at Cussac, make long-lived, Cabernet-driven reds that compete with classed growths. The appellation is also home to many Crus Bourgeois, including five 2025 Exceptionnels (Malescasse, de Malleret, Paloumey, Reysson, du Taillan).
appellations.terroir: Mixed Garonne gravels near the river, with sand, clay and limestone further inland. Southern estates on sandy gravel (La Lagune, Cantemerle) give softer, more perfumed wine; northern ones on gravel over clay give firmer, Saint-Estèphe-like structure.
appellations.nerd_note: Château Cantemerle was added to the 1855 list in September 1855, months after the original April document, because its owner protested that it had been forgotten; its name was squeezed in at the bottom of the fifth growths.

appellations.name: Saint-Estèphe
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
appellations.summary:
Saint-Estèphe is the northernmost of the great Médoc communes, separated from Pauillac by the Jalle du Breuil stream, which also separates Lafite from Cos d'Estournel. Its wines have a reputation for sturdiness: deep colour, firm tannin and acidity, and a savoury, earthy core that needs ten or more years to relax. That reputation has softened since the 2000s as estates picked riper and used more Merlot, but the structure remains.

There are five classed growths: Cos d'Estournel and Montrose (seconds), Calon-Ségur (third), Lafon-Rochet (fourth) and Cos Labory (fifth). The appellation is also unusually strong below the classed level. Phélan Ségur, Les Ormes de Pez, de Pez, Haut-Marbuzet and Meyney make some of the best value in the Médoc, and two 2025 Crus Bourgeois Exceptionnels (Le Crock and Lafitte Carcasset) are here.
appellations.terroir: More clay sits under the gravel than in Pauillac, and the soils are cooler and slower to drain, which preserves acidity and gives a slightly later harvest. The gravel croupes of Montrose and Cos face the estuary; the plateau around Saint-Estèphe village and Pez is heavier. Merlot often makes up 30 to 50% of blends.
appellations.nerd_note: The name Cos is thought to come from the Gascon *caux*, 'pebbly hill'; Montrose takes its name from the pink heather that covered its gravel mound before vines were planted in the early nineteenth century.

appellations.name: Pauillac
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
appellations.summary:
If one appellation defines Cabernet Sauvignon, it is Pauillac. Three of the five first growths (Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild) and 18 classed growths in all share about 1,200 ha around a small river port, and the style they make is the template copied around the world: blackcurrant and cedar, pencil shavings and tobacco, firm but fine tannins, and the ability to age for half a century. Cabernet Sauvignon often makes up 70 to 90% of the grand vin.

The commune has three main gravel plateaus. In the north, by the hamlet of Le Pouyalet, Lafite and Mouton face each other across a lane, with Pontet-Canet, d'Armailhac, Clerc Milon and Duhart-Milon around them. In the centre, the Bages plateau carries Lynch-Bages, Haut-Bages Libéral and Croizet-Bages; inland are Grand-Puy-Lacoste, Batailley and Haut-Batailley. In the south, at Saint-Lambert, Latour and the two Pichons sit against the Saint-Julien border, separated from Léoville Las Cases by the Juillac stream. Lafite's wines tend to perfume and finesse, Latour's to power and density, Mouton's to exotic richness.

Below the classed growths, Pauillac is almost entirely accounted for: few appellations have so little room for unknowns. The cooperative La Rose Pauillac and second wines (Carruades de Lafite, Les Forts de Latour, Le Petit Mouton, Réserve de la Comtesse) are the entry points.
appellations.terroir: Deep Garonne gravel croupes, up to 30 m high and several metres deep, over a subsoil of marl, clay and the iron-cemented *alios*. The gravel forces roots down several metres, gives excellent drainage after rain, and stores heat. Latour's 47-ha Enclos runs down to the estuary meadows, which reduces frost and cools hot nights.
producers: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande
appellations.nerd_note: The tower on Latour's label is not the medieval fort of Saint-Maubert that gave the estate its name; that tower vanished long ago, and the round tower in the vines is a seventeenth-century dovecote.

appellations.name: Saint-Julien
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
appellations.summary:
Saint-Julien is the smallest of the big four Médoc communes and the most consistent. There is no first growth, but eleven classed growths farm most of its 900-odd hectares: the three Léovilles (Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton), Gruaud Larose and Ducru-Beaucaillou as seconds; Lagrange and Langoa Barton as thirds; Saint-Pierre, Talbot, Branaire-Ducru and Beychevelle as fourths. Almost all the land is in the hands of classified estates or of Gloria, the domain Henri Martin assembled from classed-growth parcels in the twentieth century.

The style sits between Pauillac's power and Margaux's perfume: dense, cedar-scented Cabernet with polished tannins and a recognisable balance. Léoville Las Cases, with its walled Grand Clos running up to Latour, is often called a 'super second' and priced close to the firsts. Ducru-Beaucaillou, whose name refers to its 'beautiful stones', sits on the gravel nearest the river.
appellations.terroir: A compact block of deep gravel ridges facing the estuary, bordered by the Juillac stream to the north and the Jalle de Saint-Julien to the south. The riverside estates (Las Cases, Ducru, Beychevelle) are on the finest gravel; Gruaud Larose, Talbot and Lagrange lie on higher, more clay-rich gravel inland and give broader wines.
appellations.nerd_note: Beychevelle's name is said to come from *baisse-voile*, 'lower the sail': ships passing on the Gironde lowered their sails in salute to the Duc d'Épernon, admiral of France, who owned the estate in the seventeenth century. The ship on the label remembers it.

appellations.name: Margaux
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
appellations.summary:
Margaux is the largest and the most southerly of the Médoc's great communal appellations, and the one with the most classed growths: 21, from first growth Château Margaux to fifth growths Dauzac and du Tertre. It spreads across five communes: Margaux and Cantenac (merged as Margaux-Cantenac in 2017), Soussans, Labarde and Arsac. The appellation was finalised in 1954 after long arguments about which villages belonged.

Margaux's reputation is for perfume: violets, roses and red fruit layered over Cabernet's cassis, with silkier tannins than Pauillac. The best wines (Margaux, Palmer, Rauzan-Ségla, Brane-Cantenac, Giscours, Malescot Saint-Exupéry, Durfort-Vivens) combine that fragrance with real depth. The size and number of estates also mean variable quality; the 1970s and 1980s saw several underperformers, and the turnaround since then is one of the Médoc's success stories.

Palmer is the cult name here, regularly priced above several seconds, and its biodynamic farming and *Historical XIXth Century Wine* (a blend with northern Rhône Syrah, recalling the old practice of 'hermitaging' claret) show a progressive streak.
appellations.terroir: The thinnest, finest gravel of the Médoc, often over limestone, with less clay than further north. Poor, well-drained soils restrict vigour and give delicacy rather than power. The Cantenac plateau and the gravel around Margaux village are the classic sites; Arsac and Soussans sit on sandier, later-ripening soils.
appellations.nerd_note: A bottle of 1787 Margaux engraved 'Th.J.', supposedly from Thomas Jefferson's order, was valued at 500,000 dollars until a New York merchant knocked it over at a dinner in 1989. All the 'Jefferson bottles' came from the collector Hardy Rodenstock and are now widely regarded as forgeries.

appellations.name: Listrac-Médoc
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary: Listrac sits inland, on the edge of the pine forest west of Moulis, and it is the 'roof of the Médoc', reaching 43 m above sea level. Its wines are firmer and fresher than the riverside communes, traditionally a bit austere in youth, with dark fruit and a mineral, limestone-driven finish. More Merlot is planted here than anywhere else in the Haut-Médoc because the clay-limestone soils suit it. Château Clarke (Edmond de Rothschild Heritage), Fourcas Hosten, Fourcas Dupré and Fonréaud are the reference estates, and Château Reverdi was named a Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel in 2025.
appellations.terroir: Three gravel ridges of Pyrenean origin run through a plateau of clay and limestone, the only real limestone of the Médoc.
appellations.nerd_note: Listrac also makes a significant amount of dry white wine (Château Clarke's Le Merle Blanc, Fonréaud's Le Cygne), sold as Bordeaux because the appellation is red-only.

appellations.name: Moulis-en-Médoc
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary: Moulis is the smallest communal appellation of the Médoc and one of its most rewarding for drinkers. Its heart is the Grand Poujeaux gravel ridge on the border with Listrac and Arcins, where Château Chasse-Spleen, Poujeaux, Maucaillou and Branas Grand Poujeaux make dense, long-lived reds that often taste like classed growths at half the price. No estate was classified in 1855, partly because the area was less fashionable with brokers at the time.
appellations.terroir: Western Moulis shares Listrac's clay-limestone; the eastern Grand Poujeaux area has deep Garonne gravel similar to Margaux and Saint-Julien.
appellations.nerd_note: Chasse-Spleen ('chase away melancholy') is often said to have been named after a remark by Lord Byron or a poem by Baudelaire; the story is unproven, but the estate has leaned into it with a contemporary art centre.

appellations.name: Pessac-Léognan
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc for red; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Sauvignon Gris for white
appellations.summary:
Pessac-Léognan is the northern Graves, carved out in 1987 so that the historic estates closest to Bordeaux could stand apart from the cheaper southern Graves. Its ten communes run from Mérignac and Pessac (now suburbs, with vineyards between houses and tram lines) south to Léognan and Martillac, where the vines sit in clearings in the pine forest. All the estates of the Graves classification are here.

It is the one Bordeaux appellation that is great for both red and dry white. The reds blend Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot in near-equal proportions and have a signature smoky, mineral, tobacco-leaf character, sometimes described as hot gravel. The whites, barrel-fermented Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, are among France's finest: Haut-Brion Blanc, La Mission Haut-Brion Blanc, Domaine de Chevalier and Smith Haut Lafitte age 20 years or more. The late Denis Dubourdieu's research at the University of Bordeaux on skin contact, lees ageing and thiols shaped modern white Bordeaux, much of it here.

Haut-Brion, a 1855 first growth, and La Mission Haut-Brion face each other across the Avenue Jean Jaurès in Pessac, surrounded by the city.
appellations.terroir: Deep gravel terraces mixed with sand and clay, warmer than the Médoc because of the urban heat island and distance from the estuary. In the south, gravel croupes in forest clearings give cooler nights that keep the whites fresh.
appellations.nerd_note: Haut-Brion is the only wine estate mentioned in Samuel Pepys's diary: on 10 April 1663 he drank 'a sort of French wine called Ho Bryan' at the Royal Oak tavern in London.

appellations.name: Graves
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Graves takes its name from its gravel, the only major French appellation named after a soil. Since 1987 it has meant the southern part of the old district, from Cadaujac and Saint-Médard-d'Eyrans south past Podensac, Portets and Langon, wrapping around Cérons, Barsac and Sauternes.
