The reds are softer and earlier-drinking than Pessac-Léognan, with the same smoky earthiness; the dry whites, often Sémillon-rich and barrel-fermented, are some of the best value white wines in France. Clos Floridène, created by Denis and Florence Dubourdieu, Château de Chantegrive, Vieux Château Gaubert and Château Rahoul are reliable.
appellations.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces on the left bank of the Garonne, with more sand and clay in the south. The pine forest at the back gives cool nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Graves is one of the few places in Bordeaux where Sémillon still dominates dry whites, and old-vine Sémillon from here is the closest thing to the region's historic white style.

appellations.name: Graves Supérieures
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Graves Supérieures is a sweet or medium-sweet white wine appellation covering the Graves area. It is a survivor from the days when much of the southern Graves made semi-sweet wine for the Dutch and Belgian markets. Production is small today, mostly late-harvested Sémillon from estates near Cérons and Barsac, and the wines are softer and lighter than Sauternes. It is useful for nerds hunting rare aged bottles, which can be surprisingly cheap.
appellations.terroir: The same gravel and sand as Graves, with sweet-wine sites near the Ciron and the Garonne where morning mists encourage botrytis in good years.
appellations.nerd_note: Graves Supérieures does not require botrytis, so wines range from late-harvest moelleux to genuinely nobly rotten liquoreux depending on vintage and estate.

appellations.name: Sauternes
appellations.grapes: Sémillon (about 80%), Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Muscadelle
appellations.summary:
Sauternes is the most famous sweet wine in the world, and its making is a gamble against the weather. The appellation covers four communes on the south side of the Ciron (Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac) plus Barsac, whose wines may be sold as either Barsac or Sauternes. In 2010 the zone had over 2,200 ha of vines and around 190 estates producing about 41,000 hl a year; both figures have since fallen as estates switched land to dry white or red.

Everything depends on noble rot. *Botrytis cinerea* thrives when the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and autumn nights produce fog, followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The fungus perforates the skins of ripe Sémillon, water evaporates, and the berries shrivel into brown, sticky raisins whose juice can exceed 350 g/l of sugar. Rot does not arrive evenly, so pickers go through the vineyard several times, sometimes berry by berry, over six to ten weeks: these passes are the *tries successives*. The rules demand hand harvesting by successive tries, must of at least 221 g/l of sugar (15% potential alcohol), at least 12% actual alcohol and 45 g/l residual sugar, and a maximum yield of 25 hl/ha. In practice the best estates make far less: Yquem's often-quoted rule of thumb is one glass of wine per vine.

Fermentation in barrel is slow and stops naturally, or is stopped, around 13.5 to 14% alcohol with 100 to 150 g/l of sugar left. The wines then age 18 to 36 months in oak. Young Sauternes tastes of apricot, peach, pineapple, honey, saffron and botrytis's signature notes of orange marmalade and beeswax; with decades in bottle the colour turns amber and the flavours move to crème brûlée, dried fig, tea and spice. The high sugar and acidity let great vintages live a century.

The 1855 list classed Sauternes and Barsac separately from the Médoc: Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, then Premiers and Deuxièmes Crus (27 châteaux today). Sales have struggled for decades as diners moved away from sweet wine, and many estates now also make dry whites (Y, R de Rieussec, G de Guiraud, S de Suduiraut) and promote Sauternes young, chilled or with tonic as an aperitif.
appellations.terroir: Gravel and sand over clay in Sauternes and Bommes, with clay-limestone at Fargues and on the slopes around Yquem's hill, the highest point at about 75 m. The Ciron's cold water and the gallery forest along it are essential; so is the sunshine that follows the fog. Wet autumns bring grey rot instead, and some vintages (1992, 2012 at Yquem) yield no grand vin at all.
appellations.nerd_note: Botrytis produces the enzyme laccase and compounds such as sotolon (also found in fenugreek and vin jaune), which is why old Sauternes can smell of curry spice and walnuts.

appellations.name: Barsac
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Muscadelle
appellations.summary:
Barsac is the largest of the five Sauternais communes, on the north bank of the Ciron where it flows into the Garonne. It has its own appellation, but by a historic right its estates may label their wines either Barsac or Sauternes; most top estates use Barsac on the label to stress their identity. Ten classed growths of 1855 are here, including two Premiers Crus, Climens and Coutet, plus Doisy-Daëne, Doisy-Védrines, Doisy-Dubroca, Nairac, Caillou, Broustet, Suau and de Myrat.

The difference is geology. Barsac is a low limestone plateau (the *calcaire à astéries*) covered by a thin layer of red, iron-rich sand and clay, unlike the gravel of Sauternes and Bommes. The soils drain fast but the limestone keeps vines supplied in drought, and the wines tend to be a touch lighter, fresher and more citrus-driven, with a mineral, almost saline finish. Climens, made from 100% Sémillon and farmed biodynamically since 2010, is the benchmark, and the estate's ability to make elegant wine even in hot years shows what limestone brings.

The village is also known for its stone walls: many vineyards are enclosed by walls of local limestone, a reminder that the Barsac quarries supplied building stone for Bordeaux.
appellations.terroir: Flat to gently rolling limestone plateau at 10 to 20 m altitude, with shallow red sand (*sables rouges*) over fissured limestone; lower-lying vineyards towards the Garonne have more alluvium.
appellations.nerd_note: Château Coutet's Cuvée Madame, made only in exceptional years from a few of the oldest parcels and the richest tries, is one of the rarest wines of the Sauternais.

appellations.name: Cérons
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Cérons is a tiny sweet-wine appellation in the Graves, covering the communes of Cérons, Illats and Podensac just north of Barsac. It is the forgotten sibling of Sauternes: the same Garonne climate and botrytis, lighter and cheaper wines, and only a few dozen hectares now declared as sweet each year because most growers find dry Graves easier to sell. Château de Cérons and Grand Enclos du Château de Cérons keep the flame alive, and old vintages are among the best bargains in sweet wine.
appellations.terroir: Gravel and sand over limestone, close to the Garonne and the Ciron's mouth.
producers: Grand Enclos du Château de Cérons
appellations.nerd_note: Growers in Cérons can declare the same vines as Cérons (sweet) or Graves (dry or red) depending on the year, so the appellation's size changes with each vintage's weather.

appellations.name: Loupiac
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Loupiac faces Barsac across the Garonne on the right bank, and makes sweet wines from botrytised Sémillon on south and west-facing clay-limestone slopes. The wines are generally a little lighter and fresher than Sauternes, closer to a rich moelleux in lesser years, and they are excellent value. Château Loupiac-Gaudiet, Clos Jean and Château du Cros are references.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and gravel slopes above the river, with morning fogs rising from the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: Loupiac has a Gallo-Roman villa with mosaics beside its church, and local tradition claims it as the estate of the poet Ausonius, a claim Saint-Émilion makes too.

appellations.name: Cadillac
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Cadillac AOC is for sweet white wine from 22 communes on the right bank of the Garonne around the walled town of Cadillac. Since 2008 the name has also been used for the separate red appellation Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux, which confuses everyone. The sweet wines, from botrytised or late-picked Sémillon, are soft and honeyed and usually drunk within 10 years. The town's Château des Ducs d'Épernon, built in the 1600s, houses an interpretation of the area's wine heritage.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes facing the river, warmer than the Sauternais but with less consistent botrytis.
appellations.nerd_note: The town's Château des Ducs d'Épernon, begun in 1599 for the Duc d'Épernon, served as a women's prison from the nineteenth century until the 1950s before becoming a monument open to visitors.

appellations.name: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont is the best of the right-bank sweet appellations, a hilltop village facing Sauternes across the Garonne. Its steep south-facing slopes and limestone give wines with real botrytis character and the freshness to age 20 years, at a fraction of Sauternes prices. Château Loubens, La Rame and Crabitan-Bellevue lead.
appellations.terroir: The hill is built on a bank of giant fossil oysters from the Miocene sea, visible in a cliff face below the church, over limestone and clay.
appellations.nerd_note: The fossil oyster bank of Sainte-Croix-du-Mont is so thick that a cave carved into it serves as a tasting room.

appellations.name: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux once covered red and white wines from a 60 km strip of slopes on the right bank of the Garonne, from Bordeaux to Cadillac. Since the 2008 vintage its reds have moved to Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux, and the name now applies only to sweet and semi-sweet white wines. It is a small, mostly local category of moelleux.
appellations.terroir: Steep clay-limestone and gravel slopes overlooking the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: The 'Premières' in the name meant the first slopes upstream from the city, not a quality ranking.

appellations.name: Entre-deux-Mers
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle; Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc for red
appellations.summary: Entre-deux-Mers is the large district between the Garonne and the Dordogne, and the appellation of the same name has long been Bordeaux's crisp, dry white: Sauvignon Blanc-led, often with Sémillon and Muscadelle, unoaked and meant for oysters from Arcachon. From the 2023 vintage the INAO also allowed red Entre-deux-Mers with stricter rules than Bordeaux rouge, such as a planting density of at least 4,500 vines per hectare, a ban on thermovinification, and 21 months of ageing before release, so the first reds reached shelves in 2025. It is an attempt to lift a district hit hard by the collapse of bulk red prices. The sub-denomination Entre-deux-Mers-Haut-Benauge covers nine communes in the south.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone plateaus and slopes, with gravel patches and silty boulbènes; cooler and later than the Médoc.
appellations.nerd_note: The red Entre-deux-Mers rules ban thermovinification, the heat-extraction technique widely used for cheap, fruity reds, a deliberate signal that the new wines are meant to sit above basic Bordeaux rouge.

appellations.name: Graves de Vayres
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon
appellations.summary: Graves de Vayres is a small island of gravel on the left bank of the Dordogne opposite Libourne, around the communes of Vayres and Arveyres. It makes supple, Merlot-based reds and some dry whites, and owes its separate appellation to its gravelly soils, unusual in the Entre-Deux-Mers. The Renaissance Château de Vayres overlooks the river.
appellations.terroir: Gravel terraces left by the Dordogne, distinct from the surrounding clay-limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: The name refers to a gravel terrace of the Dordogne and has nothing to do with the Graves district on the Garonne, which makes it the only 'Graves' on the right bank.

appellations.name: Sainte-Foy-Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Sainte-Foy-Bordeaux sits at the eastern tip of the Gironde, next to Bergerac, around the Protestant bastide of Sainte-Foy-la-Grande. Reds, dry and sweet whites are made; since 2016 growers can also use Sainte-Foy Côtes de Bordeaux. The appellation is small and many growers farm organically.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes along the Dordogne, similar to neighbouring Bergerac.
appellations.nerd_note: Sainte-Foy-la-Grande was a Huguenot stronghold, and its growers' links with Protestant merchants in Holland and England shaped the area's early export trade.

appellations.name: Saint-Émilion
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
appellations.summary: Saint-Émilion AOC is the basic appellation of the medieval hill town and its eight neighbouring communes, which together form the old Jurisdiction of Saint-Émilion, listed by UNESCO in 1999 as the first vineyard landscape on the World Heritage list. The zone is the same as Saint-Émilion Grand Cru; the difference lies in rules (yields, ageing, tasting) and in what growers choose to declare. Most serious estates use the Grand Cru appellation, so plain Saint-Émilion is mostly the softer, earlier-drinking wine of the sandy plain toward the Dordogne and from cooperatives such as the Union des Producteurs de Saint-Émilion.
appellations.terroir: The same mosaic as the Grand Cru: limestone plateau, clay-limestone slopes, sands and gravel. Plain Saint-Émilion comes largely from the sandy and alluvial lower land.
appellations.nerd_note: The word 'Grand Cru' in Saint-Émilion is an appellation, not a ranking; only the separate classification (Grand Cru Classé, Premier Grand Cru Classé) ranks estates.

appellations.name: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
appellations.summary:
Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is the heart of the right bank: about 5,400 ha shared by the Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellations in nine communes around a limestone hill town honeycombed with quarries, catacombs and a monolithic church carved from the rock in the twelfth century. More than 800 estates share it, most of them small family holdings, and the wines range from juicy Merlot to some of the most expensive bottles on earth.

The classification, created in 1955, applies only to this appellation and is revised about every ten years, which makes it the only Bordeaux ranking where estates can be promoted or demoted. That flexibility made it litigious. The 2006 list was annulled by the courts; the 2012 list was challenged for a decade by demoted owners until the Conseil d'État finally upheld it in March 2024; and in late 2021 a Bordeaux criminal court found Hubert de Boüard, co-owner of Angélus, guilty of illegal taking of interest (*prise illégale d'intérêts*) over his role in the 2012 process. Partly in protest at criteria that weighed wine tourism, reputation and social media presence alongside tasting, Cheval Blanc and Ausone announced in mid-2021 that they would not apply for 2022, and Angélus followed in January 2022. They still use the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation, simply without a classification mention.

The 2022 classification, published in September 2022 and valid until 2032, names 85 estates: two Premiers Grands Crus Classés A (Pavie and Figeac, the latter promoted after decades of campaigning), twelve Premiers Grands Crus Classés B (Beau-Séjour Bécot, Beauséjour, Bélair-Monange, Canon, Canon-la-Gaffelière, Clos Fourtet, Larcis Ducasse, La Mondotte, Pavie Macquin, Troplong Mondot, Trottevieille, Valandraud) and 71 Grands Crus Classés. La Gaffelière, a former B, also withdrew.

Styles follow the soils. Wines from the limestone plateau and its slopes (Ausone, Canon, Bélair-Monange, Pavie) are taut, mineral and slow to evolve. The gravel island beside Pomerol (Cheval Blanc, Figeac) gives Cabernet-rich, fragrant wines. The sandy plain makes soft, early wines. The 1990s 'garagiste' movement (Valandraud, La Mondotte) showed that tiny plots and extreme ripeness could command cult prices, and its excesses later gave way to fresher, less oaky wines.
appellations.terroir: A limestone plateau of *calcaire à astéries* at 60 to 100 m, edged by steep clay-limestone slopes (*côtes*) facing south toward the Dordogne. Below are sandy-clay *pieds de côte* and the sandy, alluvial plain. In the north-west, toward Pomerol, a band of gravel and sand carries Cheval Blanc and Figeac. Clay and limestone keep vines supplied in drought and give the wines freshness.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint-Émilion's quarries supplied stone for Bordeaux for centuries; the resulting 200 km of tunnels under the plateau now age wine, and roots of old vines can be seen piercing the ceilings.

appellations.name: Montagne-Saint-Émilion
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Montagne is the largest of the four Saint-Émilion satellites north of the Barbanne stream, and its hilly limestone terrain is the most varied. It absorbed the old Parsac appellation in the 1970s. Wines are Merlot-based, plump and often excellent value; the best (Vieux Château Saint-André, Château Montaiguillon, Château Faizeau) age a decade.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills and plateau similar to Saint-Émilion's, with some sand and gravel.
appellations.nerd_note: Montagne's Écomusée du Libournais and its windmill at Calon recall a time when the hills grew grain as well as vines.

appellations.name: Lussac-Saint-Émilion
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Lussac is the northernmost satellite, cooler and later-ripening, with a mix of clay-limestone in the south and sand and gravel to the north. The wines are fresh, fruit-forward Merlot. The cooperative and family estates such as Château de Barbe Blanche, Château Lyonnat and Château de Lussac are the references.
appellations.terroir: Clay, limestone, sand and gravel; the cooler northern position shows in fresher acidity.
appellations.nerd_note: The four satellites lie north of the Barbanne stream, which also marks Pomerol's northern edge; before the appellation laws of 1936 their wines were often sold simply as Saint-Émilion.

appellations.name: Puisseguin-Saint-Émilion
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Puisseguin lies east of Montagne on a hilly limestone plateau, and its wines are often the firmest and most structured of the satellites. Château Guibot-la-Fourvieille and Château Fongaban are reliable names, and the cooperative is important.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone plateau and slopes, similar to the côtes of Saint-Émilion.
appellations.nerd_note: The Puisseguin plateau rises to about 90 m, among the highest ground in the Libournais, which tends to delay ripening and keep acidity firmer than on the Saint-Émilion plain.

appellations.name: Saint-Georges-Saint-Émilion
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Saint-Georges is the smallest satellite, a single hill in the commune of Montagne whose growers can use either name. Its south-facing limestone slopes give some of the best satellite wines. The eighteenth-century Château Saint-Georges, attributed to Victor Louis, architect of Bordeaux's Grand Théâtre, dominates it.
appellations.terroir: A limestone hill facing south toward Saint-Émilion across the Barbanne.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint-Georges is part of the commune of Montagne, so it is an appellation without its own town hall, and its growers may choose to label their wine Montagne-Saint-Émilion instead.

appellations.name: Pomerol
appellations.grapes: Merlot (about 80%), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary:
Pomerol is a small, flat, unassuming plateau north-east of Libourne, with no village to speak of, no grand châteaux and no classification, and yet it makes the most expensive red wines of Bordeaux. About 800 ha are shared by around 130 producers, many farming fewer than 10 ha. Petrus, Le Pin and Lafleur sell for more than the Médoc first growths.

The style is opulent and velvety: Merlot dominates, typically 70 to 100%, with Cabernet Franc adding perfume. Great Pomerol tastes of plum, black cherry, truffle, violets and iron, with dense but silky tannins and a texture that seems to fill the mouth. It is approachable earlier than Pauillac but can age 30 years or more.

Fame came late. In the nineteenth century Pomerol was considered part of Saint-Émilion's lesser hinterland. Madame Edmond Loubat, owner of Petrus from 1925 to 1961, and the Libourne négociant Jean-Pierre Moueix, who took over distribution and then ownership, turned Petrus into a luxury brand served at the 1953 coronation of Elizabeth II and then in New York. The Thienponts of Belgium (Vieux Château Certan from 1924, Le Pin from 1979), the Guinaudeaus at Lafleur and the Durantous at L'Église-Clinet built the rest of the legend.

No classification has ever been proposed seriously; producers argue that the market, and the soil map, already rank them.
appellations.terroir: Pomerol is a plateau of gravel and clay sloping gently from about 40 m in the east to the sands near Libourne in the west. Its highest point holds a lens of dense, swelling blue-grey smectite clay, the 'buttonhole', on which Petrus sits; around it are gravel and clay (Lafleur, Vieux Château Certan, L'Évangile, La Conseillante), with sand further west. A subsoil of *crasse de fer*, iron-rich hardpan, is said to give Pomerol its iron and truffle notes. Clay keeps Merlot supplied with water in drought, which explains its consistency in hot vintages.
appellations.nerd_note: Petrus traditionally picks only in the afternoon, once the dew has dried, with a crew large enough to bring in its roughly 11.5 ha in two or three afternoons; in a rainy vintage of the 1980s it famously hired a helicopter to hover over the vines and blow-dry the grapes.

appellations.name: Lalande-de-Pomerol
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
appellations.summary: Lalande-de-Pomerol is Pomerol's northern neighbour, across the Barbanne stream, covering Lalande and Néac. It makes Merlot-dominated reds in a plush, Pomerol-like style at a third of the price, and several Pomerol and Saint-Émilion owners make wine here (La Fleur de Boüard of the Angélus family, Château Siaurac, Château de Chambrun). The twelfth-century church at Lalande was built by the Knights Hospitaller.
appellations.terroir: Gravel and sand in the south near Pomerol, more clay and limestone at Néac.
appellations.nerd_note: Néac was once a separate appellation; it merged into Lalande-de-Pomerol in 1954, one of the few cases of a Bordeaux appellation disappearing.

appellations.name: Fronsac
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
appellations.summary: Fronsac is a set of hills on the right bank of the Dordogne just west of Libourne, overlooking the confluence with the Isle. In the eighteenth century its wines were fashionable at Versailles, partly thanks to the Maréchal de Richelieu, Duc de Fronsac, and priced above Saint-Émilion. Today it is one of the best-value right-bank appellations: firm, dark, slightly rustic Merlot with Cabernet Franc, mineral and long-lived. Château de la Dauphine, Villars, Dalem, Fontenil and Les Trois Croix are references.
appellations.terroir: Limestone hills capped by clay and the *molasse du Fronsadais* (sandstone and clay), steeper and higher than most of the right bank. The Tertre de Fronsac rises 75 m above the river.
appellations.nerd_note: Legend says Charlemagne built a fort on the Tertre de Fronsac in 769 to watch the river; whatever stood there, the hill controlled traffic on the Dordogne for centuries.

appellations.name: Canon-Fronsac
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Canon-Fronsac is a small enclave within Fronsac on the steepest limestone slopes in Fronsac and Saint-Michel-de-Fronsac, facing south over the Dordogne. Its wines are deeper and more structured than Fronsac, often compared to the côtes of Saint-Émilion. Château Canon de Brem, Moulin Pey-Labrie and Vrai Canon Bouché are the references.
appellations.terroir: Steep south-facing limestone slopes with thin clay soils over the calcaire à astéries.
appellations.nerd_note: In the nineteenth century the wines of 'Canon' hill were shipped and priced separately from other Fronsac wines, which is how a village slope became an appellation.

appellations.name: Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Côtes de Bordeaux is an umbrella created in 2009 (from the 2008 vintage) to bring together several hillside appellations on the right banks of the Garonne, Dordogne and Gironde under one marketable name. Four areas joined first: Blaye (formerly Premières Côtes de Blaye), Cadillac (the reds of the Premières Côtes de Bordeaux), Castillon (formerly Côtes de Castillon) and Francs (formerly Bordeaux-Côtes de Francs); Sainte-Foy joined in 2016. Wines can be sold under the plain Côtes de Bordeaux name, made from any of the areas, or with the area name in front. They are mostly Merlot-based reds, ripe and fresh, often the best value in Bordeaux.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills and plateaus on the 'côtes' facing the rivers, generally cooler and later-ripening than the Libournais.
appellations.nerd_note: Côtes de Bordeaux is one of the few cases where several existing appellations voluntarily merged their identity to gain export clout.

appellations.name: Castillon Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Castillon lies immediately east of Saint-Émilion and shares its limestone plateau and slopes, which is why investors from Saint-Émilion moved in from the 1990s. Stephan von Neipperg (Château d'Aiguilhe) and the consultant Stéphane Derenoncourt (Domaine de l'A) showed what the côtes could do, and Clos Puy Arnaud became a biodynamic reference. The wines are Merlot with Cabernet Franc, fresh and mineral. The town is where the English were defeated in 1453, ending the Hundred Years War and three centuries of English Bordeaux.
appellations.terroir: The eastward continuation of Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau and clay-limestone slopes, with sandy-gravel terraces near the Dordogne.
appellations.nerd_note: Every summer the town re-enacts the 1453 Battle of Castillon with hundreds of volunteers, horses and cannon.

appellations.name: Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Colombard
appellations.summary: Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux covers the hilly right bank of the Gironde estuary opposite the Médoc, and is the largest of the Côtes. Its reds are generous Merlot, its whites fresh Sauvignon. Château Bel-Air La Royère, Les Jonqueyres and Haut-Bertinerie are among the best.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills with gravel and sand patches near the estuary.
appellations.nerd_note: Blaye's growers use three names for three tiers: Côtes de Blaye (white only), Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, and the stricter red Blaye AOC.

appellations.name: Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux is the red-wine appellation of the steep slopes along the right bank of the Garonne from Bordeaux to Cadillac, formerly the reds of Premières Côtes de Bordeaux. The views across the river to the Graves are spectacular and the wines, mostly Merlot, are fresh and juicy. Château Reynon (Dubourdieu family), Château Carignan and Clos Chaumont are good examples.
appellations.terroir: Steep clay-limestone and gravel slopes along the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: Not to be confused with the sweet white Cadillac AOC from the same villages.

appellations.name: Francs Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Francs is the smallest of the Côtes, north-east of Castillon on the border with the Dordogne department, and one of the highest and coolest parts of the Gironde. The Thienpont family (Château Puygueraud) put it on the map, and Château Le Puy, farmed without chemicals by the Amoreau family for generations, is a cult name among natural-wine drinkers.
appellations.terroir: High clay-limestone plateaus and slopes, cooler than Saint-Émilion.
appellations.nerd_note: When the Japanese manga *Les Gouttes de Dieu* (Kami no Shizuku) featured Château Le Puy's 2003 vintage, the estate's stock sold out almost overnight.

appellations.name: Sainte-Foy Côtes de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon
appellations.summary: Sainte-Foy Côtes de Bordeaux is the newest member of the Côtes family, added in 2016, covering the same zone as Sainte-Foy-Bordeaux at the eastern edge of the Gironde. Growers can choose either name.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes on the left bank of the Dordogne bordering Bergerac.
appellations.nerd_note: It is the only Côtes appellation on the left bank of the Dordogne.

appellations.name: Côtes de Bordeaux-Saint-Macaire
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: A small appellation for dry, medium-sweet and sweet white wines from ten communes around the medieval town of Saint-Macaire, on the right bank of the Garonne upstream of Sainte-Croix-du-Mont. Production is tiny and mostly local.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and gravel slopes above the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint-Macaire is one of the best-preserved medieval towns of the Gironde, a former river port whose ramparts and arcaded square date from its trading heyday on the Garonne.

appellations.name: Blaye
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary: Blaye AOC is a stricter red appellation for the Blayais, with lower yields, higher planting density and longer ageing than Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux. It is used by a minority of ambitious estates for their top cuvées.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills around the citadel of Blaye.
appellations.nerd_note: Blaye AOC demands denser planting and lower yields than Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, so only a handful of estates claim it, usually for their top cuvée.

appellations.name: Côtes de Blaye
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle, Colombard
appellations.summary: Côtes de Blaye is now a white-only appellation for dry wines from the Blayais, often with Colombard alongside Sauvignon and Sémillon, a legacy of the Cognac-grape plantings on the northern edge of Bordeaux.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and sandy soils north of the citadel.
appellations.nerd_note: Blaye is one of the few places in Bordeaux where Colombard, a Cognac grape, is still a traditional component of white wine.

appellations.name: Côtes de Bourg
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec
appellations.summary: Côtes de Bourg covers the steep, hilly country around the old port of Bourg, just upstream of where the Dordogne and Garonne meet. Vines here predate the Médoc, and the Romans planted these slopes. Reds dominate, Merlot with a notable share of Malbec, and they are dark, firm and great value. François Mitjavile of Tertre Rôteboeuf makes Roc de Cambes here, a wine that showed what the appellation can do; Château Falfas is biodynamic, and Fougas, Brulesécaille and Martinat are reliable.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills and steep slopes facing the Gironde, with gravel patches near the water and limestone caves under Bourg.
appellations.nerd_note: Roc de Cambes, a natural amphitheatre of vines facing the Gironde, was bought in 1988 by François Mitjavile of Tertre Rôteboeuf, and its success showed that Bourg could make wine of classed-growth depth.

appellations.name: Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Carmenère, plus small shares of Marselan, Touriga Nacional, Castets, Arinarnoa; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle, Colombard, Ugni Blanc, Alvarinho, Liliorila
appellations.summary:
Bordeaux AOC is the regional appellation that can be used anywhere in the Gironde's delimited vineyard, and it is where the region's crisis has been most visible. In good times it supplied supermarket claret, rosé and dry white to the world; when demand for red Bordeaux collapsed after 2018, prices for bulk Bordeaux fell below production costs and much of the land pulled up in 2023 to 2026 was regional AOC vineyard.

The appellation still makes excellent everyday wine. Juicy Merlot-based reds, crisp Sauvignon whites and a growing amount of rosé come from estates and cooperatives across the Entre-Deux-Mers, Blaye and the Libournais. Many top châteaux sell white wines as Bordeaux because their communal AOCs are red-only (Pavillon Blanc de Château Margaux, Aile d'Argent from Mouton). Bordeaux Clairet, a deep pink wine with a short maceration, keeps alive the colour of the medieval claret that England once drank.

In January 2021, after a vote by the growers in 2019, the INAO approved six climate-adaptation varieties for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur: the reds Arinarnoa, Castets, Marselan and Touriga Nacional and the whites Alvarinho and Liliorila, limited to 5% of a property's vineyard and 10% of a blend.
appellations.terroir: Any of the region's soils, though most regional AOC wine comes from the clay-limestone and sandy-gravel soils of the Entre-Deux-Mers and the outer Libournais.
appellations.nerd_note: Castets is a near-extinct Gironde red variety rediscovered in the 2000s; its inclusion among the 2019 climate varieties is a rare case of an old local grape returning through climate policy.

appellations.name: Bordeaux Haut-Benauge
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Bordeaux Haut-Benauge is a seldom-used name, attached to AOC Bordeaux, for white wines from the Haut-Benauge, a hilly area in the south of the Entre-Deux-Mers around the castle of Benauge. The wines, dry to medium-sweet, must come from Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle; most growers in the zone prefer to sell under the better-known Entre-deux-Mers-Haut-Benauge name for dry wine.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills, among the highest in the Entre-Deux-Mers.
appellations.nerd_note: The medieval Château de Benauge, a stronghold of the counts of Benauge, still stands over the vineyards that give the appellation its name.

appellations.name: Bordeaux Supérieur
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Carmenère
appellations.summary: Bordeaux Supérieur covers the same area as Bordeaux with stricter rules: lower yields, higher minimum alcohol, denser plantings, and red wines aged until at least the June after the harvest. It is the home of many serious family estates outside the famous districts, such as Château Reignac, Château Penin and Château de Parenchère, and its best wines outperform many cheaper communal labels. Whites under the name must be medium-sweet; Y d'Yquem is sold as Bordeaux (dry white), not Supérieur.
appellations.terroir: Mostly clay-limestone and gravel of the Entre-Deux-Mers and the outer Libournais.
appellations.nerd_note: Bordeaux Supérieur was briefly the home of 'Bordeaux garage' wines in the 2000s, when ambitious growers made tiny, extracted cuvées that challenged the hierarchy.

appellations.name: Crémant de Bordeaux
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle, Ugni Blanc, Colombard, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Crémant de Bordeaux is traditional-method sparkling wine, made white or rosé with at least nine months on the lees. It grew from a nineteenth-century tradition of Bordeaux sparkling wine centred on Bourg and the Entre-Deux-Mers, and has become one of the few growth categories in the region as growers look for alternatives to red. The rosés, often Merlot and Cabernet Franc, are especially popular.
appellations.terroir: Grapes come from across the Gironde, mostly cool clay-limestone sites in the Entre-Deux-Mers and Blaye that keep acidity.
appellations.nerd_note: Bordeaux had its own sparkling wine houses before the First World War, and Crémant production has grown sharply since 2020 as growers redirect vineyards away from unsold red.

appellations.name: Champagne
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Meunier, Chardonnay (plus tiny amounts of Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, and the trial hybrid Voltis)
appellations.summary:
Champagne is the only French wine region where a single appellation covers everything: 34,200 ha in 319 villages, from the Montagne de Reims to the Aube, all producing wine sold under one name. The legal area was delimited in 1908, extended to the Aube in 1927, and defined as an AOC in 1936. The rules govern every step: hand harvesting of whole bunches (machine harvesting is banned), pressing in fractions (the first 2,050 litres from 4,000 kg are the *cuvée*, the next 500 the *taille*), a maximum yield set each year, second fermentation in the bottle in which the wine is sold, and minimum cellar ageing of 15 months for non-vintage (12 on the lees) and three years for vintage wines.

What you taste comes from that process: the tension between Champagne's cold-climate acidity and the creamy, toasty, brioche notes of yeast autolysis during long lees ageing. Blending across villages, grapes and years (most non-vintage Champagne includes 20 to 50% reserve wine) gives each house its consistent style: Krug's richness, Bollinger's Pinot-driven power, Taittinger's Chardonnay elegance, Pol Roger's balance.

Economics shape everything. Grapes sell for some of the highest prices in the wine world, over 7 euros per kilo in recent years, and land in grand cru villages can exceed 1.5 million euros per hectare. Sales dipped to about 266 million bottles in 2025, 152 million of them exported, and stocks are high, so producers cut the 2026 yield to 8,800 kg/ha. Meanwhile the grower movement, led by Anselme Selosse from the 1980s and later by a generation of small producers bottling single villages and parcels, has shifted attention from house blends to terroir.

The appellation area debate, opened in 2003 to adjust the boundary and add about 40 villages, was formally dropped by the growers' union in October 2026, leaving the 319 communes unchanged.
appellations.terroir: Mostly Belemnite and Micraster chalk in the Marne, Kimmeridgian marl in the Aube, with clay, sand and marl in the Marne valley. Cool continental-oceanic climate, average about 11°C, with spring frost and hail risk.
appellations.nerd_note: The pressure inside a Champagne bottle, about 6 atmospheres, is roughly three times that of a car tyre; a cork can leave the bottle at over 40 km/h.

appellations.name: Coteaux Champenois
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Meunier, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Coteaux Champenois is the appellation for still wines from the Champagne zone: red, white and rosé. It is rare (often under 0.1% of production) because it uses grapes that could become Champagne, which sells for far more. But it holds history: before bubbles took over, Champagne was known for still red and pale wines, and villages such as Bouzy, Aÿ, Ambonnay and Cumières still make pale, perfumed Pinot Noir. Warmer vintages since 2015 have led growers such as Egly-Ouriet, Bérêche, Bollinger (La Côte aux Enfants in Aÿ) and Paul Bara to make serious, Burgundy-like reds. Village names are often added to the label, such as Bouzy Rouge.
appellations.terroir: Same chalk and marl as Champagne; the warmest south-facing slopes are used for red.
appellations.nerd_note: Still Champagne was served at Louis XIV's court, and Bouzy Rouge was a fashionable wine in nineteenth-century Paris.

appellations.name: Rosé des Riceys
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: One of the rarest appellations in France: a still, dark rosé made only in the commune of Les Riceys in the Aube, from Pinot Noir. The grapes are macerated in open vats, and the winemaker tastes constantly to stop the maceration when the 'goût des Riceys', a flavour of hazelnut, red fruit and spice, appears. Only a few tens of thousands of bottles are made, and only in good years. Legend says Louis XIV drank it when he visited the area.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone on south-facing slopes in Les Riceys.
appellations.nerd_note: Les Riceys is the only commune in France with three AOCs: Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys.

appellations.name: Languedoc
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault, Lledoner Pelut; Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne, Vermentino, Bourboulenc, Clairette, Picpoul, Viognier
appellations.summary:
AOC Languedoc is the regional appellation that replaced the old Coteaux du Languedoc. Approved by the INAO in 2006 and applied from 2007, it covers the whole Languedoc and Roussillon, from Nîmes to the Spanish border, so any AOC wine in the region can be declassified into it. Reds must blend at least two of the main grapes (Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre), and many are excellent value.

Beneath it sit 'dénominations géographiques complémentaires' that can follow the Languedoc name. Some are well known: Grès de Montpellier (the terraces around Montpellier), older village names such as Saint-Georges-d'Orques, Saint-Christol, Saint-Drézéry and La Méjanelle, Pézenas (volcanic and schist hills around the town of Molière), Sommières (near the Gard), Cabrières (schist and limestone near Clermont-l'Hérault, on its way to its own AOC), Saint-Saturnin (Larzac foothills), and Quatourze (gravel near Narbonne). Montpeyroux, long one of them, became an AOC in its own right in 2026.

The appellation can feel like a catch-all, but it gives estates a recognisable name and lets the best terroirs climb toward cru status.
appellations.terroir: Every soil of the Mediterranean arc: limestone garrigue, schist, galets roulés, villafranchian terraces, basalt and marl; altitude from sea level to 400 m.
producers: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
appellations.nerd_note: Molière toured the Languedoc with his troupe from the 1640s and staged plays at Pézenas, whose growers now use his name on their wines.

appellations.name: Pic Saint-Loup
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Carignan
appellations.summary: Pic Saint-Loup takes its name from the 658-m limestone peak that rises north of Montpellier like a shark's fin. Its vineyards, in 17 communes around Saint-Martin-de-Londres, Valflaunès and Lauret, are the coolest and wettest in the Languedoc, with cold nights from the Cévennes. That made it the first area of the region to specialise in Syrah, which gives fresh, peppery, violet-scented reds with Grenache and Mourvèdre. It was recognised as an AOC in its own right in 2017, starting with the 2016 vintage, and registered as an EU PDO in July 2023, after decades as a named area of Coteaux du Languedoc. Domaine de l'Hortus (Jean Orliac), Château de Cazeneuve, Clos Marie, Mas Bruguière and Ermitage du Pic Saint-Loup are references.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic and Cretaceous limestone, marl and scree in a combe between the Pic Saint-Loup and the Montagne de l'Hortus; altitude 150 to 300 m; one of the wettest parts of the Languedoc.
appellations.nerd_note: Legend says three brothers, Loup, Guiral and Clair, fell in love with the same woman; when she died, each retreated to a peak to live as a hermit, and the highest peak took Loup's name.

appellations.name: Terrasses du Larzac
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault
appellations.summary: Terrasses du Larzac covers 32 communes on the foothills of the Larzac plateau north-west of Montpellier, around Aniane, Saint-Jean-de-Fos, Jonquières and Saint-Saturnin. Its great asset is the big difference between day and night temperatures (often 20°C), because cold air flows down from the plateau. The reds are fresh, dark and mineral. AOC since 2014, it is home to the Languedoc's most famous estates: Mas de Daumas Gassac, Grange des Pères and Mas Jullien, as well as Domaine de Montcalmès and Clos du Serres.
appellations.terroir: Very varied: limestone scree, red ruffe (iron-rich sandstone and clay, especially near the Lac du Salagou), schist, basalt and glacial deposits; altitudes up to 400 m.
producers: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
appellations.nerd_note: Mas de Daumas Gassac and Grange des Pères, the two most famous estates in the area, sell their wines as IGP, outside the appellation, because their grape blends do not fit the rules.

appellations.name: Montpeyroux
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault
appellations.summary: Montpeyroux, in the foothills of the Larzac, became the Languedoc's newest communal AOC in 2026 after nearly 30 years of campaigning. The INAO's national committee approved its specification in June 2025, and the appellation replaces the former 'Languedoc Montpeyroux' name. It covers Montpeyroux and three neighbouring communes (Arboras, Lagamas and Saint-Jean-de-Fos), about 500 ha, and is red only. The campaign was led by 35 producers, 16 of them independent estates, and began with a first INAO visit in 1996. Domaine d'Aupilhac (Sylvain Fadat), Domaine Alain Chabanon and the Castelbarry cooperative are references. The village's name comes from 'Mont Pierreux', stony mountain.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree, marl and the blue marl of the Larzac foothills; altitudes of 150 to 400 m with cool nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Sylvain Fadat of Aupilhac plants old Carignan and Cinsault on north-facing terraces at Les Cocalières, a high, cool amphitheatre of volcanic and limestone soils.

appellations.name: La Clape
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan; Bourboulenc, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne, Vermentino
appellations.summary: La Clape is a limestone massif between Narbonne and the sea that was an island in Roman times, before silt from the Aude joined it to the mainland. Its vineyards sit in hollows among garrigue and pines, with the sea on two sides. The cru is famous for whites based on Bourboulenc (here called Malvoisie), which keep a saline freshness despite the heat. Reds are Syrah and Mourvèdre-rich. AOC since 2015. Château Pech Redon, Château de la Négly, Château Rouquette-sur-Mer and Gérard Bertrand's Château l'Hospitalet are references.
appellations.terroir: Limestone massif with marl and clay; sea influence, wind and very little rain.
appellations.nerd_note: La Clape is one of the few Languedoc crus where white wine has equal standing with red.

appellations.name: Corbières
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut, Cinsault; Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Macabeu, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
appellations.summary: Corbières is the largest appellation of the Languedoc, roughly 10,000 ha in the wild hills of the Aude south of Narbonne and east of Carcassonne. It is a country of Cathar castles (Quéribus, Peyrepertuse), garrigue and scattered villages, and its wines, mostly red and often led by Carignan, range from rustic to impressive. Eleven terroir zones have been identified, from the coastal Fontfroide and Sigean to the high Hautes-Corbières. The best estates include Château de Lastours, Domaine de Villemajou (Gérard Bertrand), Maxime Magnon, Domaine Ledogar and Château La Voulte-Gasparets, whose Cuvée Romain Pauc helped make the area's name.
appellations.terroir: Very varied: limestone, schist, marl, sandstone and gravel; maritime near the coast, mountain climate inland.
appellations.nerd_note: The Cathar castles that dominate the Corbières sheltered heretics during the Albigensian Crusade (1209 to 1229); Quéribus, the last to fall, surrendered in 1255.

appellations.name: Corbières-Boutenac
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah
appellations.summary: Corbières-Boutenac is the first cru of Corbières, created in 2005, covering ten communes around Boutenac in the north-east. Its rules give old Carignan a leading role in the blend, a deliberate statement that this once-despised grape can make great wine. The reds are deep and long-lived.
appellations.terroir: Sandstone, clay-limestone and gravel on a natural basin around the Pinada hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Boutenac was the first part of Corbières promoted to its own appellation, a model for the cru tier the Languedoc has built since.

appellations.name: Minervois
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Lledoner Pelut, Cinsault; Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Macabeu, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
appellations.summary: Minervois lies on the southern slopes of the Montagne Noire, between Narbonne and Carcassonne, in an amphitheatre facing south toward the Canal du Midi and the Aude. It takes its name from Minerve, a cliff-top village where 140 Cathars were burned in 1210. The reds, Syrah and Grenache-led, are smoother and more fragrant than Corbières. The area is divided into several zones, from the cool, high Petit Causse to the warm, lower Canal du Midi area. In June 2025 the INAO opened consultation on Cazelles, a proposed new named area (DGC).
appellations.terroir: Limestone, schist, sandstone and marl, on terraces descending from the Montagne Noire (up to 400 m) to the Aude valley.
appellations.nerd_note: The village of Minerve, on a rocky spur between two gorges, was besieged by Simon de Montfort in 1210; 140 Cathars who refused to recant were burned.

appellations.name: Minervois-la-Livinière
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan
appellations.summary: Minervois-La Livinière was the Languedoc's first communal cru, recognised in 1999, covering six communes around La Livinière on the limestone Petit Causse. Its reds are deep, structured and age well. Clos Centeilles, Château Sainte Eulalie, Château Maris and Domaine Combe Blanche are leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on the south-facing slopes of the Petit Causse, at 150 to 300 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Patricia Boyer-Domergue of Clos Centeilles planted and saved old varieties such as Piquepoul Noir, Riveyrenc and Œillade.

appellations.name: Fitou
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut
appellations.summary: Fitou was the first Languedoc red AOC, in 1948, ahead of the region's revival. It has two separate parts: a coastal zone around Fitou, Leucate and Treilles on limestone near the Étang de Leucate, and an inland mountain zone around Tuchan, Paziols and Villeneuve-les-Corbières on schist. Reds are dark, spicy and sturdy. The Mont Tauch cooperative in Tuchan is the largest producer.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone near the coast; schist and limestone in the mountain zone.
appellations.nerd_note: Fitou's two zones are separated by part of the Corbières appellation, so the appellation is cut in two.

appellations.name: Faugères
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Lledoner Pelut, Cinsault; Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
appellations.summary: Faugères, north of Béziers in the foothills of the Cévennes, is entirely on schist, the same rock as Banyuls and Priorat. Its reds are smooth and fragrant, with dark fruit, garrigue and a mineral, slightly smoky edge. It was among the first Languedoc AOCs (1982 for reds and rosés). Domaine Léon Barral, Domaine Alquier, Château des Estanilles and Mas d'Alezon are leading estates. The village's old windmills overlook the vineyards.
appellations.terroir: Devonian and Carboniferous schist, hard and fractured, on hills at 200 to 400 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Faugères whites became AOC only in 2005; before that the area was red and rosé only.

appellations.name: Saint-Chinian
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault, Lledoner Pelut; Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
appellations.summary: Saint-Chinian, north-west of Béziers, is divided by the Vernazobre river: schist in the north and limestone and clay in the south. The northern schist gives fine, fragrant reds; the southern limestone gives more powerful, structured wines. Two villages on the schist, Berlou and Roquebrun, have their own crus (since 2005), and the Roquebrun cooperative is among the best in France. Borie La Vitarèle, Canet-Valette, Mas Champart and Domaine des Jougla are references.
appellations.terroir: Schist in the north (Berlou, Roquebrun), clay-limestone and marl in the south, on hills facing the Mediterranean.
appellations.nerd_note: Roquebrun, on the Orb, is so warm that it is called 'the little Nice of the Hérault' and has a Mediterranean garden of cacti and citrus.

appellations.name: Limoux
appellations.grapes: Mauzac, Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc, Pinot Noir; Merlot, Malbec, Cabernet, Syrah, Grenache for red
appellations.summary:
Limoux, in the upper Aude valley south of Carcassonne, is cool for the south of France: influenced by both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, at 200 to 500 m. It makes three sparkling wines. Blanquette de Limoux, mostly Mauzac, is made by the traditional method; Blanquette Méthode Ancestrale is pure Mauzac, fermented once in the bottle without added sugar or yeast, and low in alcohol; and Crémant de Limoux, more Chardonnay and Chenin. Limoux also makes barrel-fermented still Chardonnay (Limoux blanc, with a famous charity auction, Toques et Clochers) and reds.

Limoux claims to have made the world's first sparkling wine. A document from 1531 records the monks of the abbey of Saint-Hilaire buying flasks of 'blanquette', and local legend says they discovered that wine bottled before fermentation finished would sparkle. The claim predates Dom Pérignon by over a century, but the 1531 document does not prove the wine was sparkling; it is a beloved local story rather than established fact.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone, sandstone and gravel in four zones: Autan, Méditerranéen, Océanique and Haute Vallée, with altitudes up to 500 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Blanquette means 'little white one', from the white down on the underside of Mauzac leaves.

appellations.name: Crémant de Limoux
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc, Mauzac, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Crémant de Limoux, created in 1990, is the traditional-method sparkling wine of Limoux, with Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc dominant, Mauzac in a minor role, and Pinot Noir for rosé. It has more finesse and less of Mauzac's green-apple tang than Blanquette, and is a well-priced alternative to Champagne.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone at altitude, cooler than the Mediterranean plain.
appellations.nerd_note: The Sieur d'Arques cooperative is by far the largest producer, alongside family houses such as Antech, whose ancestors made Blanquette in the nineteenth century.

appellations.name: Picpoul de Pinet
appellations.grapes: Piquepoul Blanc
appellations.summary: Picpoul de Pinet is the Languedoc's oyster wine: a crisp, lemony, saline white made only from Piquepoul Blanc, grown around Pinet on the shores of the Étang de Thau, where Bouzigues oysters are farmed. The grape's name means 'lip stinger' for its acidity. It became a separate AOC in 2013 (registered in the EU from 2017) after decades as a named area of Coteaux du Languedoc. It is one of the region's great commercial success stories, with distinctive embossed 'Neptune' bottles. Cooperatives at Pomérols and Pinet make most of it, alongside estates like Château de Pinet and Domaine Félines Jourdan.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, clay and sand near the Étang de Thau, with sea breezes.
appellations.nerd_note: The Thau lagoon produces about 10% of France's oysters, and Picpoul growers and oyster farmers jointly market 'the perfect pairing'.

appellations.name: Clairette du Languedoc
appellations.grapes: Clairette Blanche
appellations.summary: One of the oldest Languedoc AOCs (1948), pure Clairette from the area around Adissan and Aspiran in the Hérault valley. It is made dry, sweet, or as a 'rancio' aged oxidatively, and as a vin de liqueur. Production is small.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and red ruffe soils in the Hérault valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Clairette du Languedoc was France's first white AOC in the Languedoc, granted in 1948.

appellations.name: Cabardès
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Grenache, Syrah, Fer Servadou
appellations.summary: Cabardès, north of Carcassonne, is unique in France: it is the meeting point of the Atlantic and Mediterranean climates, and its rules require a blend of Bordeaux grapes (at least 40% of Merlot, Cabernets, Malbec) and Mediterranean grapes (at least 40% of Grenache, Syrah). The wines are fresh and balanced. Château de Pennautier, owned by the Lorgeril family since 1620, is the reference.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, schist and gravel on the southern slopes of the Montagne Noire.
appellations.nerd_note: Cabardès's blending rule, half Atlantic and half Mediterranean grapes, makes it the only French AOC that requires both families.

appellations.name: Malepère
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Lledoner Pelut, Syrah
appellations.summary: Malepère, south-west of Carcassonne, is the most Atlantic-influenced Languedoc appellation, and Merlot leads its blends, with Cabernet Franc and Malbec alongside Grenache and Syrah. Its wines are close to Bordeaux in style, with soft tannins and fresh fruit. It was promoted from VDQS to AOC in 2007.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and sandstone hills around the Malepère massif.
appellations.nerd_note: Malepère has the highest proportion of Bordeaux grapes of any Languedoc AOC.

appellations.name: Muscat de Frontignan
match: Muscat de Frontignan / Frontignan / Vin de Frontignan
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains (Blanc and Rouge)
appellations.summary: Muscat de Frontignan, from the coast between Sète and Montpellier, is one of France's oldest and most famous sweet wines; Voltaire and Thomas Jefferson ordered it, and it was one of the first AOCs (1936). It is a vin doux naturel: fermentation of Muscat à Petits Grains is stopped by adding grape spirit, keeping at least 110 g/l of sugar. The result is golden and aromatic, with apricot, orange blossom and honey. The cooperative makes most of it, and its twisted bottle is famous. There is also a vin de liqueur version.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay with pebbles, between the Étang de Thau and the sea, near the Gardiole massif.
appellations.nerd_note: Muscat à Petits Grains is often called Muscat de Frontignan in other countries, including Australia, after this town.

appellations.name: Muscat de Lunel
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains
appellations.summary: A small VDN appellation around Lunel, east of Montpellier, on terraces of galets roulés. Its Muscats are rich and aromatic. In 2025 the INAO launched a revised specification adding controlled irrigation and environmental rules.
appellations.terroir: Villafranchian terraces of pebbles and red clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Lunel's Jewish community was famous in the Middle Ages for its rabbinical school; the town's wine trade goes back to the same era.

appellations.name: Muscat de Mireval
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains
appellations.summary: A small VDN appellation next to Frontignan, on the slopes of the Gardiole massif facing the Étang de Vic. Its Muscat à Petits Grains gives aromatic, honeyed wines with at least 110 g/l of sugar. Rabelais, who studied medicine in Montpellier, is said to have enjoyed its wine.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree and red clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Mireval and Frontignan share the slopes of the Gardiole massif, but Mireval's vines face the Étang de Vic on red clay and limestone scree.

appellations.name: Muscat de Saint-Jean-de-Minervois
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains
appellations.summary: The highest and freshest of the Languedoc Muscats, from a limestone plateau at about 250 m in the north of the Minervois. Late harvest gives lighter, more delicate VDN with good acidity. Domaine de Barroubio is the reference.
appellations.terroir: Limestone causse, cool for the region.
appellations.nerd_note: It is harvested later than other Languedoc Muscats, sometimes in October.

appellations.name: Clairette de Bellegarde
appellations.grapes: Clairette Blanche
appellations.summary: Clairette de Bellegarde is a tiny white-wine appellation for pure Clairette from the commune of Bellegarde, in the Gard between Nîmes and the Camargue, on the edge of the Costières de Nîmes. The wines are soft, floral and low in acidity, best drunk young. It is one of the oldest appellations of the eastern Languedoc and today one of France's smallest by volume, kept alive by a handful of growers.
appellations.terroir: Terraces of rounded pebbles (galets roulés) and red clay, left by the ancient Rhône and Durance.
appellations.nerd_note: Clairette is one of the oldest grapes of the French Midi; in Bellegarde it has survived as a single-variety appellation while most of the region moved to blends.

appellations.name: Côtes du Roussillon
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut; Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
appellations.summary: The regional dry-wine appellation of Roussillon, covering most of the Pyrénées-Orientales. Reds blend Grenache, Carignan, Syrah and Mourvèdre; the whites, from Grenache Blanc and Gris and Macabeu, have improved greatly. The best dry wines of the region are often sold under it or as IGP Côtes Catalanes.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial terraces, schist, granite, limestone; dry, windy, sunny.
appellations.nerd_note: The Côtes Catalanes IGP is used by many top Roussillon growers for wines that do not fit AOC rules, such as single-variety Carignan or Grenache Gris.

appellations.name: Côtes du Roussillon Villages
match: Côtes du Roussillon Villages Les Aspres
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut
appellations.summary: Côtes du Roussillon Villages is red only, from the northern half of the department, mainly the Agly valley. Five villages may add their names: Caramany (granite and gneiss), Latour-de-France (schist), Lesquerde (granite), Tautavel (limestone, near the famous prehistoric cave) and Les Aspres (clay-limestone terraces south of the Têt, the only one outside the Agly). The wines are dense, spicy and powerful, from old Grenache and Carignan, often on very low yields.
appellations.terroir: Agly valley schist, granite and limestone; Les Aspres clay-silt terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: Tautavel is famous for 'Tautavel Man', fossils about 450,000 years old found in the Caune de l'Arago cave, some of the oldest human remains in Europe.

appellations.name: Collioure
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Carignan; Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Vermentino
appellations.summary: Collioure covers the same steep terraced schist slopes as Banyuls, between the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean near the Spanish border, but for dry wines. Its reds, built on Grenache with Mourvèdre and Syrah, are dense, spicy and mineral; its whites (AOC since 2002) are rich and saline. The harbour town of Collioure, painted by Matisse and Derain in 1905 when they invented Fauvism, is the centre. Domaine de la Rectorie, Domaine du Mas Blanc, Coume del Mas and Domaine Vial-Magnères are references.
appellations.terroir: Steep terraces of Cambrian schist, held up by dry-stone walls and drained by 'peu de gall' (rooster's foot) channels.
appellations.nerd_note: The Collioure and Banyuls terraces are held up by thousands of kilometres of dry-stone walls; the 'peu de gall' channels, shaped like a rooster's foot, stop storms from washing the soil into the sea.

appellations.name: Banyuls
appellations.grapes: Grenache Noir (at least 50%), Grenache Gris, Grenache Blanc, Carignan, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Muscat
appellations.summary:
Banyuls is France's great fortified red, made on the steep schist terraces of four communes (Banyuls-sur-Mer, Collioure, Port-Vendres and Cerbère) where the Pyrenees fall into the Mediterranean. It is a vin doux naturel: the fermentation of very ripe Grenache is stopped by adding neutral grape spirit (mutage), which keeps natural sugar and lifts alcohol to about 16%. Banyuls winemakers often add the spirit *sur grains*, onto the skins, and macerate for weeks, which extracts colour and tannin, much like Port.

What happens next defines the style. In the *oxidative* tradition, the wine ages for years in old barrels or in glass demijohns called *bonbonnes* left outdoors in the sun, where it oxidises, concentrates and develops a nutty, maderised character: flavours of walnut, coffee, prune, cocoa and dried fig, and the prized *rancio* note. Some houses age wine in large barrels for decades, refreshing old wine with younger, like a solera. In the *reductive* tradition, called *rimage* (Catalan for 'vintage'), the wine is bottled young to keep its fresh red and black fruit, and it is closer to a vintage Port. There are also white and rosé Banyuls, and *hors d'âge* wines aged at least five years.

The Cellier des Templiers cooperative makes most Banyuls and keeps a huge collection of old barrels; Domaine de la Rectorie, Domaine du Mas Blanc (whose founder, Dr André Parcé, led the campaign for the appellation) and Coume del Mas are leading estates. Banyuls is one of the few wines that can match chocolate.
appellations.terroir: Steep terraces of Cambrian schist with very thin soil, often under a few centimetres of topsoil, facing the sea; tiny yields (often under 20 hl/ha); extreme wind and drought.
appellations.nerd_note: Arnau de Vilanova, a physician at Montpellier in the 1280s, described adding spirit to fermenting grape must to stop fermentation; tradition holds that the King of Majorca granted him a patent for it in 1299.

appellations.name: Banyuls grand cru
appellations.grapes: Grenache Noir (at least 75%)
appellations.summary: Banyuls Grand Cru is the top tier of Banyuls, with at least 75% Grenache Noir, a maceration of at least five days on the skins, and at least 30 months of ageing in oak before release. The wines are deep, complex and oxidative, with notes of dried fruit, walnut, coffee and rancio, and they last for decades.
appellations.terroir: The same schist terraces as Banyuls; the best old-vine plots.
appellations.nerd_note: Grand Cru Banyuls is one of the very few French appellations that requires a specific period of oak ageing.

appellations.name: Maury
appellations.grapes: Grenache Noir, Grenache Gris, Grenache Blanc, Macabeu, Muscat; Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre for Maury Sec
appellations.summary: Maury, in the upper Agly valley in the north of Roussillon, sits on a band of black schist between the limestone ridges of the Corbières and the Fenouillèdes, beneath the Cathar castle of Quéribus. It makes Grenache-based vins doux naturels in both oxidative and reductive (grenat, vintage) styles. Its old *hors d'âge* wines, aged in barrels and bonbonnes left in the sun, are among the great oxidative wines of the world. Since 2011, Maury Sec has been a separate category for dry reds, recognising the area's success with old-vine Grenache, Carignan and Syrah. Mas Amiel, founded in 1816, with its famous field of glass bonbonnes, and the Vignerons de Maury are the main producers.
appellations.terroir: Black schist (Albian marl) in a valley sheltered by limestone ridges; very dry and windy.
appellations.nerd_note: According to the estate's story, Raymond Amiel won Mas Amiel from the Bishop of Perpignan in a game of cards in 1816.

appellations.name: Rivesaltes
appellations.grapes: Grenache Noir, Grenache Gris, Grenache Blanc, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Muscat
appellations.summary:
Rivesaltes is the largest VDN appellation, covering much of Roussillon and a few communes of the Aude. Its wines are made by mutage: neutral grape spirit is added to fermenting Grenache, Macabeu or Malvoisie once part of the sugar has turned to alcohol, which keeps natural sweetness and brings the wine to 15 to 18% alcohol. There are four styles. *Grenat* is a young red, bottled after a short reductive ageing to keep its black-cherry fruit. *Tuilé* is red aged oxidatively for years until it turns the colour of old roof tiles. *Ambré* is white aged oxidatively until it turns amber, with notes of orange peel, apricot and toasted almond. *Rosé* is the newest, fresh and fruity.

The oxidative wines are where Rivesaltes becomes extraordinary. Many estates leave young wine in glass bonbonnes in the sun for a year, then age it in large old casks for decades, sometimes topping up old wine with younger wine like a solera. *Hors d'âge* wines must be at least five years old, and *rancio* is a mention for wines that have developed the nutty, maderised, curry-and-walnut character that comes with long oxidation. Sales have fallen sharply since the 1980s, when Rivesaltes was a mass-market aperitif, which means that old vintages are surprisingly affordable. Domaine Cazes, Domaine Sarda-Malet and Domaine des Chênes keep old wines.
appellations.terroir: Schist, limestone, granite and alluvial terraces of the Agly, Têt and Tech valleys.
appellations.nerd_note: Rivesaltes made Marshal Joffre, born in the town in 1852, its most famous son; his statue stands in the main square.

appellations.name: Muscat de Rivesaltes
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains, Muscat of Alexandria
appellations.summary: Muscat de Rivesaltes is a VDN made from Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria across most of Roussillon. It is bottled young to keep its aromas of citrus, mint, peach and flowers, and drunk chilled. 'Muscat de Noël' is released before Christmas.
appellations.terroir: Schist, granite, limestone and alluvial terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: Muscat de Rivesaltes covers more ground than any other French Muscat appellation, overlapping with most of Roussillon's other zones.

appellations.name: Grand Roussillon
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Muscat
appellations.summary: An old regional VDN appellation covering the whole of Roussillon, with the same grapes and mutage rules as Rivesaltes. It is almost never used today, since producers prefer Rivesaltes, Maury or Banyuls. Wines labelled 'rancio' can be found under the name in old stocks.
appellations.terroir: All of Roussillon.
appellations.nerd_note: Grand Roussillon is one of France's most obscure AOCs, with production in some years close to zero.

appellations.name: Muscadet
appellations.grapes: Melon de Bourgogne
appellations.summary: Regional Muscadet covers the whole Nantais area and is the lightest, simplest version of the wine: dry, crisp, saline white for the seafood platters of the Atlantic coast. Most volume is sold under the more precise sub-regional names, especially Sèvre et Maine.
appellations.terroir: Mixed Armorican rocks; flatter, more fertile land than the sub-regions.
appellations.nerd_note: The grape's name, Melon de Bourgogne, recalls its Burgundian origin; it is a natural cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc, sibling of Chardonnay and Aligoté.

appellations.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
appellations.grapes: Melon de Bourgogne
appellations.summary:
Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, named after the two rivers that cross it south-east of Nantes, produces the large majority of Muscadet and almost all the best. The traditional *sur lie* style means the wine stays on its fine lees through the winter in underground glass-lined tanks and is bottled directly off them, often with a light prickle of carbon dioxide; the lees add texture, a breadlike note and freshness.

The story of the last fifteen years is the crus communaux, sub-zones defined by bedrock with minimum lees ageing of 18 months or more (24 months or more for some) and lower yields. Clisson (granite), Gorges (gabbro and quartzite) and Le Pallet (gneiss and gabbro) were recognised in 2011; Château-Thébaud, Goulaine, Monnières-Saint-Fiacre and Mouzillon-Tillières followed in 2019. In August 2025 the INAO opened public consultation on three more (Champtoceaux, La Haye-Fouassière and Vallet), which were still awaiting final approval in 2026. The cru wines show a depth, smoky minerality and ageing potential (10 to 20 years) that few people expect from Muscadet. Producers such as Domaine de l'Écu, Jo Landron, Domaine de la Pépière, Luneau-Papin, Jérémie Huchet and Michel Brégeon proved the point.
appellations.terroir: Rolling plateau cut by the Sèvre and Maine rivers. Each cru maps to a rock: granite at Clisson and Château-Thébaud, gabbro at Gorges and Mouzillon-Tillières, gneiss at Le Pallet and Monnières-Saint-Fiacre, and schist and gneiss at Goulaine.
appellations.nerd_note: Muscadet sur lie must spend the winter on its lees and cannot be bottled before 1 March after the harvest; the cru wines spend far longer on lees, which is why they are usually released two or more years after the vintage.

appellations.name: Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire
appellations.grapes: Melon de Bourgogne
appellations.summary: The smallest and least known of the Muscadet appellations, on schist and granite slopes along both banks of the Loire upstream of Nantes, around Ancenis and Champtoceaux. The wines are firmer and more mineral than Sèvre et Maine, with a hint of the Anjou schist.
appellations.terroir: Steep schist and granite slopes overlooking the river, with good drainage.
appellations.nerd_note: Champtoceaux, proposed as a cru communal in 2025, would be the first cru outside Sèvre et Maine.

appellations.name: Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu
appellations.grapes: Melon de Bourgogne
appellations.summary: Created in 1994, this appellation surrounds the Lac de Grand-Lieu south-west of Nantes, one of France's largest natural lakes in winter. Sandy and granitic soils give soft, aromatic Muscadet, best drunk young.
appellations.terroir: Granite, schist and sandy soils; the lake moderates temperatures.
appellations.nerd_note: The Lac de Grand-Lieu's water level varies hugely between seasons, and the lake is a major bird reserve.

appellations.name: Gros Plant du Pays nantais
appellations.grapes: Folle Blanche
appellations.summary: Gros Plant is the local name for Folle Blanche, a Cognac grape, and its wine is famously lean and tart. It was a VDQS until it became AOC in 2011. With sur lie ageing, the best examples are bracing, saline and perfect with oysters.
appellations.terroir: Same soils as Muscadet; the grape is prone to rot, so it is planted on the driest sites.
appellations.nerd_note: Folle Blanche was the main Cognac grape before phylloxera; in Nantes it survives as a wine grape.

appellations.name: Coteaux d'Ancenis
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon; Pinot Gris (Malvoisie)
appellations.summary: A small appellation around Ancenis on the Loire, between the Pays Nantais and Anjou, specialising in light Gamay reds and rosés, with some Cabernet. Its curiosity is the sweetish Coteaux d'Ancenis Malvoisie, made from Pinot Gris. It was promoted from VDQS to AOC in 2011.
appellations.terroir: Schist and granite slopes on both banks.
appellations.nerd_note: Malvoisie here means Pinot Gris, a reminder of how many unrelated grapes have borne that name across Europe.

appellations.name: Fiefs Vendéens
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Négrette; Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Grolleau Gris
appellations.summary: Fiefs Vendéens covers five scattered zones in the Vendée department south of Nantes (Brem, Mareuil, Pissotte, Vix and Chantonnay). Its fresh rosés, light reds and whites are mostly drunk by the summer crowds on the Atlantic beaches. Domaine Saint-Nicolas at Brem, biodynamic, is the reference producer.
appellations.terroir: Schist and clay near the coast; limestone further inland.
appellations.nerd_note: Cardinal Richelieu began his career as bishop of Luçon in the Vendée, and local tradition says he favoured the wines of Mareuil.

appellations.name: Anjou
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc; Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Gamay, Pineau d'Aunis, Grolleau
appellations.summary: Anjou is the regional appellation for the department of Maine-et-Loire and neighbouring parts of Deux-Sèvres and Vienne. Anjou Blanc, made from Chenin, is the star: a group of growers on the dark schists since the 1990s (Richard Leroy, Mark Angeli, Thibaud Boudignon, Patrick Baudouin, Stéphane Bernaudeau) has made some of the world's most sought-after dry Chenin under this humble name. Anjou Rouge and Anjou Gamay are juicy and light; Anjou Mousseux is sparkling.
appellations.terroir: The 'Anjou Noir' schist and volcanic rock to the west, the 'Anjou Blanc' tuffeau to the east.
producers: Mark Angeli (La Ferme de la Sansonnière)
appellations.nerd_note: Several of the best Anjou Blancs are labelled as Vin de France because their makers refused to follow appellation rules, so the most famous Anjou is sometimes not legally Anjou.

appellations.name: Anjou Villages
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: A red-only appellation for the best Cabernet sites in 46 communes of Anjou, created in 1987. The wines are deeper and more structured than Anjou Rouge, and Cabernet Sauvignon ripens unusually well on the warm schist.
appellations.terroir: Schist and volcanic soils in the Layon and Aubance valleys.
appellations.nerd_note: Anjou is one of the few places in the Loire where Cabernet Sauvignon can ripen fully, thanks to dark, heat-retaining schist.

appellations.name: Anjou Villages Brissac
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: A red appellation for ten communes around Brissac-Quincé, between the Aubance and the Loire. Firm, dark Cabernet with a mineral finish; Domaine de Montgilet and Domaine de Bablut are leading names. The Château de Brissac, the tallest château in France at seven storeys, presides.
appellations.terroir: Schist and sandstone, with some limestone at the border with the Saumurois.
appellations.nerd_note: Brissac sits right on the boundary between the dark schists of the Armorican Massif and the pale limestone of the Paris Basin.

appellations.name: Anjou-Coteaux de la Loire
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: A small appellation for sweet Chenin from slopes along the Loire west of Angers, around Montjean and Ingrandes. The wines are lighter and more mineral than the Layon.
appellations.terroir: Schist and limestone slopes above the river.
appellations.nerd_note: Its limestone patches, rare in Anjou Noir, once supplied lime kilns along the river.

appellations.name: Savennières
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary:
