Savennières is a tiny appellation on the north bank of the Loire just west of Angers, and the most uncompromising dry Chenin Blanc on earth. Its south-facing slopes on volcanic rock and schist give wines of searing acidity and intense minerality, notes of quince, chamomile, beeswax and wet stone, and a reputation for being closed for years after release; the best need a decade or more and last half a century.

Three names share it: Savennières itself and two Grand Cru enclaves with their own appellations, La Roche aux Moines and La Coulée de Serrant. In the nineteenth century the sweet and dry wines of Savennières were among the most valuable in France. Today the style is mostly dry, sometimes demi-sec in warm years. Domaine des Baumard, Domaine du Closel (Évelyne de Pontbriand), Damien Laureau, Eric Morgat and Thibaud Boudignon are leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Steep south-facing slopes over violet schist, sandstone and volcanic rhyolite, with thin soil and little water. The river reflects heat and keeps frost away.
appellations.nerd_note: Chenin in Savennières often shows a slightly bitter, phenolic grip because growers tolerate some botrytis and skin contact; that grip is part of why the wines need time.

appellations.name: Savennières Roche aux Moines
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: La Roche aux Moines, 'the monks' rock', is a set of south-facing slopes east of the Coulée de Serrant, once owned by the monks of Saint-Nicolas in Angers. In 1214 the French Prince Louis defeated King John of England here, in a battle that led to the loss of Anjou by the Plantagenets. The wines are powerful, dense dry Chenin; Domaine aux Moines (Tessa Laroche) and Pierre Soulez's Château de Chamboureau are the references. A 2011 decree gave it its own appellation status, with stricter yields.
appellations.terroir: Schist and volcanic rock on steep slopes facing the river.
appellations.nerd_note: The 1214 Battle of La Roche-aux-Moines was fought the same summer as Bouvines; together they ended England's hold on Anjou.

appellations.name: Savennières Coulée de Serrant
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: One of the few French appellations owned by a single estate: 7 ha of steep slope over a small valley running down to the Loire, planted by Cistercian monks in 1130. Nicolas Joly's family bought it in 1962; he converted to biodynamics in 1981 and became the most famous evangelist of biodynamic winemaking in the world. The wine, harvested in several tries with some botrytis, is rich and powerful, notoriously variable, and capable of decades of ageing.
appellations.terroir: Schist and volcanic rhyolite with very thin soils on a steep, south-facing ravine.
producers: Nicolas Joly (Clos de la Coulée de Serrant)
appellations.nerd_note: Joly writes that the vines are cultivated by horse and that the estate's purpose is to let the vineyard express itself; he founded the group La Renaissance des Appellations in 2001.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Layon
match: Coteaux du Layon Premier Cru Chaume
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary:
The Layon is a small river that runs north-west into the Loire south of Angers, cutting a valley of steep schist slopes, and its sweet Chenin Blanc is one of France's great dessert wines. Morning fogs from the river encourage botrytis; growers pick by successive tries, sometimes into November, to make wines from moelleux to luscious liquoreux, with Chenin's high acidity balancing the sugar. They taste of quince, apricot, honey and acacia, and the best age for decades.

Six villages may add their names (Beaulieu-sur-Layon, Faye-d'Anjou, Rablay-sur-Layon, Rochefort-sur-Loire, Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné, Saint-Lambert-du-Lattay), and Chaume, on the slopes above Rochefort, has the right to 'Premier Cru'. The appellation peaked in fame in the nineteenth century; since the 1990s growers such as Jo Pithon, Patrick Baudouin, Domaine des Forges and Château Pierre-Bise have revived it, with a debate between rich, sugar-laden styles and lighter, fresher wines.
appellations.terroir: Schist, sandstone, carboniferous coal measures (around Saint-Aubin and Chaudefonds) and volcanic rocks, on steep south-facing slopes. The river's mists and the slopes' heat suit botrytis.
appellations.nerd_note: Coal was mined near Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné until the twentieth century, and growers say the coal-bearing schist gives a smoky note to the wines.

appellations.name: Quarts de Chaume
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Quarts de Chaume is a tiny amphitheatre of south-facing slopes above the Layon at Rochefort-sur-Loire, and since 2011 it has been the first and only Loire appellation with 'Grand Cru' in its name. The name comes from the medieval lord's right to a quarter of the harvest from the best plots. The rules ban chaptalisation and require hand harvesting and must of at least 298 g/l of sugar, giving some of the most concentrated sweet Chenins anywhere. Château Pierre-Bise, Domaine des Baumard, Château de Bellerive and Domaine de la Bergerie are references.
appellations.terroir: South-facing schist slopes in a sheltered bowl near the river, warm and well exposed, where botrytis develops reliably.
appellations.nerd_note: In 2011 the INAO also banned cryoextraction (freezing grapes to concentrate sugar) for Quarts de Chaume, after a long dispute with a producer who used it.

appellations.name: Bonnezeaux
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Bonnezeaux is a small appellation on three steep schist hillsides above the Layon in the commune of Thouarcé, and with Quarts de Chaume it is the best sweet-wine site of the Layon. The wines are rich, honeyed and long-lived. Château de Fesles, Domaine de Petit Val and Mark Angeli (La Ferme de la Sansonnière) are names to know.
appellations.terroir: South-facing schist hillsides with quartz, warm and dry.
appellations.nerd_note: Mark Angeli's Bonnezeaux, made without chaptalisation and with long ageing, helped inspire the natural wine scene in Anjou.

appellations.name: Coteaux de l'Aubance
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: The Aubance is the next river north of the Layon, and its slopes make lighter, fresher sweet Chenin. 'Sélection de Grains Nobles' may appear on wines from richer musts. Domaine de Montgilet and Domaine de Bablut are reliable.
appellations.terroir: Schist slopes, cooler and less exposed than the Layon.
appellations.nerd_note: Aubance wines are often more mineral and less overtly sweet than the Layon's, which makes them good food wines.

appellations.name: Rosé d'Anjou
appellations.grapes: Grolleau, Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Côt, Pineau d'Aunis
appellations.summary: Rosé d'Anjou is a medium-sweet rosé, mostly from Grolleau, and one of the best-selling appellation wines in France. Light, fruity and slightly sweet, it is a supermarket staple. Its reputation is modest, but well-made examples are refreshing and cheap.
appellations.terroir: Across Anjou, mostly on schist.
appellations.nerd_note: Grolleau, its main grape, is named for the 'grolle', a local word for crow, because of its dark berries.

appellations.name: Cabernet d'Anjou
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Cabernet d'Anjou is a medium-sweet rosé made from the two Cabernets, richer and fuller than Rosé d'Anjou, and one of the biggest-selling wines of the Loire. Good examples age surprisingly well; old Cabernet d'Anjou can develop notes of dried fruit and tea.
appellations.terroir: Anjou schist and tuffeau.
appellations.nerd_note: Many Anjou rosés are made by direct pressing and stopping fermentation by chilling, which keeps the natural sweetness.

appellations.name: Rosé de Loire
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Gamay, Grolleau, Pineau d'Aunis, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Rosé de Loire is a dry rosé appellation covering Anjou, Saumur and Touraine. Created in 1974 to give the region a dry alternative to the off-dry Rosé d'Anjou, it is crisp and light.
appellations.terroir: The Anjou, Saumur and Touraine areas.
appellations.nerd_note: Rosé de Loire must contain at least 30% Cabernet, a rule designed to give it more structure than Grolleau alone.

appellations.name: Saumur
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc; Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pineau d'Aunis
appellations.summary:
Saumur, on the tuffeau cliffs of the south bank of the Loire, makes red, white and especially sparkling wine. It is the Loire's sparkling-wine capital: Jean Ackerman founded the first house in 1811 after working in Champagne, and Bouvet-Ladubay, Gratien & Meyer, Langlois-Chateau and Veuve Amiot followed, ageing their bottles in kilometres of tuffeau galleries. Saumur Brut is mostly Chenin Blanc, often with Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.

The still whites, pure Chenin, have become some of the Loire's best since Clos Rougeard, Domaine Guiberteau, Arnaud Lambert and Romain Guiberteau's Brézé hill showed what the tuffeau can do. Saumur Rouge is fresh Cabernet Franc. Saumur Puy-Notre-Dame, a named sub-zone in the south recognised in 2009, makes reds with stricter rules (Cabernet Franc with at most 15% Cabernet Sauvignon and lower yields).
appellations.terroir: Turonian tuffeau chalk covered by clay, sand and flint. The tuffeau stores water and regulates temperature, and the slopes facing the Loire and the Thouet are the best sites.
appellations.nerd_note: The hill of Brézé produced one of the most famous white wines of eighteenth-century France, said to be sold at the price of Montrachet; growers today are trying to reclaim that status.

appellations.name: Saumur-Champigny
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pineau d'Aunis
appellations.summary: Saumur-Champigny is red-only, from nine communes east of Saumur, and in the 1980s it was the fashionable Paris bistro wine: juicy, fragrant Cabernet Franc with red fruit and violet, served lightly chilled. Its serious side came from the Foucault brothers of Clos Rougeard in Chacé, whose old-vine, barrel-aged Le Bourg and Les Poyeux became among the most sought-after wines of France. Domaine Filliatreau, Château du Hureau, Domaine des Roches Neuves (Thierry Germain) and Château de Villeneuve continue the line.
appellations.terroir: Tuffeau chalk with clay and sand on top; the 'Champigny' name may come from Latin *campus igni*, 'field of fire', for its warm slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos Rougeard's Charly and Nady Foucault refused to use new technology for decades; after Charly's death in 2015 the estate was sold to Martin Bouygues in 2017.

appellations.name: Coteaux de Saumur
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: A tiny appellation for sweet Chenin from the Saumur tuffeau, picked overripe or with botrytis. Rare and charming, it shows the lighter, chalkier side of sweet Loire Chenin.
appellations.terroir: Tuffeau slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: In the nineteenth century, sweet Saumur was more famous than the sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Cabernet de Saumur
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: A small appellation for dry or off-dry rosé from Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon grown on the Saumur tuffeau. It is drier and lighter than Cabernet d'Anjou. Volumes are small and the wine is rarely seen outside the region.
appellations.terroir: Tuffeau.
appellations.nerd_note: Cabernet de Saumur is drier and lighter than Cabernet d'Anjou.

appellations.name: Haut-Poitou
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay; Cabernet Franc, Gamay, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A small appellation north of Poitiers, best known for crisp Sauvignon Blanc from the cooperative of Neuville-de-Poitou, which made the name in the 1980s. It became AOC in 2011.
appellations.terroir: Limestone plateau with clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Haut-Poitou lies on the plateau north of Poitiers, about 70 km south of the Loire itself, on the road toward Cognac country.

appellations.name: Chinon
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc (Breton), up to 10% Cabernet Sauvignon; Chenin Blanc for white
appellations.summary:
Chinon is the Loire's most famous red-wine appellation, a band of vineyards along the Vienne river around the medieval town where Joan of Arc met the future Charles VII in 1429. Rabelais, born nearby, praised its wines, calling it 'Chinon, little town, great fame'. The grape is Cabernet Franc, locally called Breton, and Chinon shows its full range: light, crunchy reds from the sandy and gravel terraces by the river for drinking cool in their first years, and deep, structured, long-lived wines from the clay-limestone slopes and tuffeau hillsides.

Charles Joguet in Sazilly began bottling single-site Chinons in the 1960s and 1970s, notably Clos de la Dioterie, and Bernard Baudry, Olga Raffault, Philippe Alliet and Couly-Dutheil (Clos de l'Écho, once Rabelais's family vineyard) are references. A little white Chenin and rosé are also made. Good Chinon tastes of raspberry, violet, graphite and pencil lead, with fine tannins, and the best reach 20 years or more.
appellations.terroir: Three terroirs: sand and gravel terraces by the Vienne; clay and flint on the plateau; tuffeau slopes (*coteaux*) with clay-limestone topsoil. The best sites face south above the Vienne in Cravant-les-Coteaux, Sazilly and Chinon itself.
appellations.nerd_note: Couly-Dutheil's Clos de l'Écho was said to have belonged to the family of François Rabelais, who grew up at La Devinière just south of Chinon.

appellations.name: Bourgueil
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, up to 10% Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Bourgueil faces Chinon across the Loire on the north bank, and its Cabernet Franc is a touch firmer and more tannic, especially from the tuffeau slopes. The Benedictine abbey founded at Bourgueil in 990 is traditionally credited with bringing Cabernet Franc (Breton) to the area. Pierre-Jacques Druet, Domaine de la Butte (Jacky Blot), Catherine and Pierre Breton and Yannick Amirault are leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces by the Loire give lighter wines; clay-limestone and tuffeau on the slopes give structure.
appellations.nerd_note: The local name Breton for Cabernet Franc may come from Abbot Baudry of Bourgueil, who is said to have brought it from Brittany via the Nantes trade, but the evidence is thin.

appellations.name: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, up to 10% Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil is a single commune west of Bourgueil with its own appellation. Its vines sit mostly on sand and gravel, giving lighter, more fragrant, earlier-drinking Cabernet Franc than Bourgueil, though the slopes at the north make serious wines. Yannick Amirault and Frédéric Mabileau are leading names.
appellations.terroir: Mostly sand and gravel terraces; tuffeau slopes in the north.
appellations.nerd_note: Because most of its vines grow on sand and gravel, Saint-Nicolas is often the first Loire red ready to drink, best served cool within a few years of release.

appellations.name: Vouvray
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc (a little Orbois/Menu Pineau tolerated)
appellations.summary:
Vouvray is Chenin Blanc's spiritual home, on the tuffeau cliffs on the north bank of the Loire just east of Tours. Its range is unmatched: sparkling (mousseux and pétillant, more than half the production), dry (sec), off-dry (tendre, demi-sec), and in hot, botrytis-rich years sweet (moelleux, liquoreux). The style is chosen each year based on the vintage, which makes Vouvray hard to market and endlessly fascinating.

The great Vouvrays age for a century: honey, quince, chamomile, and a mineral, chalky backbone held together by Chenin's acidity. The plateau above the cliffs is covered in clay and flint (*perruches*) and clay-limestone (*aubuis*). Domaine Huet, with its Le Haut-Lieu, Clos du Bourg and Le Mont vineyards, is the reference; Gaston Huet, mayor of Vouvray and former prisoner of war, ran it from 1947 and converted to biodynamics with his son-in-law Noël Pinguet in the 1990s. Philippe Foreau's Clos Naudin, Domaine des Aubuisières, Vincent Carême and François Pinon are other leaders. The cellars in the tuffeau cliffs along the river road hold bottles from the nineteenth century.
appellations.terroir: Tuffeau cliffs and slopes, with clay-flint (perruches) and clay-limestone (aubuis) on the plateau; the best sites are on the edges of the plateau above the Loire and the small Brenne and Cisse valleys.
producers: Domaine de la Taille aux Loups
appellations.nerd_note: Huet's Le Haut-Lieu was the first vineyard bought by Victor Huet in 1928, and Gaston Huet's 1947 moelleux is one of the legendary sweet wines of France.

appellations.name: Montlouis-sur-Loire
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Montlouis faces Vouvray across the Loire on the south bank, between the Loire and the Cher. It makes the same Chenin styles (dry, sweet and sparkling), and was long considered Vouvray's little brother. Since the 2000s a group of growers led by Jacky Blot (Domaine de la Taille aux Loups) and François Chidaine has made it a source of some of the Loire's finest dry Chenin, often more precise and mineral than Vouvray. Montlouis growers also launched 'Pétillant Originel', a méthode ancestrale sparkling wine bottled before fermentation ends.
appellations.terroir: Clay-flint and sand over tuffeau on a plateau between the two rivers; slightly sandier and earlier-ripening than Vouvray.
producers: Domaine de la Taille aux Loups
appellations.nerd_note: Montlouis was historically sold as Vouvray until a 1938 ruling gave it its own appellation.

appellations.name: Touraine
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Orbois; Gamay, Côt, Cabernet Franc, Pineau d'Aunis, Grolleau
appellations.summary: Touraine is the regional appellation of the Tours area, and its volume is mostly crisp, affordable Sauvignon Blanc from the Cher valley, plus Gamay, Côt (Malbec) and Cabernet Franc reds. It has five named sub-areas: Amboise and Mesland (Chenin, Gamay, Côt), Azay-le-Rideau (Chenin and Grolleau rosé), Chenonceaux (Sauvignon and Côt-based reds, created 2011) and Oisly (Sauvignon Blanc, created 2011). The Cher valley, with its flint and clay soils, is also home to natural wine pioneers such as Thierry Puzelat and Noëlla Morantin.
appellations.terroir: Clay-flint, sandy clay and tuffeau around the Cher and the Loire.
appellations.nerd_note: Henry Marionnet grows ungrafted vines of Romorantin dating from before phylloxera, as well as ungrafted Gamay planted in 1992 to see how wines tasted before grafting.

appellations.name: Touraine Noble Joué
appellations.grapes: Pinot Meunier, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A rare vin gris (very pale rosé) from five communes south of Tours, from Pinot Meunier, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir. Popular at the court of Louis XI in the fifteenth century, it nearly vanished in the twentieth century as Tours expanded and was revived by a few growers and recognised in 2001.
appellations.terroir: Clay-flint and sand south of Tours.
appellations.nerd_note: Its mix of Meunier, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir echoes the grapes of Champagne, but it is made as a still, very pale vin gris.

appellations.name: Jasnières
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Jasnières is a single south-facing slope of tuffeau about 4 km long above the Loir river (the Loire's tributary, without the 'e'), north of Tours. Its dry and occasionally sweet Chenin is lean, piercing and mineral. Domaine de Bellivière (Éric and Christine Nicolas) and Pascal Janvier put it back on the map in the 1990s.
appellations.terroir: South-facing tuffeau slope with clay-flint on top; a cool, northern site.
appellations.nerd_note: The Loir valley's growers dig cellars and homes into the tuffeau cliffs, and some still live in troglodyte houses.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Loir
appellations.grapes: Pineau d'Aunis, Cabernet Franc, Gamay, Côt; Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Coteaux du Loir is the area around Jasnières on the Loir. It is the heartland of Pineau d'Aunis, a pale, peppery red grape that gives light, spicy reds and rosés. Domaine de Bellivière and Le Briseau make good examples.
appellations.terroir: Tuffeau and clay-flint slopes along the Loir.
appellations.nerd_note: Pineau d'Aunis takes its name from the priory of Aunis near Saumur, and tradition says Henry III of England drank its wine; despite the name it is unrelated to Pinot.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Vendômois
appellations.grapes: Pineau d'Aunis, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Cabernet Franc; Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Further up the Loir around Vendôme, this small appellation is known for its vin gris made from Pineau d'Aunis, one of the few appellations where that grape must dominate.
appellations.terroir: Tuffeau and clay-flint slopes along the Loir.
appellations.nerd_note: The Vendômois vin gris is made essentially from Pineau d'Aunis, pressed quickly to give a pale, peppery rosé.

appellations.name: Cheverny
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Orbois, Chenin Blanc; Pinot Noir, Gamay, Côt, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: Cheverny, in the Sologne south of Blois, makes blended wines: whites from Sauvignon with Chardonnay or Orbois, reds from Pinot Noir with Gamay. The blending rules make it unusual in the Loire. The château of Cheverny inspired Hergé's Marlinspike Hall in the Tintin books.
appellations.terroir: Sand and clay over limestone in the Sologne.
appellations.nerd_note: Cheverny is one of the few Loire appellations where blending is compulsory: reds combine Pinot Noir with Gamay, and whites combine Sauvignon Blanc with Chardonnay or Orbois.

appellations.name: Cour-Cheverny
appellations.grapes: Romorantin
appellations.summary: Cour-Cheverny is one of France's rarest appellations and the only one for Romorantin, a white grape that King François I is said to have brought from Burgundy to the town of Romorantin in 1519. The wines are dry or off-dry, with high acidity, notes of honey, beeswax and citrus, and can age decades. Philippe Tessier, François Cazin and Hervé Villemade make it.
appellations.terroir: Sand and clay with flint in the Sologne.
appellations.nerd_note: DNA work shows Romorantin is one of the offspring of Pinot and Gouais Blanc, which makes it a full sibling of Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Valençay
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Orbois; Gamay, Pinot Noir, Côt, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: Valençay, south of Cheverny near the château Talleyrand owned, makes fresh Sauvignon whites and light blended reds. It is also the name of a pyramid-shaped goat cheese coated in ash, whose flat top is said to have been cut off at Talleyrand's table to avoid reminding Napoleon of Egypt.
appellations.terroir: Clay-flint and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Talleyrand, who owned Château de Valençay, used it to host diplomatic feasts prepared by the chef Antonin Carême.

appellations.name: Orléans
appellations.grapes: Pinot Meunier, Pinot Noir; Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A small appellation around Orléans, with pale rosé and reds from Pinot Meunier (here called Gris Meunier) and Pinot Noir, and whites from Chardonnay (Auvernat). It was among the great vineyards of France in the Middle Ages.
appellations.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces on the Loire.
appellations.nerd_note: Orléans vinegar, a famous slow-fermented wine vinegar, comes from the city's wine trade.

appellations.name: Orléans-Cléry
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: A tiny red-only appellation of Cabernet Franc from five communes around Cléry-Saint-André, south-west of Orléans. The gravel terraces give light, crunchy reds. It survives thanks to a handful of growers on the edge of the Orléans suburbs.
appellations.terroir: Sandy-gravel terraces of the Loire.
appellations.nerd_note: Louis XI, who loved Cléry, was buried in the basilica there in 1483.

appellations.name: Sancerre
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc; Pinot Noir for red and rosé
appellations.summary:
Sancerre is the world's reference for Sauvignon Blanc: a hilltop town above the Loire, surrounded by 14 communes of steep chalky hills that make a crisp, minerally white with notes of citrus, gooseberry, cut grass and flint. It became France's most popular bistro white in the 1960s and 1970s. About 80% of the production is white; the rest is Pinot Noir red and rosé, which has improved greatly since the 1990s.

Three soils define it. The *terres blanches*, Kimmeridgian marl with fossil oysters, as in Chablis, on the western hills (Chavignol, Bué, Verdigny), give the fullest, longest-lived wines. The *caillottes*, small stones of Oxfordian limestone, give aromatic, early-drinking wines. And *silex*, flint on clay near the town and the Loire, gives smoky, tight wines. The Monts Damnés above Chavignol (a slope so steep it was 'damned' to work) is the most famous lieu-dit. Producers such as Vacheron, Cotat, Alphonse Mellot, Gérard Boulay, Henri Bourgeois, Lucien Crochet and Edmond Vatan made Sancerre a wine of place. Chavignol is also the home of the Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese, Sancerre's classic partner.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl (terres blanches), Oxfordian limestone (caillottes) and flint (silex), on steep hills rising to 400 m. A semi-continental climate, cooler and frostier than western Loire.
appellations.nerd_note: Sancerre was a Protestant stronghold that resisted a royal siege for eight months in 1572 and 1573; the town's inhabitants were reduced to eating leather and parchment.

appellations.name: Pouilly-Fumé
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
Pouilly-Fumé sits on the east bank of the Loire facing Sancerre, around the town of Pouilly-sur-Loire. The name 'Fumé', smoky, refers to the grey bloom on ripe Sauvignon berries or to the smoky, gunflint note of wines from the flint soils, depending on whom you ask. The wines are white only, Sauvignon Blanc, often a little rounder and spicier than Sancerre.

Didier Dagueneau (1956 to 2008), a former motorcycle racer known for his wild hair and uncompromising standards, changed Pouilly-Fumé by showing it could rival the world's great whites: he cut yields, used barrels and made single-terroir wines such as Silex and Pur Sang. His son Louis-Benjamin continues the work. Château du Nozet (Ladoucette), Château de Tracy and Jonathan Pabiot are other leaders.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl, Portlandian limestone and flint (silex) on clay, on gentle slopes above the Loire; Saint-Andelain's flint hill is the most famous site.
appellations.nerd_note: Alexandre Bain, a natural-wine producer whose Pouilly-Fumé was refused the appellation in the mid-2010s as atypical, now sells it as Vin de France; his case is often cited in debates about how appellations judge typicity.

appellations.name: Pouilly-sur-Loire
appellations.grapes: Chasselas, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: A survivor of the pre-phylloxera Loire: white wine from Chasselas, once the grape of the area, which supplied table grapes to Paris. Only a few hectares remain, with Domaine Serge Dagueneau et Filles among the last producers.
appellations.terroir: The same soils as Pouilly-Fumé.
appellations.nerd_note: Pouilly-sur-Loire is one of the last French appellations built on Chasselas, a grape that once covered the Pouilly hills.

appellations.name: Menetou-Salon
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc; Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Menetou-Salon is Sancerre's neighbour to the south-west, near Bourges, on the same Kimmeridgian marl. The Sauvignon whites and Pinot Noir reds are similar to Sancerre, often fresher and better value. Domaine Henry Pellé and Philippe Gilbert are the leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Jacques Cœur, the great merchant and treasurer of Charles VII, owned a château at Menetou-Salon in the fifteenth century.

appellations.name: Quincy
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris
appellations.summary: Quincy, on the Cher river west of Bourges, was one of the first French AOCs (1936). Its Sauvignon Blanc grows on sand and gravel terraces and is light, citrusy and floral.
appellations.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces over limestone on the left bank of the Cher.
appellations.nerd_note: Quincy was recognised as an AOC in 1936, one of the very first, along with Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Arbois.

appellations.name: Reuilly
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc; Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: Reuilly, on the Arnon river near Quincy, makes Sauvignon whites, Pinot Noir reds and a distinctive pale rosé or vin gris from Pinot Gris. Its Kimmeridgian and limestone slopes give wines close to Sancerre in style. Claude Lafond helped revive the area from near abandonment in the 1970s.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl, limestone and sand.
appellations.nerd_note: Reuilly is one of the few places in France that makes a rosé from Pinot Gris.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Giennois
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc; Pinot Noir, Gamay
appellations.summary: A small appellation north of Pouilly-Fumé, on both banks of the Loire around Gien and Cosne-sur-Loire. The Sauvignon is light and fresh; reds blend Pinot Noir and Gamay.
appellations.terroir: Flint and clay, limestone and sand.
appellations.nerd_note: Its red wines must blend Gamay and Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Châteaumeillant
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Châteaumeillant, south of Bourges near the geographical centre of France, is red and rosé only, from Gamay and Pinot Noir on volcanic and schist soils. Its vin gris is a local speciality. It became AOC in 2010.
appellations.terroir: Mica-schist, sandstone and volcanic rocks, unusual for the Centre-Loire.
appellations.nerd_note: Châteaumeillant was known as a wine town in Roman times; amphorae from Italy have been found in excavations of the Gallic oppidum here.

appellations.name: Côte Roannaise
appellations.grapes: Gamay (Gamay Saint-Romain)
appellations.summary: The Côte Roannaise lies on the east-facing granitic slopes of the Monts de la Madeleine above Roanne. Gamay here gives juicy, mineral reds, closer to the Beaujolais crus than to Touraine. Domaine Sérol and Domaine des Pothiers are leading the revival; the Troisgros family's famous restaurant in Roanne is a big supporter.
appellations.terroir: Granite and volcanic rocks on east-facing slopes at 400 to 550 m.
appellations.nerd_note: The local Gamay strain is often called Gamay Saint-Romain, after the village of Saint-Romain-la-Motte.

appellations.name: Côtes du Forez
appellations.grapes: Gamay
appellations.summary: The Côtes du Forez lie on the eastern slopes of the Monts du Forez, near Boën. The volcanic and granitic soils give fresh Gamay. The cooperative and Domaine Verdier-Logel are the main producers.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic basalt and granite on east-facing slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Côtes du Forez is among the furthest-upstream appellations on the Loire itself.

appellations.name: Saint-Pourçain
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir; Chardonnay, Tressallier, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Saint-Pourçain, on the Sioule and Allier rivers in the Allier department, claims to be one of the oldest vineyards in France. In the Middle Ages its wine was served at the court of Saint Louis and the papal court of Avignon. It became AOC in 2009. Whites must include the local Tressallier grape; reds blend Gamay and Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, sand and granite on terraces and slopes along the Sioule.
appellations.nerd_note: Tressallier, Saint-Pourçain's own white grape, turns out to be Sacy, an old Yonne variety.

appellations.name: Côtes d'Auvergne
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir; Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Côtes d'Auvergne covers scattered vineyards around Clermont-Ferrand on volcanic soils, with five village names (Boudes, Chanturgue, Châteaugay, Corent, Madargue). Gamay dominates; Corent is famous for rosé. Before phylloxera the Puy-de-Dôme had one of the largest vineyards in France.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic basalt, marl and limestone on the slopes of the Limagne plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Before phylloxera the Puy-de-Dôme was one of France's largest wine departments, with tens of thousands of hectares; today only a few hundred remain.

appellations.name: Crémant de Loire
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Grolleau, Orbois
appellations.summary: Crémant de Loire is the Loire's regional traditional-method sparkling wine, covering Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Cheverny, with at least 12 months on the lees. Chenin and Chardonnay dominate the whites; the rosés use Cabernet Franc and Pinot Noir. It is one of France's three largest crémants, with Alsace and Burgundy, and a growing alternative to Champagne.
appellations.terroir: Mostly the tuffeau of Saumur and Touraine; houses age it in tuffeau caves.
appellations.nerd_note: Saumur's houses can sell the same wine as Saumur Brut or Crémant de Loire; the difference lies in production rules such as whole-cluster pressing and minimum lees ageing.

appellations.name: Côtes de Provence
match: Côtes de Provence Notre-Dame des Anges
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Tibouren, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon; Vermentino (Rolle), Clairette, Sémillon, Ugni Blanc
appellations.summary:
Côtes de Provence is the largest appellation of Provence, about 20,300 ha across 84 communes of the Var, the Bouches-du-Rhône and a corner of the Alpes-Maritimes, and the engine of the pale-rosé boom. Around 90% of its production is rosé: dry, light salmon-pink, made by direct pressing or short maceration, mostly from Grenache and Cinsault with Syrah and the local Tibouren. The appellation also makes reds and whites, often from the same estates.

It is a huge and diverse area. Five 'dénominations de terroir' highlight distinct zones: Sainte-Victoire (2005, limestone at the foot of Cézanne's mountain, east of Aix), Fréjus (2005, volcanic red rhyolite near the coast, known for Tibouren rosé), La Londe (2008, schist near the sea in the Maures, with whites and rosés), Pierrefeu (2013, between the Maures and the limestone hills) and Notre-Dame des Anges (2019, the inland Maures foothills near Pignans).

The 1955 crus classés are a curiosity: 23 estates were classified while the area was a VDQS, and 18 still use the title, including Château Minuty, Château Sainte-Roseline, Clos Mireille (Domaines Ott), Château de Selle (Ott), Château Roubine and Clos Cibonne, a champion of Tibouren. The classification has never been revised. Rosé's economics are spectacular: a well-branded Provence rosé sells at two to three times the price of a red Côtes du Rhône, and investors including LVMH, Pernod Ricard and the Pitt-Jolie partnership (Miraval) have bought in.
appellations.terroir: Two Provences: limestone hills in the north and west (Sainte-Victoire, the Haut-Var) and crystalline schist, gneiss and volcanic rock in the south-east (Maures, Esterel), plus the inland Permian depression of red sandstone and clay. Mistral and sea breezes.
producers: Domaines Ott (Clos Mireille, Château de Selle)
appellations.nerd_note: Clos Cibonne, near Toulon, ages its Tibouren rosé under a thin veil of yeast in old casks, a traditional technique that gives it nutty, savoury depth unlike any other Provence rosé.

appellations.name: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Counoise, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carignan; Vermentino, Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Ugni Blanc
appellations.summary: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence is the western part of Provence, between the Durance and the Mediterranean around Aix. It is cooler and windier than the Var, swept by the mistral. Cabernet Sauvignon has a long history here: Georges Brunet planted it at Château Vignelaure in the 1960s, which inspired Domaine de Trévallon. Rosé dominates, but the reds and whites are serious. Château La Coste, Château Vignelaure and Château Revelette are references.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay hills with gravel and marl, from the Étang de Berre to the Durance.
appellations.nerd_note: Château La Coste mixes wine with contemporary architecture and art, with pavilions by Tadao Ando, Frank Gehry, Renzo Piano and Jean Nouvel among the vines.

appellations.name: Coteaux Varois en Provence
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon; Vermentino, Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Ugni Blanc, Sémillon
appellations.summary: Coteaux Varois en Provence is the cooler heart of the Var, around Brignoles and Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, at 350 to 500 m. Its rosés are fresher and more mineral than those of the coast. Château Miraval in Correns, a village that set out in the 1990s to become France's first fully organic commune, is the most famous estate, although most of Miraval's rosé is sold as Côtes de Provence. Domaine du Deffends and Château La Calisse are good names.
appellations.terroir: Limestone hills and plateaus of the Haut-Var, cooler at altitude.
appellations.nerd_note: Correns, where Miraval is located, is known as the first French village to convert nearly all its farmland to organic agriculture.

appellations.name: Bandol
appellations.grapes: Mourvèdre (at least 50% of reds), Grenache, Cinsault; Clairette, Ugni Blanc, Bourboulenc
appellations.summary:
Bandol is the great red wine of Provence, from a natural amphitheatre of terraced hills (restanques) above the fishing port of Bandol, between Marseille and Toulon. Its grape is Mourvèdre, which needs heat to ripen, and the sun-baked south-facing slopes, sheltered from the mistral, provide it. The rules require at least 50% Mourvèdre in the red (top wines often use 75 to 95%) and at least 18 months of ageing in wood before release. The wines are dark, structured and long-lived, with notes of black fruit, garrigue, liquorice, leather and game. Bandol rosé, also built on Mourvèdre, is one of the most serious rosés in France.

Bandol was a famous wine in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, exported through its port. After phylloxera it almost disappeared. Lucien Peyraud of Domaine Tempier, who married into the family in 1936, led the fight for the appellation (1941) and the return of Mourvèdre. Tempier, Château de Pibarnon, Château Pradeaux, Domaine de la Bégude and Château Vannières are among the leading estates.
appellations.terroir: Terraces (restanques) of limestone, marl and sandstone facing south toward the sea, sheltered by the Sainte-Baume massif; the sea moderates temperatures.
appellations.nerd_note: Lucien Peyraud is called the 'father of Bandol'; his friend Richard Olney, the American food writer, made Tempier famous in the United States through Kermit Lynch and Alice Waters.

appellations.name: Cassis
appellations.grapes: Marsanne, Clairette, Ugni Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Bourboulenc; Grenache, Cinsault, Mourvèdre
appellations.summary: Cassis, a small fishing town east of Marseille, was one of the first French AOCs (1936) and is one of the few in Provence known for white wine. Its vines grow on terraces between the sea and Cap Canaille, among the highest sea cliffs in Europe. The whites, from Marsanne and Clairette, are fresh and saline, the classic partner for bouillabaisse. Urban growth and land prices put constant pressure on its small vineyard of around 200 ha. Clos Sainte-Magdeleine, on a promontory above the sea, Domaine du Bagnol and Clos Val Bruyère are references.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl terraces between the sea and the Cap Canaille cliffs.
appellations.nerd_note: The Provençal poet Frédéric Mistral praised Cassis wine in his 1859 epic *Mirèio* as shining like a clear diamond and smelling of the rosemary, heather and myrtle of its hills.

appellations.name: Bellet
appellations.grapes: Vermentino (Rolle), Chardonnay; Braquet, Folle Noire, Grenache, Cinsault
appellations.summary: Bellet is a tiny appellation in the hills above Nice, one of the few vineyards inside a large French city. Only a few dozen hectares survive among the villas. It uses grapes found almost nowhere else in France: Braquet (Brachetto) and Folle Noire (Fuella) for reds and rosés, and Rolle (Vermentino) for whites. The whites are fresh and aromatic. Château de Bellet, Château de Crémat and Clos Saint-Vincent are the main producers.
appellations.terroir: Steep terraces of poudingue (conglomerate) and sand above the Var river, at 200 to 400 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Bellet's history reflects that Nice was part of the Kingdom of Sardinia until 1860, which explains its Italian grapes.

appellations.name: Palette
appellations.grapes: Mourvèdre, Grenache, Cinsault and many others; Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Ugni Blanc, Muscat and others
appellations.summary: Palette is one of the smallest AOCs in France, a few dozen hectares on north-facing limestone slopes on the outskirts of Aix-en-Provence, and it is largely the creation of a single estate, Château Simone. The Rougier family has owned Simone since 1830, and its old vines, a mix of dozens of varieties including some pre-phylloxera survivors, give red, white and rosé wines of unusual depth and longevity. Château Simone's white, mostly Clairette, ages in old barrels and develops honey, herbs and resin over decades. Château Crémade and Château Henri Bonnaud are the other producers.
appellations.terroir: North-facing slopes of limestone scree (calcaire de Langesse) and clay, cooler than the surroundings, near the Arc river.
appellations.nerd_note: Château Simone's cellars were dug by Carmelite monks in the sixteenth century, and some of its vines are among the oldest in Provence.

appellations.name: Les Baux de Provence
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carignan; Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Vermentino, Marsanne, Roussanne
appellations.summary: Les Baux-de-Provence is a small appellation around the limestone Alpilles hills and the medieval village of Les Baux. It is often called France's most organic appellation: most of its estates are organic or biodynamic, partly because the dry, mistral-swept climate makes it easy. The reds are spicy and herbal. Domaine de Trévallon, founded by Eloi Dürrbach in 1973, is the most famous estate, but it sells as IGP Alpilles because its blend of roughly equal Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah exceeds the Cabernet limit set when the AOC was created in 1995. Domaine Hauvette, Château Romanin and Mas de la Dame are references.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree and clay on the slopes of the Alpilles; windy, dry.
appellations.nerd_note: Domaine de Trévallon, Provence's most famous red, is not allowed to use the appellation because it has too much Cabernet Sauvignon.

appellations.name: Pierrevert
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Carignan; Grenache Blanc, Vermentino, Clairette, Roussanne, Marsanne
appellations.summary: Pierrevert is a small appellation in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, along the Durance near Manosque, at the cool northern edge of Provence, with vineyards up to 600 m. It is the only appellation in the department. Its wines, mostly rosé, are fresh and mineral.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and gravel terraces along the Durance, at altitude.
appellations.nerd_note: Pierrevert's altitude makes it one of the coolest Mediterranean appellations in France, close to the lavender fields of Valensole.

appellations.name: Patrimonio
appellations.grapes: Nielluccio (dominant in reds); Vermentinu (Vermentino) for white
appellations.summary: Patrimonio, at the base of Cap Corse near Saint-Florent, was Corsica's first AOC (1968) and is its most famous. It sits in an amphitheatre of limestone and schist facing the Gulf of Saint-Florent, and Nielluccio, Corsica's name for Sangiovese, gives firm, dark, spicy reds that age well. The Vermentinu whites are rich and saline. Antoine Arena (and his sons), Domaine Leccia, Yves Leccia, Domaine Gentile and Clos de Bernardi are leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone (unusual in Corsica), clay and schist in an amphitheatre facing the sea.
appellations.nerd_note: Patrimonio is the only part of Corsica with large limestone outcrops, which is why Nielluccio does particularly well there.

appellations.name: Ajaccio
appellations.grapes: Sciaccarellu (dominant), Barbarossa, Nielluccio, Vermentinu, Grenache
appellations.summary: Ajaccio, around Napoleon's birthplace on the west coast, is the home of Sciaccarellu, a pale, fragrant red grape that grows best on granite. Its name is usually explained as 'crunchy', for its firm berries, and the wines are light in colour but intense, with notes of red fruit, pepper and maquis. Comte Abbatucci, Clos Capitoro and Domaine de Vaccelli are references.
appellations.terroir: Granite hills around the Gulf of Ajaccio, up to 500 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Sciaccarellu has been identified as Mammolo, a Tuscan variety, but it has developed a distinct Corsican identity on granite.

appellations.name: Vin de Corse
match: Vin de Corse Coteaux du Cap Corse
appellations.grapes: Nielluccio, Sciaccarellu, Grenache, Carcajolu Neru, Minustellu, Aleatico; Vermentinu, Biancu Gentile, Codivarta, Genovese
appellations.summary: Vin de Corse, now often labelled simply Corse, is the island's regional AOP, and it has five named sub-areas. Calvi, in the north-west Balagne, makes elegant wines on granite (Clos Culombu, Domaine d'Alzipratu). Coteaux du Cap Corse, on the schist of the northern peninsula, makes mineral Vermentinu (Clos Nicrosi). Figari, the southernmost and windiest, uses granite and gives intense wines (Clos Canarelli, which revived the old Carcajolu Neru and Biancu Gentile grapes). Porto-Vecchio, on the south-east coast, has granitic soils and cooling sea breezes (Domaine de Torraccia). Sartène, in the south-west, is a land of granite and old family estates. Rosé is the largest category, and many estates make serious reds from Nielluccio and Sciaccarellu.
appellations.terroir: Granite in the west and south, schist in Cap Corse, alluvial plain in the east; altitude and sea breezes.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos Canarelli in Figari replanted Carcajolu Neru, a nearly forgotten Corsican grape that DNA work has matched to Parraleta, a variety of Aragon in Spain.

appellations.name: Muscat du Cap Corse
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains
appellations.summary: Muscat du Cap Corse is a vin doux naturel from the narrow, mountainous northern peninsula of Corsica, made from Muscat à Petits Grains, often slightly raisined on the vine. The mutage keeps it sweet and aromatic, with notes of apricot, orange and honey, and the island's schist gives freshness. It is one of the finest Muscats in France. Clos Nicrosi, Domaine Antoine Arena and Domaine Leccia make it.
appellations.terroir: Schist slopes on the Cap Corse peninsula and around Patrimonio.
appellations.nerd_note: It is the only Corsican vin doux naturel and one of the youngest VDN appellations in France.

appellations.name: Bergerac
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Fer Servadou, Mérille; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle, Ondenc, Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Bergerac is the regional appellation for the vineyards around the town of Bergerac on the Dordogne, east of Bordeaux. It uses Bordeaux grapes on similar soils, which long made it a cheaper Bordeaux substitute. Reds are Merlot-led and supple; Bergerac Sec whites are fresh Sauvignon and Sémillon; rosés are growing. A small number of growers showed that Bergerac can be much more: Luc de Conti at Château Tour des Gendres, Château de Tiregand in Pécharmant, and Claudie and Bruno Bilancini at Tirecul la Gravière.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes and molasse on both banks of the Dordogne, river gravels, and sandy terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: Bergerac's Protestant growers exported their wine to Holland after the 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes, and Dutch buyers favoured them over Bordeaux for a century.

appellations.name: Côtes de Bergerac
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Côtes de Bergerac is the stricter version of Bergerac, with lower yields and higher minimum ripeness. The reds are fuller and often oak-aged, and many of the area's best estates use it for their top cuvées. The whites must be medium-sweet (moelleux).
appellations.terroir: The same area as Bergerac; the best clay-limestone slopes are used.
appellations.nerd_note: Côtes de Bergerac Blanc must be moelleux, so a dry white from the same vines is sold as Bergerac Sec.

appellations.name: Monbazillac
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Monbazillac is the Southwest's answer to Sauternes: sweet white wine from botrytised grapes on the south bank of the Dordogne, facing Bergerac. The same autumn mists that rise from the river encourage noble rot, and the rules require hand harvesting in successive tries. The wines are rich, honeyed and often lighter and cheaper than Sauternes, with Muscadelle adding a floral note. Château Tirecul la Gravière, whose Cuvée Madame shows what great Monbazillac can be, and the cooperative that owns the sixteenth-century Château de Monbazillac are reference points. The appellation went through a crisis in the 1990s when some producers made wine from machine-harvested, chaptalised grapes; it has since banned machine harvesting.
appellations.terroir: North-facing clay-limestone slopes above the Dordogne, cool enough for slow ripening and humid enough for botrytis.
appellations.nerd_note: Monbazillac's vineyards face north, unlike most sweet-wine sites; the cooler exposure keeps acidity and helps mists linger.

appellations.name: Saussignac
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle, Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Saussignac is a tiny sweet-wine appellation west of Monbazillac with some of the strictest rules in France: hand picking by tries, no chaptalisation, and high minimum must weight. Growers such as Château Les Miaudoux, Château Richard and Château Le Payral make intense, botrytised wines that rival Sauternes.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes south of the Dordogne.
appellations.nerd_note: Rabelais mentions Saussignac in *Gargantua*, as one of the great sweet wines of his day.

appellations.name: Pécharmant
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec
appellations.summary: Pécharmant is the best red appellation of the Bergerac area, on the hills north-east of the town. Its name is said to come from 'pech charmant', the charming hill. A subsoil of iron-rich clay called *tran* gives firm, deep, long-lived reds. Château de Tiregand and Domaine du Haut-Pécharmant lead.
appellations.terroir: Sand and gravel over an iron-rich clay hardpan ('tran').
appellations.nerd_note: The 'tran' hardpan is so hard that it blocks roots, keeping yields low.

appellations.name: Montravel
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle; Merlot for red
appellations.summary: Montravel lies at the western end of the Bergerac area, next to Saint-Émilion's eastern neighbours. It makes dry whites (Sauvignon and Sémillon), and since 2001, Merlot-dominated reds. The philosopher Michel de Montaigne lived at his castle in Saint-Michel-de-Montaigne in the heart of the appellation, where his library tower survives.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes continuing those of Castillon.
appellations.nerd_note: Montaigne wrote his *Essais* in the tower of his château in Montravel.

appellations.name: Côtes de Montravel
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: A small appellation for medium-sweet (moelleux) white wines from the Montravel area at the western end of the Bergerac vineyard, made from Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle picked late. The wines are softer and lighter than Monbazillac, with honey and white-peach notes, and are mostly sold locally. Only a handful of growers still declare it.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: It is part of a trio with Montravel (dry) and Haut-Montravel (sweeter).

appellations.name: Haut-Montravel
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: The sweetest of the Montravel trio, from a few villages in the east of the area, made from overripe or botrytised Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle picked in successive passes. In good years it rivals Monbazillac, but production is tiny because most growers now prefer to make dry Montravel.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Very small production; most growers prefer to make dry Montravel.

appellations.name: Rosette
appellations.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: One of France's smallest appellations, on the hills just north of Bergerac next to Pécharmant, for semi-sweet (moelleux) whites with delicate, floral sweetness. It was a fashionable aperitif in the early twentieth century. Its sand and gravel soils give light, fragrant wines that are best drunk within a few years.
appellations.terroir: Sand and gravel over clay, similar to Pécharmant.
appellations.nerd_note: Rosette was nearly extinct by the 1990s; a handful of growers keep it alive.

appellations.name: Côtes de Duras
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle; Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec
appellations.summary: Côtes de Duras lies south of Bergerac, around the castle of Duras, with Bordeaux grapes and a particular strength in crisp Sauvignon Blanc. Many growers are organic, and Domaine Mouthes Le Bihan and Domaine de Laulan are good names.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and molasse hills between the Dropt and the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: The novelist Marguerite Duras took her pen name from this village, where her father owned a house.

appellations.name: Buzet
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
appellations.summary: Buzet, in the Lot-et-Garonne between the Garonne and the Landes forest, makes Bordeaux-style reds. The cooperative Vignerons de Buzet, founded in 1953, makes most of the wine and has its own cooperage, one of the first French cooperatives to do so.
appellations.terroir: Gravel terraces, clay-limestone hills and sand.
appellations.nerd_note: Buzet was called Côtes de Buzet until 1986.

appellations.name: Côtes du Marmandais
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Abouriou, Fer Servadou, Malbec, Syrah
appellations.summary: On both banks of the Garonne around Marmande, upstream of Bordeaux. What sets it apart is Abouriou, a local early-ripening red grape. Elian Da Ros, a former Zind-Humbrecht cellar hand, made the appellation known with his natural, Abouriou-based wines.
appellations.terroir: Gravel and clay-limestone along the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: Abouriou was grown for years in California under the name 'Early Burgundy' before DNA work identified it.

appellations.name: Brulhois
appellations.grapes: Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Fer Servadou
appellations.summary: A small area on both banks of the Garonne around Agen, known for its 'vin noir', a dark, tannic red from Tannat blended with Bordeaux grapes. Most wine comes from the Vignerons du Brulhois cooperative at Donzac. It was promoted from VDQS to AOC in 2011.
appellations.terroir: Gravel and clay terraces along the Garonne.
appellations.nerd_note: Brulhois markets its 'vin noir' as a tribute to the dark wines that the Haut-Pays sent to England in the Middle Ages.

appellations.name: Cahors
appellations.grapes: Malbec (Côt, Auxerrois) at least 70%, Merlot, Tannat
appellations.summary:
Cahors is the homeland of Malbec, here called Côt or Auxerrois. Its 'black wine' was famous in the Middle Ages: the grapes' dark colour, sometimes intensified by heating part of the must, gave wines so deep that they were used to colour paler Bordeaux. English merchants shipped it through Bordeaux, and the Russian Orthodox Church adopted it as communion wine. The vineyard almost disappeared after phylloxera and the February 1956 frost; replanted from the 1960s, Cahors became AOC in 1971.

Its rules require at least 70% Malbec, completed with Merlot and Tannat, and many top wines are pure Malbec. Two terroirs give two styles: the gravel and clay terraces along the Lot make supple, fruity wines; the limestone causse plateau, at about 300 m, gives tight, mineral, long-lived wines. The success of Argentine Malbec from the 1990s prompted Cahors to rebrand itself as the 'birthplace of Malbec', and a new generation, alongside established estates such as Château du Cèdre, Clos Triguedina and Château Lagrézette, has made fresher, less extracted wines.
appellations.terroir: The meandering Lot valley: three alluvial terraces of gravel and clay, and the causse, a Jurassic limestone plateau with red clay (*terres rouges*) and siderolithic deposits.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos Triguedina's 'The New Black Wine' revives the old technique of heating the grapes before fermentation to make an inky, concentrated wine.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Quercy
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Merlot, Tannat, Gamay
appellations.summary: South of Cahors on the Quercy limestone, between the Lot and the Aveyron, this former VDQS became an AOC in 2011. Its reds are based on Cabernet Franc, blended with Malbec, Merlot and Tannat, giving supple, fresh wines that are lighter than Cahors.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone causse.
appellations.nerd_note: Cabernet Franc must make up at least 40% of the blend, unusual for the Southwest.

appellations.name: Gaillac
appellations.grapes: Duras, Braucol (Fer Servadou), Prunelard, Syrah, Gamay; Mauzac, Len de l'El (Loin de l'Œil), Ondenc, Muscadelle, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
Gaillac, on the Tarn east of Toulouse, is one of the oldest vineyards in France and probably the most varied. Roman potters at Montans made amphorae for the local wine, and the Benedictines of Saint-Michel (972) built its medieval trade. It makes every style: red, white, rosé, dry, sweet and sparkling.

Its secret weapon is its grapes. Reds blend Duras and Braucol (the local name for Fer Servadou), often with Syrah; whites use Mauzac (green-apple and pear), Len de l'El (an Occitan name meaning 'far from the eye', for its long stalks), Ondenc and Muscadelle. The *méthode gaillacoise*, or ancestral method, makes a sparkling wine in a single fermentation, finished in the bottle without added sugar or yeast, a technique much older than Champagne's second fermentation. Robert Plageoles and his son Bernard revived forgotten grapes (Ondenc, Prunelard, Verdanel, Mauzac Noir) and a sherry-like *vin de voile*. Today, natural-wine producers such as Domaine de Brin, Causse Marines and Nicolas Carmarans keep up the experimentation.
appellations.terroir: Three zones: gravel terraces of the Tarn's left bank, limestone plateau on the right bank (the premières côtes and Cordes area), and the sand and granite of the Cunac plateau near Albi. The south-easterly 'vent d'autan' dries the grapes.
appellations.nerd_note: Gaillac's 'vin de voile', aged under a veil of yeast in old barrels like Jura's vin jaune, was revived by Robert Plageoles from local tradition.

appellations.name: Gaillac premières côtes
appellations.grapes: Mauzac, Len de l'El, Ondenc, Muscadelle, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: A sub-appellation for dry and sweet whites from the limestone hills on the right bank of the Tarn, with stricter ripeness rules than plain Gaillac. It is rarely seen on labels, since most growers sell under the better-known Gaillac name or with mentions such as doux or perlé.
appellations.terroir: Limestone hillsides on the right bank of the Tarn.
appellations.nerd_note: Despite its age, the name appears on only a handful of bottles.

appellations.name: Fronton
appellations.grapes: Négrette (at least 50%), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Gamay, Malbec, Fer Servadou
appellations.summary: Fronton is Toulouse's local wine, from terraces between the Tarn and the Garonne. It is the home of Négrette, a red grape with violet and liquorice notes, which must make up at least half of the blend. Local legend says the Knights Hospitaller brought it from Cyprus in the Middle Ages; the story is colourful but unproven, and the grape appears to be a local variety. Reds are supple and aromatic; rosés are popular. Château Bellevue la Forêt and Château Plaisance lead.
appellations.terroir: Three terraces of the Tarn: gravel and boulbènes (silty clay) on the lower terraces, and red, iron-rich 'rouget' soils higher up.
appellations.nerd_note: Négrette is prone to rot in humid weather, so it thrives only in Fronton's well-drained terraces and dry autan wind.

appellations.name: Saint-Sardos
appellations.grapes: Syrah (at least 40%), Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Merlot
appellations.summary: A small appellation on the left bank of the Garonne west of Montauban, promoted to AOC in 2011 and dominated by the Saint-Sardos cooperative. Syrah is the main grape, blended with Tannat, giving dark, peppery reds and rosés that suit the region's cassoulet and confit.
appellations.terroir: Gravel terraces and clay-limestone hills.
appellations.nerd_note: One of the few Southwest appellations where Syrah is the main grape.

appellations.name: Madiran
appellations.grapes: Tannat (60 to 80%), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fer Servadou (Pinenc)
appellations.summary:
Madiran is the kingdom of Tannat, a grape with more tannin and colour than almost any other, and its wines are among the most structured reds in France: black fruit, liquorice and spice, with tannins that need years to soften. In the 1980s Alain Brumont of Château Montus and Château Bouscassé showed that 100% Tannat aged in new oak could rival great Bordeaux, and his Montus Prestige made the appellation's name.

Madiran is also where micro-oxygenation was invented: in the early 1990s Patrick Ducournau of Domaine Mouréou developed a technique to bubble tiny, controlled amounts of oxygen into wine to soften Tannat's tannins, and it spread worldwide. A 2006 study in *Nature* by Roger Corder linked the high procyanidin content of Tannat wines to the longevity of people in the Gers, which briefly made Madiran famous as a 'healthy wine'. Today, growers like Château d'Aydie and Domaine Labranche-Laffont make fresher, less oaky styles.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone, siliceous clay and pebbly boulbènes on hills rising from the Adour, with Pyrenean influence and dry, warm autumns.
appellations.nerd_note: Tannat is also Uruguay's national grape, taken there by Basque immigrants in the nineteenth century.

appellations.name: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh
appellations.grapes: Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Arrufiac, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon
appellations.summary: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh is the white-wine twin of Madiran, from the same area. Its name in Gascon means 'posts in a row' (*piquets en rang*), from the old way of training vines on stakes. It is made dry or sweet; the sweet versions, from Petit and Gros Manseng shrivelled on the vine (passerillé), can be picked as late as December. The local Arrufiac grape, nearly extinct, was revived by the Plaimont cooperative and Alain Brumont.
appellations.terroir: The same clay-limestone and boulbènes as Madiran.
appellations.nerd_note: Some producers pick a last batch of shrivelled Manseng for sweet Pacherenc as late as the end of December.

appellations.name: Saint-Mont
appellations.grapes: Tannat, Pinenc (Fer Servadou), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon; Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Arrufiac, Petit Manseng
appellations.summary: Saint-Mont, in the Gers, is almost entirely the work of the Plaimont cooperative, founded in 1979 by André Dubosc, whose campaign to save local grapes and old vineyards earned it the AOC in 2011. In Sarragachies, Plaimont protects a pre-phylloxera vineyard of under a hectare with about 20 varieties, some found nowhere else; in 2012 it became the first vineyard in France listed as a Monument Historique. The reds are Tannat blends, less tannic than Madiran; the whites are fresh and floral.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone, sandy and boulbènes soils on Gers hillsides.
appellations.nerd_note: The Sarragachies vineyard is planted 'en foule', haphazardly, with vines layered (provignés) from older vines, a method used before rows were the norm.

appellations.name: Tursan
appellations.grapes: Baroque, Gros Manseng, Sauvignon Blanc; Tannat, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: Tursan, in the Landes south of the Adour, is the home of Baroque, a white grape found almost nowhere else, giving round, nutty wines. The chef Michel Guérard of Eugénie-les-Bains revived the appellation's image with his Château de Bachen.
appellations.terroir: Sandy and clay-limestone hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Baroque's high natural sugar made it popular in Armagnac before phylloxera; Tursan is now almost its last refuge.

appellations.name: Béarn
appellations.grapes: Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fer Servadou; Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Raffiat de Moncade, Petit Courbu
appellations.summary: Béarn covers scattered vineyards in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques around Jurançon, Madiran and Salies-de-Béarn, mostly for rosés and reds built on Tannat and the Cabernets. Béarn-Bellocq is a small sub-zone around the village of Bellocq, where the cooperative makes most of the wine. The appellation is a useful outlet for red grapes in an area best known for white Jurançon.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone and pebbles in the Gave valleys.
appellations.nerd_note: Raffiat de Moncade, a white grape found almost only here, is named after the Moncade tower in Orthez.

appellations.name: Jurançon
appellations.grapes: Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Camaralet, Lauzet
appellations.summary:
Jurançon, in the foothills of the Pyrenees south and west of Pau, makes one of France's great sweet wines without relying on botrytis. Petit Manseng's tiny, thick-skinned berries are left on the vine into November or December, shrivelling (passerillage) in the dry foehn wind from Spain while keeping vibrant acidity. The result tastes of pineapple, mango, quince, ginger and honey, with a tangy freshness that sets it apart from Sauternes.

The legend says that when the future Henri IV was born in Pau in 1553, his grandfather rubbed his lips with garlic and a drop of Jurançon. In 1975 the appellation added Jurançon Sec, now about half the production, mostly from Gros Manseng. Vineyards on steep slopes are often trained high to avoid frost and rot, and the best are terraced. Henri Ramonteu of Domaine Cauhapé, Charles Hours of Clos Uroulat, Domaine de Souch and Clos Lapeyre are the reference producers.
appellations.terroir: Steep hills of clay, limestone and *poudingue* (a conglomerate of Pyrenean pebbles) at 300 to 400 m, with the warm, dry foehn wind in autumn.
appellations.nerd_note: Late-harvest Petit Manseng can hang into December, and in some years pickers bring in shrivelled bunches after the first snow on the Pyrenees.

appellations.name: Irouléguy
appellations.grapes: Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon; Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Petit Courbu
appellations.summary: Irouléguy is France's only Basque wine appellation, a small vineyard in the Pyrenean foothills near Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port on the pilgrimage route to Santiago. Monks of the Roncesvalles abbey planted the first vines. Steep slopes are terraced on red sandstone at up to 400 m. Tannat dominates the reds, which are fresher and more mineral than Madiran's. Domaine Arretxea, Domaine Ilarria, Domaine Brana and the cooperative are the main producers.
appellations.terroir: Red sandstone (grès rouge), schist, ophite and limestone on steep, terraced mountain slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Labels often say 'Irulegi', the Basque spelling, and the cooperative's top wines bear Basque names.

appellations.name: Floc de Gascogne
appellations.grapes: Colombard, Gros Manseng, Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche; Merlot, Cabernet, Tannat for rosé
appellations.summary: Floc de Gascogne is a liqueur wine (vin de liqueur), made by adding young Armagnac to unfermented grape juice, in the Armagnac area, then resting it for several months before release. Its name means 'bouquet of flowers' in Gascon. Served chilled as an aperitif, it comes in white and rosé versions.
appellations.terroir: The Armagnac area's sandy (Bas-Armagnac) and clay-limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The Armagnac must be from the same estate as the grape juice, a rule that keeps Floc a farm product.

appellations.name: Pineau des Charentes
appellations.grapes: Ugni Blanc, Colombard, Montils, Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc; Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Pineau des Charentes is the liqueur wine of the Cognac region, made by blending fresh grape must with Cognac at least a year old, then ageing it, partly in oak, for at least 18 months before release. A legend says a sixteenth-century grower accidentally poured must into a barrel containing Cognac and found the result delicious years later. It is made white or rosé and served chilled.
appellations.terroir: The chalky soils of Cognac (Grande and Petite Champagne, Borderies, Fins Bois).
appellations.nerd_note: Pineau is made by mutage, like the vins doux naturels, but with Cognac instead of neutral spirit, and before fermentation starts.

appellations.name: Marcillac
appellations.grapes: Fer Servadou (Mansois, at least 90%)
appellations.summary: Marcillac is a tiny appellation in the Aveyron near Rodez, in a natural amphitheatre of red soils, and its wine is made almost entirely from Fer Servadou, called Mansois here. The wines are bright, peppery and redcurrant-scented, with a mineral iron note from the soil. Domaine du Cros and the Valon cooperative are the main producers. Monks of the abbey of Conques, a major stop on the pilgrimage to Santiago, planted the vineyards.
appellations.terroir: The 'rougier', red, iron-rich clay and sandstone of the Permian, on steep slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: The miners and steelworkers of nearby Decazeville kept the wine alive in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; it was their daily wine.

appellations.name: Entraygues - Le Fel
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Mauzac; Fer Servadou, Cabernet Franc, Gamay
appellations.summary: Tiny terraced vineyards on granite and schist at the confluence of the Lot and Truyère, in the north of the Aveyron. The whites, mostly Chenin Blanc, are crisp and mineral, and the reds blend Fer Servadou and Cabernet Franc. Laurent Mousset is the reference producer.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: Entraygues means 'between waters' in Occitan, referring to the two rivers.

appellations.name: Estaing
appellations.grapes: Fer Servadou, Gamay; Chenin Blanc, Mauzac
appellations.summary: A tiny appellation on the Lot below the medieval village and castle of Estaing, a stop on the pilgrimage road to Santiago, with vines on steep schist and limestone terraces. Reds blend Fer Servadou and Gamay; whites use Chenin Blanc and Mauzac. Production is very small and almost all drunk in the Aveyron.
appellations.terroir: Terraced slopes of schist and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: With only about twenty hectares, Estaing is one of France's smallest AOCs.

appellations.name: Côtes de Millau
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Syrah, Fer Servadou, Cabernet Sauvignon; Chenin Blanc, Mauzac
appellations.summary: Vineyards in the Tarn gorges near Millau, close to Norman Foster's famous viaduct, on old limestone and schist terraces that cling to the valley sides. Reds blend Gamay and Syrah with Fer Servadou and Cabernet; whites use Chenin Blanc and Mauzac. The local cooperative makes most of the wine, which is light, peppery and fresh.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and schist terraces in the Tarn gorges.
producers: Les Vignerons des Gorges du Tarn
appellations.nerd_note: Before phylloxera the Tarn gorges had thousands of hectares of terraced vines; the terraces can still be seen in the scrub.

sites.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
sites.text: Listed first among the first growths in 1855, Lafite sits on the northern edge of Pauillac, its vines running down to the Jalle du Breuil stream that separates it from Cos d'Estournel in Saint-Estèphe. The Marquis Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur made it famous in the eighteenth century; Baron James de Rothschild bought it in 1868 and died three months later, and his descendants still own it. The style is the most perfumed of the Pauillac firsts: cedar, graphite and violets over a fine-grained frame. Its second wine is Carruades de Lafite.

sites.name: Château Latour
sites.text: Latour takes its name from a fourteenth-century fort that guarded the estuary; the domed tower in the vines is a later dovecote. The heart of the estate is the 47-ha Enclos around the château, deep gravel sloping to the riverside meadows that blunt frost and cool hot nights. Latour is the most powerful and slowest-maturing of the first growths, famous for consistency in poor vintages. François Pinault's Artémis group has owned it since 1993, and in 2012 Latour left the en primeur system to release wines only when it judges them ready.

sites.name: Château Margaux
sites.text: The only first growth in the Margaux appellation, and the only one whose château is a true neoclassical palace: Louis Combes built it between 1810 and 1816, columns and all. The Mentzelopoulos family bought the estate in 1977 and, with director Paul Pontallier, restored its reputation after a weak spell. The wine is the archetype of Margaux perfume, violets and red fruit over silky tannins. Its Pavillon Blanc, pure Sauvignon Blanc, is sold as Bordeaux because the appellation is red-only. Norman Foster designed the new cellars, opened in 2015.

sites.name: Château Haut-Brion
sites.class: Premier Cru Classé (1855); Cru Classé de Graves (red, and white from 1960)
sites.text: The only red outside the Médoc ranked in 1855, and arguably the first estate wine sold by name: Arnaud III de Pontac shipped 'Ho Bryan' to London, where Samuel Pepys drank it in 1663. The vineyard sits on a deep gravel ridge in Pessac, now surrounded by the city. American banker Clarence Dillon bought it in 1935; his descendant Prince Robert of Luxembourg runs it. The red is smoky and tobacco-scented; the white, rare and expensive, ages for decades.

sites.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
sites.class: Premier Cru Classé (1973; Deuxième Cru in 1855)
sites.text: The only estate ever promoted in the 1855 classification. Ranked first among the seconds in 1855, two years after Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild bought it, Mouton was raised to first growth in 1973 after half a century of lobbying by Baron Philippe de Rothschild, who also pioneered château bottling in 1924. Its motto changed from 'Premier ne puis, second ne daigne, Mouton suis' to 'Premier je suis, second je fus, Mouton ne change'. Every vintage since 1945 carries a label by an artist, from Braque and Picasso to Bacon and Warhol.

sites.name: Château Rauzan-Ségla
sites.text: Pierre de Rauzan created this estate in 1661, and it was split in the eighteenth century into Rauzan-Ségla and Rauzan-Gassies. In 1855 Rauzan-Ségla headed the second growths, just behind Mouton. After a long slump, the Wertheimer family (owners of Chanel) bought it in 1994 and invested heavily in drainage and replanting; it is now one of the finest Margaux, perfumed and silky with real depth.

sites.name: Château Rauzan-Gassies
sites.text: The other half of Pierre de Rauzan's seventeenth-century estate, owned by the Quié family since 1946. Its parcels interlock with Rauzan-Ségla on the gravel around Margaux village. The wine has improved markedly since the 2000s, with more precision and freshness than its old reputation suggests.

sites.name: Château Léoville Las Cases
sites.text: The largest share of the old Léoville estate, which was divided after the Revolution into Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton. Its walled Grand Clos, entered through a stone gateway with a lion on top (the label's emblem), runs right up to Latour's vineyards. Under the Delon family, especially Michel Delon from the 1970s, it became the archetypal 'super second', with Pauillac-like density and prices to match. Clos du Marquis is a separate wine, not a second wine.

sites.name: Château Léoville Poyferré
sites.text: Named after Baron Jean-Marie de Poyferré, who inherited this third of the Léoville estate in the early nineteenth century. The Cuvelier family has owned it since 1920; Didier Cuvelier's modernisation from 1979 made it one of Saint-Julien's richest, most plush wines. Its château faces Las Cases across the road in the village of Saint-Julien.

sites.name: Château Léoville Barton
sites.text: Hugh Barton, of an Irish family of Bordeaux merchants, bought a third of the Léoville vineyard in 1826, five years after buying Langoa. There is no Léoville Barton château: the wine is made in the cellars of Langoa. Anthony Barton, who ran both estates from 1983 until his death in 2022, kept prices fair through the boom years, and his daughter Lilian Barton Sartorius continues the line. The wine is classic, firm, cedary Saint-Julien that rewards patience.

sites.name: Château Durfort-Vivens
sites.text: Named after the Durfort de Duras family, who owned it from the fourteenth century. The Lurton family took it over in 1961, and Gonzague Lurton converted it to biodynamics in the 2010s; it now experiments with amphorae and bottlings of single Cabernet parcels. The wine is one of the more Cabernet-driven, mineral Margaux.

sites.name: Château Gruaud Larose
sites.text: Founded in the 1720s by the abbé Gruaud and later passed to his heir, Monsieur de La Rose, it is one of the largest estates in Saint-Julien, set inland on a broad gravel plateau. The Merlaut family has owned it since 1997. Gruaud makes dense, long-lived wine, a little more rustic and broad-shouldered than the riverside Saint-Juliens.

sites.name: Château Lascombes
sites.text: Named after Antoine de Lascombes, a seventeenth-century owner. The American writer and merchant Alexis Lichine bought it in 1952 and expanded it to over 100 ha, making it one of the largest Margaux estates. A large share of Merlot on clay-rich parcels gives it a riper, rounder style than most Margaux.

sites.name: Château Brane-Cantenac
sites.text: Baron Hector de Brane, nicknamed the 'Napoleon of the vines', sold Brane-Mouton (now Mouton Rothschild) in 1830 to concentrate on his estate in Cantenac. The Lurton family has owned it since 1925, and Henri Lurton has run it since 1992. Its central gravel plateau gives one of the most fragrant and refined Margaux.

sites.name: Château Pichon Baron
sites.text: In 1850 the Pichon-Longueville estate was divided between Baron Raoul de Pichon-Longueville and his sisters; the baron kept this half and built the turreted fairytale château in 1851. AXA Millésimes bought it in 1987 and, under Christian Seely, restored its reputation. The wine is dense, structured Pauillac, the vineyard facing Latour across the D2 road.
