sites.name: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande
sites.text: The sisters' share of the 1850 Pichon division, named after Virginie, Comtesse de Lalande. May-Eliane de Lencquesaing ran it from 1978 to 2007, when she sold it to Champagne Louis Roederer. Some of its vines lie across the border in Saint-Julien, and a relatively high share of Merlot gives a famously silky, perfumed style for Pauillac.

sites.name: Château Ducru-Beaucaillou
sites.text: The name means Ducru (a nineteenth-century owner) plus 'beaux cailloux', beautiful stones, for the large gravel that covers its riverside vineyard. The Borie family has owned it since 1941; Bruno Borie runs it. The château, with its Victorian towers, faces the Gironde, and the wine is the most refined and polished of the Saint-Julien seconds.

sites.name: Château Cos d'Estournel
sites.text: Louis-Gaspard d'Estournel, who traded horses and wine with India, built the extraordinary chai with pagoda towers and a carved door from Zanzibar in the 1830s. Nicknamed the 'Maharajah of Saint-Estèphe', he died in debt. Cos faces Lafite across the Jalle du Breuil, on a gravel ridge facing south-east. Owned by Michel Reybier since 2000, it makes rich, exotic, spicy Saint-Estèphe from gravity-fed cellars rebuilt in 2008.

sites.name: Château Montrose
sites.text: Montrose did not exist as a vineyard until the early nineteenth century, when Étienne Théodore Dumoulin cleared a heath of pink heather on a gravel mound above the estuary. Fifty years later it was a second growth. The estuary breeze and gravel over clay give one of the most powerful, long-lived wines of the Médoc. Martin and Olivier Bouygues bought it in 2006 and rebuilt it with a strong environmental focus, including solar panels and geothermal energy.

sites.name: Château Kirwan
sites.text: Named after Mark Kirwan, an Irishman from Galway who married into the estate in the eighteenth century. The Schÿler family, Bordeaux négociants of German origin, have owned it since 1925, and their botanical gardens around the château are listed. Kirwan was named first of the third growths in 1855; its Cantenac vineyard gives supple, aromatic wine.

sites.name: Château d'Issan
sites.text: A moated seventeenth-century château built on the foundations of the medieval Château de la Mothe-Cantenac, beside the estuary meadows. Its motto, 'Regum mensis arisque deorum' (for the tables of kings and the altars of the gods), appears on the gate. The Cruse family has owned it since 1945 and was joined by Jacques Thienpont in 2013. The wine is classic, elegant Margaux.

sites.name: Château Lagrange
sites.text: The largest estate in Saint-Julien, inland on two gravel hills behind Gruaud Larose, with an Italianate tower. Japan's Suntory bought it in 1983, the first Japanese investment in a classed growth, and replanted most of the vineyard. It makes firm, good-value Saint-Julien and a white wine, Les Arums de Lagrange, sold as Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château Langoa Barton
sites.text: Bought by Hugh Barton in 1821, Langoa is the oldest classed growth to have remained with the same family, now the seventh and eighth Barton generations. Its eighteenth-century chartreuse houses the family and the cellars for both Langoa and Léoville Barton. The wine is a slightly softer, earlier-drinking cousin of Léoville.

sites.name: Château Giscours
sites.text: A large estate in Labarde with a grand Second Empire château and a park landscaped by Eugène Bühler. The Dutch Albada Jelgersma family has owned it since 1995 and also owns du Tertre. Giscours made famous wines in the 1970s, then slipped; it has steadily regained form with generous, dark-fruited Margaux.

sites.name: Château Malescot Saint-Exupéry
sites.text: Simon Malescot, counsellor to King Louis XIV, bought the estate in 1697; Count Jean-Baptiste de Saint-Exupéry, an ancestor of the author of *The Little Prince*, owned it in the nineteenth century. The Zuger family has run it since 1955. Its château stands in the middle of Margaux village, and the wine is deep and spicy, among the most concentrated in the appellation.

sites.name: Château Boyd-Cantenac
sites.text: Named after Jacques Boyd, of an Irish family, who bought vines in Cantenac in the 1750s. Owned by the Guillemet family, who also make Château Pouget in the same cellars. A small estate making traditional, firm Margaux with a good share of Cabernet.

sites.name: Château Cantenac Brown
sites.text: John Lewis Brown, of a Scottish family and father of the animal painter of the same name, built the château in the 1830s in an English Tudor style that looks nothing like any other building in the Médoc. Its vineyard lies on gravel in Cantenac, giving firm, deep-coloured wine. A new low-carbon winery, built with traditional materials such as rammed earth, opened in the 2020s.

sites.name: Château Palmer
sites.text: Major-General Charles Palmer, a British officer who fought under Wellington, bought the estate in 1814 and ruined himself on it; the Pereire banking brothers took it over in 1853. Today owned by the Sichel and Mähler-Besse families, Palmer consistently sells above many second growths. Farmed biodynamically since 2014, it uses a high share of Merlot (often 40% or more), which gives a sensual, velvety style. Its *Historical XIXth Century Wine* blends Margaux with northern Rhône Syrah, as merchants did when 'hermitaging' claret.

sites.name: Château La Lagune
sites.text: The first classed growth heading north from Bordeaux, in Ludon on sandy gravel close to the estuary. Its eighteenth-century chartreuse is attributed to the architect Victor Louis. The Frey family (also owners of Paul Jaboulet Aîné and Château Corton C) has owned it since 2000, with Caroline Frey making the wine and converting to biodynamics. The style is supple and perfumed.

sites.name: Château Desmirail
sites.text: Named after Jean Desmirail, who married into the Rauzan family in the eighteenth century. Its vines were absorbed into Palmer and other estates in the twentieth century, and the name survived only as a brand until Lucien Lurton revived it in 1981. His son Denis Lurton now runs a small estate making elegant Margaux.

sites.name: Château Calon-Ségur
sites.text: The most northerly classed growth, once owned by the Marquis de Ségur, who also owned Lafite and Latour but said his heart was at Calon: hence the heart on the label, a favourite Valentine's Day wine. The vineyard is largely walled. Since 2012, new owners have replanted and rebuilt the cellars, and the wine has become one of Saint-Estèphe's best, with a high share of Cabernet Sauvignon.

sites.name: Château Ferrière
sites.text: One of the smallest classed growths, at under 25 ha, named after Gabriel Ferrière, a royal shipbroker. Leased to Château Lascombes for decades, it was revived by the Villars-Merlaut family in 1992 and is now run by Claire Villars-Lurton, who converted it to biodynamics. The wine is fine-boned and floral.

sites.name: Château Marquis d'Alesme
sites.text: Formerly Marquis d'Alesme Becker, this small estate in Margaux village was bought by the Perrodo family (also owners of Labégorce) in 2006. They dropped 'Becker' from the name in 2009 and built a new winery with Chinese-inspired gardens, a nod to Hubert Perrodo's Asian business links.

sites.name: Château Saint-Pierre
sites.text: A small Saint-Julien estate bought in 1982 by Henri Martin, mayor of Saint-Julien and creator of Château Gloria, and now run by his descendants, the Triaud family. Its vines are scattered parcels of excellent gravel in the village, and the wine is plush and generous for Saint-Julien.

sites.name: Château Talbot
sites.text: Named after John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the English commander killed at Castillon in 1453, though there is no proof he ever owned it. The Cordier family has owned Talbot since 1917 and now runs it with the Rustmann and Bignon families. A large inland estate, it makes sturdy, savoury red and a well-known white, Caillou Blanc, sold as Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château Branaire-Ducru
sites.text: Facing Beychevelle across the road, Branaire takes its name from Jean-Baptiste Braneyre, who bought it in 1680, and from the Ducru family of the nineteenth century. The Maroteaux family has owned it since 1988 and built one of the first gravity-flow cellars in the Médoc in 1991. The wine is elegant, mid-weight Saint-Julien of real charm.

sites.name: Château Duhart-Milon
sites.text: Bought by the Rothschilds of Lafite in 1962, Duhart-Milon's vines lie on the slopes of the Carruades plateau west of Lafite, next to the hamlet of Milon. The name recalls a legendary eighteenth-century pirate, Monsieur Duhart, said to have lived in Pauillac; it is a story more than a fact. The wine is a firmer, more affordable sibling of Lafite.

sites.name: Château Pouget
sites.text: One of the smallest classed growths, about 10 ha in Cantenac, owned by the Guillemet family and made alongside Boyd-Cantenac. It makes traditional, firm Margaux at modest prices.

sites.name: Château La Tour Carnet
sites.text: A genuine medieval castle with a moat and a thirteenth-century keep, in Saint-Laurent-Médoc. Bernard Magrez bought it in 2000 and changed it radically, with heavy investment in the vineyard and a ripe, modern style. Its name comes from Jean de Foix's squire, Carnet, who won it by defending it in the Hundred Years War, according to tradition.

sites.name: Château Lafon-Rochet
sites.text: Instantly recognisable by its yellow château and label, painted that colour by the Tesseron family, who owned it from 1960 until 2021, when Jacky Lorenzetti (owner of Pédesclaux) bought it. The vineyard is next to Cos d'Estournel and Lafite, and the wine is firm, fresh Saint-Estèphe.

sites.name: Château Beychevelle
sites.text: Its name is said to derive from *baisse-voile*, lower the sail: ships on the Gironde dipped their sails to salute the Duc d'Épernon, admiral of France, who owned the estate in the seventeenth century. Hence the ship on the label. The eighteenth-century château is among the most elegant in the Médoc. Owned since the 1980s by a partnership led by Castel and Suntory, Beychevelle makes supple, aromatic Saint-Julien that often outperforms its rank.

sites.name: Château Prieuré-Lichine
sites.text: Once the priory of the Benedictine monks of Cantenac, it was bought in 1951 by Alexis Lichine, the Russian-born wine writer and merchant, who added his name and opened it to visitors when such hospitality was unheard of in the Médoc. The vineyard is a patchwork of parcels across Margaux's five communes, giving a blended picture of the appellation.

sites.name: Château Marquis de Terme
sites.text: Named after the Marquis de Terme, who acquired it by marriage in 1762. The Sénéclauze family has owned it since 1935. A mid-sized estate in Margaux village whose wine has gained finesse since the 2010s.

sites.name: Château Pontet-Canet
sites.text: Owned by the Tesseron family since 1975, Pontet-Canet became the most talked-about fifth growth of the 2000s. Alfred Tesseron converted to biodynamics, certified in 2010, brought back horses for ploughing, and introduced concrete amphorae made from the estate's own gravel. The wines, from vineyards next to Mouton, are now priced and scored like seconds.

sites.name: Château Batailley
sites.text: Its name recalls a battle of the Hundred Years War said to have been fought on the site. Owned by the Castéja family (of Borie-Manoux), it sits inland in a wooded park in south-western Pauillac. Batailley makes classic, firm, fairly priced Pauillac.

sites.name: Château Haut-Batailley
sites.text: Split off from Batailley in 1942 when the Borie family divided its holdings, Haut-Batailley was run by the Bories of Ducru-Beaucaillou until the Cazes family of Lynch-Bages bought it in 2017. Its vines border Pichon Baron and Latour inland, and the wine is lighter-bodied and graceful.

sites.name: Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste
sites.text: 'Puy' means hill: the estate sits on a high gravel mound on the Bages plateau. The Borie family bought it in 1978, and Xavier Borie and now his daughter Emeline have made it a byword for classic, cassis-and-cedar Pauillac at a fair price.

sites.name: Château Grand-Puy Ducasse
sites.text: Unusually, its château stands on the waterfront quay of Pauillac town, while its vines are scattered across three parts of the appellation. Named after Pierre Ducasse, an eighteenth-century lawyer. It makes approachable, mid-weight Pauillac.

sites.name: Château Lynch-Bages
sites.text: Named after Thomas Lynch, of an Irish family, whose son Jean-Baptiste became mayor of Bordeaux. The Cazes family has owned it since 1939; Jean-Michel Cazes made it a 'poor man's Latour' famous for rich, cassis-laden wine, and restored the hamlet of Bages with a bakery and café. A new cellar designed by Chien Chung Pei opened in 2020.

sites.name: Château Lynch-Moussas
sites.text: The westernmost classed growth of Pauillac, on gravel at the edge of the forest. Like Lynch-Bages it was once owned by the Lynch family. The Castéja family has run it since 1919, replanting and expanding it from the 1970s.

sites.name: Château Dauzac
sites.text: In Labarde, close to the estuary, Dauzac has a famous place in wine science. In the early 1880s its manager Ernest David and the botanist Alexis Millardet noticed that vines sprayed with copper sulphate and lime, to deter grape thieves along the road, had escaped downy mildew. The result was *bouillie bordelaise*, the Bordeaux mixture that saved Europe's vineyards.

sites.name: Château d'Armailhac
sites.text: Baron Philippe de Rothschild bought this neighbour of Mouton in 1933 and renamed it several times (Mouton Baron Philippe, then Mouton Baronne Philippe) before reverting in 1989 to the name of the eighteenth-century d'Armailhacq family. The wine has a relatively high share of Cabernet Franc and is softer than Mouton.

sites.name: Château du Tertre
sites.text: 'Tertre' means a small hill, and this estate in Arsac sits on one of the highest gravel ridges in the Margaux appellation. Owned by the Albada Jelgersma family since 1997, it uses a striking share of Cabernet Franc and some Petit Verdot, giving fragrant, fresh wines.

sites.name: Château Haut-Bages Libéral
sites.text: Named after the Libéral family, eighteenth-century merchants. Part of its vineyard borders Latour. Claire Villars-Lurton has converted it to biodynamics and agroforestry, planting hedges and trees among the vines.

sites.name: Château Pédesclaux
sites.text: Founded by Pierre Urbain Pédesclaux, a Bordeaux wine broker of the early nineteenth century, when brokers (courtiers) were the men who drew up the 1855 ranking. Long underperforming, it was transformed after Jacky Lorenzetti bought it in 2009, with a glass-walled, gravity-fed cellar by architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte and replanted vineyards near Mouton and Pontet-Canet.

sites.name: Château Belgrave
sites.text: An inland estate in Saint-Laurent-Médoc, just behind Lagrange and the Saint-Julien border. Part of the Dourthe group since 1979, it makes firm, good-value Haut-Médoc from gravel over clay.

sites.name: Château de Camensac
sites.text: An eighteenth-century chartreuse in Saint-Laurent-Médoc. The Merlaut family and associates have owned it since 2005 and worked to restore its gravel vineyard. The wine is supple and approachable for a classed growth.

sites.name: Château Cos Labory
sites.text: A small estate next door to Cos d'Estournel, owned by the Audoy family. Its wine is firm, honest Saint-Estèphe at a price well below its famous neighbour's.

sites.name: Château Clerc Milon
sites.text: Bought by Baron Philippe de Rothschild in 1970, its vines lie next to Lafite and Mouton close to the estuary, around the hamlet of Milon. A new winery opened in 2011. The wine is richer and more Mouton-like than its rank suggests.

sites.name: Château Croizet-Bages
sites.text: On the Bages plateau next to Lynch-Bages, owned by the Quié family (also of Rauzan-Gassies) since 1942. Long considered an underachiever, it has improved with recent investment.

sites.name: Château Cantemerle
sites.text: Missing from the original list of April 1855, Cantemerle was added a few months later at the bottom of the fifth growths after its owner, the widow Villeneuve-Durfort, produced records proving its prices. The château stands in a wooded park in Macau, at the southern end of the Médoc. The wine is perfumed and supple, from sandy gravel.

sites.name: Château d'Yquem
sites.text: The only wine given the rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in 1855, a title no red wine received. Yquem sits on the highest hill of Sauternes, about 75 m, with a fortified manor dating back to the fifteenth century. The Sauvage family owned it from 1593; in 1785 Françoise-Joséphine de Sauvage d'Yquem married Count Louis-Amédée de Lur-Saluces, and their descendants ran it until LVMH took control at the end of the 1990s, with Alexandre de Lur-Saluces leaving in 2004. Thomas Jefferson ordered it in the 1780s. About 100 ha are in production, roughly three quarters Sémillon. Pickers make up to ten or more tries, and in poor years (1992, 2012 among them) no Yquem is released. Its dry white, Ygrec (Y), first made in 1959, is now produced every year.

sites.name: Château La Tour Blanche
sites.text: Ranked first of the Premiers Crus after Yquem in 1855. In 1907 its owner, the philanthropist Daniel Iffla Osiris, left it to the French state on condition that it house a school of viticulture, and it still runs a wine college today. Its wines, from Bommes, are rich and barrel-fermented.

sites.name: Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey
sites.text: A thirteenth-century fortified manor in Bommes with crenellated walls. Swiss businessman Silvio Denz, owner of the glassmaker Lalique, bought it in 2014 and opened a hotel and restaurant, Lalique, where crystal and Sauternes meet. The wines are among the most consistent of the Premiers Crus.

sites.name: Clos Haut-Peyraguey
sites.text: Created when the Peyraguey estate was divided in 1879, this small vineyard on the summit of the Bommes hill was owned by the Pauly family for a century before Bernard Magrez bought it in 2012. The wines are fine and lifted rather than heavy.

sites.name: Château de Rayne Vigneau
sites.text: On a hill in Bommes famous for its soil studded with semi-precious stones, agate, onyx and quartz brought by the Garonne, which a nineteenth-century owner had catalogued. The wine is fragrant and finely balanced.

sites.name: Château Suduiraut
sites.text: A grand seventeenth-century château in Preignac with gardens attributed to André Le Nôtre's school, bordering Yquem's vines. AXA Millésimes has owned it since 1992. Suduiraut is one of the richest, most opulent Sauternes; it also makes dry whites (Lions de Suduiraut and S de Suduiraut).

sites.name: Château Coutet
sites.text: The largest of the Barsac first growths, with a thirteenth-century tower that once served as an English fort. Owned by the Baly family since 1977, distributed with Baron Philippe de Rothschild SA. Its rare Cuvée Madame, made only in great years from the oldest vines, is one of the most sought-after Barsacs.

sites.name: Château Climens
sites.text: Often called the Lord of Barsac, Climens farms about 30 ha in one block on the highest point of the Barsac limestone plateau, planted entirely with Sémillon. Bérénice Lurton ran it from 1992 and converted it to biodynamics in 2010, the first Sauternais classed growth to do so. In 2022 she sold a majority stake to the Moitry family and stayed on as a consultant. The wine is a model of Barsac freshness and finesse.

sites.name: Château Guiraud
sites.text: One of the largest estates of Sauternes, on gravel next to Yquem. Since 2006 it has belonged to a group including Robert Peugeot, Xavier Planty, Olivier Bernard of Domaine de Chevalier and Stephan von Neipperg, and it was the first Sauternes classed growth certified organic (2011). It runs a conservatory of old vine selections.

sites.name: Château Rieussec
sites.text: In Fargues, on high gravel next to Yquem. The Rothschilds of Lafite (Domaines Barons de Rothschild) bought it in 1984. Rieussec is known for its deep golden colour and rich, honeyed style. Its dry wine is R de Rieussec.

sites.name: Château Rabaud-Promis
sites.text: The old Rabaud estate in Bommes was ranked as one in 1855, divided in 1903 into Rabaud-Promis and Sigalas-Rabaud, reunited in 1929 and divided again in 1952. Rabaud-Promis has been owned by the Déjean family since 1981.

sites.name: Château Sigalas Rabaud
sites.text: The smaller half of the old Rabaud estate, on a gravel slope in Bommes facing north-west. Owned by the de Lambert des Granges family, descendants of the Marquis de Sigalas, it makes delicate, pure Sauternes and was among the first to make a sulphite-free sweet wine.

sites.name: Château de Myrat
sites.text: The de Pontac family, owners since the nineteenth century, pulled up the vines in 1976 when Sauternes could not be sold. Two of the family sons replanted in 1988, and the estate returned to production in the 1990s.

sites.name: Château Doisy-Daëne
sites.text: Part of the original Doisy estate, owned by the Dubourdieu family since 1924. Denis Dubourdieu, the great white-wine scientist of the University of Bordeaux, worked here; his sons now run it. Its L'Extravagant, made in tiny quantities from the richest berries, is one of the most concentrated sweet wines of Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château Doisy-Dubroca
sites.text: The smallest of the three Doisy estates, a few hectares of old Sémillon. For many years it was owned by the Lurton family and made by the team at Climens.

sites.name: Château Doisy-Védrines
sites.text: The largest of the three Doisy estates and the original seat of the family, owned by the Castéja family since 1840. It makes rich, long-lived Barsac.

sites.name: Château d'Arche
sites.text: A seventeenth-century château on a gravel hill in Sauternes, named after the Comte d'Arche, an eighteenth-century owner who built up the estate. It makes rich, classic Sauternes with a high share of Sémillon and now hosts a small hotel among the vines, a rare chance to sleep in the heart of the Sauternais.

sites.name: Château Filhot
sites.text: A large estate in the south of Sauternes with an elegant château built in the early nineteenth century and a park. Owned by the Lur-Saluces family for a long time, it now belongs to the Vaucelles family. The wines are lighter than most, with a good share of Sauvignon Blanc.

sites.name: Château Broustet
sites.text: A small Barsac estate on the limestone plateau beside the road to Langon, with vineyards on red sand and clay over limestone. Its wines are lighter and more citrus-toned than the Sauternes heavyweights, a good introduction to the Barsac style.

sites.name: Château Nairac
sites.text: An elegant château built in 1776 for Élysée Nairac, a Protestant merchant from a family of shipowners, by an architect from the circle of Victor Louis. The Heeter-Tari family revived the estate from 1971 and makes concentrated, oak-aged Barsac.

sites.name: Château Caillou
sites.text: A small estate with a neo-Gothic château on the limestone of Barsac, run by the Bravo family. Caillou means pebble. Its wines are fresh and floral.

sites.name: Château Suau
sites.text: One of the least-known classed growths, a small Barsac vineyard of a few hectares close to the Garonne. Not to be confused with the Château Suau that makes red and white Bordeaux at Capian, across the river.

sites.name: Château de Malle
sites.text: A seventeenth-century château with Italian-style gardens and statues, classified as a historic monument, in Preignac. It has belonged to the same family since its construction, now the Bournazel line. It also makes red and dry white Graves.

sites.name: Château Romer
sites.text: The small half of the old Romer estate in Fargues, owned by the Farges family. After decades of being leased, the family took back control in 2002, and the wine has regained its place.

sites.name: Château Romer du Hayot
sites.text: The other part of the old Romer estate, in Fargues, run by the du Hayot family since the 1970s. It makes light, fresh, approachable Sauternes.

sites.name: Château Lamothe
sites.text: In 1961 the old Lamothe estate on a ridge south of Sauternes village was split between two families. Lamothe, run by the Despujols family, is the smaller half. Its steep slope of gravel over clay drains quickly and gives a fresh, mid-weight style of Sauternes.

sites.name: Château Lamothe Guignard
sites.text: The larger part of the old Lamothe estate, owned by the Guignard family since 1981, on a ridge of gravel and clay near Sauternes village. The Guignards brought it back to form with stricter tries and better barrels, and it is now one of the reliable values among the Deuxièmes Crus.

sites.name: Château La Mission Haut-Brion
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red; white since the 2009 absorption of Laville Haut-Brion)
sites.text: Facing Haut-Brion across the Avenue Jean Jaurès, La Mission was owned from 1682 to the Revolution by the Lazarist priests of the Congregation of the Mission. The Woltner family made it famous in the twentieth century, and Domaine Clarence Dillon (Haut-Brion's owner) bought it in 1983. It absorbed La Tour Haut-Brion (red) in 2006 and Laville Haut-Brion (white) in 2009, whose wine is now La Mission Haut-Brion Blanc. The red is denser and more muscular than Haut-Brion.

sites.name: Château Pape Clément
sites.text: Bertrand de Goth, archbishop of Bordeaux, received this vineyard in 1299; in 1305 he became Pope Clement V, the first Avignon pope, and gave the estate to the archdiocese. It is one of the oldest named vineyards in Bordeaux. Bernard Magrez has run it since the 1980s and made it a rich, modern-style Pessac-Léognan.

sites.name: Château Smith Haut Lafitte
sites.text: A Scottish merchant, George Smith, added his name in the eighteenth century. Daniel and Florence Cathiard, both former ski champions, bought it in 1990, made it one of the best estates in the appellation and created Les Sources de Caudalie hotel and spa; their daughter founded Caudalie cosmetics using grape-seed polyphenols. Its white, though unclassified, is among the best of Bordeaux.

sites.name: Domaine de Chevalier
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red and white)
sites.text: A vineyard in a forest clearing in Léognan, exposed to spring frost because cold air pools among the pines. Olivier Bernard's family bought it in 1983. Its white, Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon fermented in barrel, is one of the longest-lived dry whites in France and is often best after 15 years.

sites.name: Château Haut-Bailly
sites.text: Red only, on a gravel hill in Léognan. It keeps a block of vines more than a century old, with several varieties planted together in the old way. American banker Robert Wilmers bought it in 1998 and kept Véronique Sanders, granddaughter of a previous owner, as director. The wine is famous for silky elegance.

sites.name: Château Carbonnieux
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red and white)
sites.text: One of the oldest and largest estates of the Graves, run by Benedictine monks of Sainte-Croix in the eighteenth century. A popular story says the monks sold their white wine to the Ottoman court as 'mineral water of Carbonnieux' to get around the ban on alcohol. The Perrin family has owned it since 1956.

sites.name: Château Malartic-Lagravière
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red and white)
sites.text: Named after Count Hippolyte de Maurès de Malartic, an eighteenth-century admiral, whose ship is on the label. Belgian businessman Alfred-Alexandre Bonnie bought it in 1997 and rebuilt the cellars; the estate is now one of the most reliable in Léognan.

sites.name: Château de Fieuzal
sites.text: Classified only for red, though its barrel-fermented white made it famous in the 1980s, when Gérard Gribelin showed how good modern white Graves could be. The estate, on gravel in Léognan, has been owned by the Irish Quinn family since 2001, and both colours remain excellent.

sites.name: Château Olivier
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red and white)
sites.text: A moated castle with a twelfth-century keep in a hunting estate in Léognan, owned by the de Bethmann family since 1886. The Black Prince is said to have hunted here. The estate has improved greatly since the 2000s.

sites.name: Château Bouscaut
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red and white)
sites.text: In Cadaujac, close to the Garonne, owned by the Lurton family since 1979 and now run by Sophie Lurton. Its clay and limestone suit Merlot more than most Pessac-Léognan.

sites.name: Château Latour-Martillac
sites.class: Cru Classé de Graves (1959, red and white)
sites.text: Named after a tower, the remains of a twelfth-century fort, in Martillac. The Kressmann family, Bordeaux négociants, have owned it since 1930. Some white vines date from the 1880s.

sites.name: Château Couhins
sites.text: Owned since 1968 by France's national agricultural research institute (INRA, now INRAE), which uses it as an experimental vineyard and also sells its classified white. A rare case of a state-owned classed growth.

sites.name: Château Couhins-Lurton
sites.text: A small part of the old Couhins estate bought by André Lurton in 1967. Its classified white is pure Sauvignon Blanc, barrel-fermented, and ages well.

sites.name: Château Pavie
sites.text: Pavie's vines climb the south-facing côtes from the foot of the slope to the limestone plateau, giving a mix of clay, limestone and sand. Gérard Perse, a former supermarket owner, bought it in 1998 and made it a symbol of the ripe, concentrated style, which divided critics in the early 2000s. It was promoted to A in 2012 and confirmed in 2022, when it became one of only two A estates. A palatial new winery opened in 2013.

sites.name: Château Figeac
sites.text: Figeac sits on three gravel croupes near the Pomerol border, sharing the gravel island with Cheval Blanc. Unusually for the right bank, it plants about a third each of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot, so its wine is more Médoc-like in structure. Thierry Manoncourt ran it for 60 years; after decades of campaigning the family won promotion to A in 2022, the only estate raised to the top rank that year. A new underground cellar opened in 2021.

sites.name: Château Ausone
sites.class: Withdrew from the classification in 2021 (formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé A)
sites.text: Named after the fourth-century Roman poet Ausonius, who had a villa near Bordeaux, Ausone is a tiny estate of about 7 ha on the edge of the limestone plateau, facing south-east above the town. Its cellars are carved into the rock. The Vauthier family has owned it since the nineteenth century; Alain Vauthier and his daughter Pauline make a dense, mineral wine with a high share of Cabernet Franc. Ausone left the classification in 2021 in protest at its criteria.

sites.name: Château Cheval Blanc
sites.class: Withdrew from the classification in 2021 (formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé A)
sites.text: On gravel and clay right on the Pomerol border, Cheval Blanc is unusual for its high proportion of Cabernet Franc, often more than half the blend. Its 1947, a heavy, almost port-like wine from a hot year, is often called the greatest Bordeaux of the twentieth century. Owned by Bernard Arnault and the late Albert Frère since 1998. Christian de Portzamparc designed the wave-shaped winery opened in 2011. Cheval Blanc withdrew from the classification in 2021.

sites.name: Château Angélus
sites.class: Withdrew from the classification in 2022 (formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé A)
sites.text: The name comes from the Angelus bells, which could be heard from three churches in the vineyard; a bell is on the label, and the estate's tower plays a carillon. Owned by the de Boüard de Laforest family since 1909, it was promoted to A in 2012. In January 2022 it withdrew from the classification, after a court ruling against co-owner Hubert de Boüard over his role in the 2012 ranking. Stéphanie de Boüard-Rivoal now runs it.

sites.name: Château Beau-Séjour Bécot
sites.text: On the limestone plateau west of the town, it was demoted in 1986 for including vines from outside its classified area and promoted back in 1996, a story that shows how seriously the classification can be taken. The Bécot family has owned it since 1969.

sites.name: Château Beauséjour
sites.text: Owned by the Duffau-Lagarrosse family for more than 150 years, this small estate on the plateau and côtes west of the town was sold in 2021 to Joséphine Duffau-Lagarrosse and the Courtin family (Clarins), after a public family dispute. Since then it has dropped 'Duffau-Lagarrosse' from its label.

sites.name: Château Bélair-Monange
sites.text: On the edge of the limestone plateau next to Ausone, with quarried cellars beneath. The Moueix family bought Bélair in 2008, added Monange (a family name) and merged neighbouring Magdelaine in 2012. The family has since rebuilt the winery. The wine is taut and mineral.

sites.name: Château Canon
sites.text: Named after Jacques Kanon, an eighteenth-century privateer. The Wertheimer family (Chanel) bought it in 1996 and replanted much of the vineyard after the cellars were found contaminated with TCA; they later absorbed neighbouring Matras and Berliquet. Canon is a pure, limestone-driven wine with a walled clos on the plateau.

sites.name: Château Canon-la-Gaffelière
sites.text: At the foot of the côtes below the town, owned by Stephan von Neipperg since 1971. He was among the first in Saint-Émilion to farm organically, and his success at this sandy-clay site helped make the 'modern' right bank style. Promoted to B in 2012.

sites.name: Château Larcis Ducasse
sites.text: On the terraced south-facing côtes of Saint-Laurent-des-Combes, east of the town, beside Pavie. Its limestone terraces face the sun all day. Owned by the Gratiot-Attmane family, it was promoted to B in 2012 under the management of Nicolas Thienpont.

sites.name: Château Pavie Macquin
sites.text: Named after Albert Macquin, who was a pioneer in grafting vines onto American rootstock after phylloxera in the late nineteenth century. The estate is on the limestone plateau above Pavie. Promoted to B in 2006, confirmed since.

sites.name: Château Troplong Mondot
sites.text: On the highest point of Saint-Émilion, about 110 m, its water tower is a local landmark. Raymond Troplong expanded the estate in the nineteenth century. The insurer SCOR bought it in 2017, and the wine has moved from a powerful style to fresher, earlier picking.

sites.name: Château Trotte Vieille
sites.text: On the limestone plateau east of the town, owned by the Castéja family since 1949. Its name is said to come from an old woman who 'trotted' out to meet travellers on the road. It keeps a small plot of pre-phylloxera Cabernet Franc.

sites.name: Château Valandraud
sites.text: The first 'garage wine': Jean-Luc Thunevin and Murielle Andraud made their first vintage in 1991 from a few rows in a garage in Saint-Émilion town. Its rise from a garage to Premier Grand Cru Classé B in 2012 is a great Bordeaux story. The estate is now based in Saint-Étienne-de-Lisse.

sites.name: Clos Fourtet
sites.text: Right at the gates of the medieval town on the limestone plateau, with a huge network of old quarries beneath it used as cellars. The name may come from a small fort (fortet) that defended the town. The Cuvelier family has owned it since 2001.

sites.name: La Mondotte
sites.text: A small vineyard of under 5 ha on the limestone plateau of Saint-Laurent-des-Combes, owned by Stephan von Neipperg. In 1996 he made it an independent wine; it became a cult 'garage' wine and was promoted to B in 2012.

sites.name: Château La Gaffelière
sites.class: Withdrew from the classification in 2022 (formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé B)
sites.text: At the foot of the côtes below Ausone, where a Gallo-Roman mosaic with a vine motif was found. Owned by the Malet Roquefort family for more than three centuries, it withdrew from the classification in 2022.

sites.name: Château Tertre Rôteboeuf
sites.text: François Mitjavile's small amphitheatre of vines on the south-facing côtes of Saint-Laurent-des-Combes. The name means the hill where the oxen belched, because ploughing it was so hard. Mitjavile never applied for classification, yet his late-picked, voluptuous wine sells above many Premiers Grands Crus Classés.

sites.name: Monolithic Church of Saint-Émilion
sites.text: Carved out of the limestone in the eleventh and twelfth centuries below a bell tower that rises from the plateau, it is the largest underground church in Europe. It stands above the cave where the Breton monk Émilion lived in the eighth century. The quarries that run under the town and its vineyards supplied stone for Bordeaux and now age wine. The church is the symbol of the UNESCO-listed Jurisdiction of Saint-Émilion, the first vineyard landscape on the World Heritage list.

sites.name: Petrus
sites.text: The most famous wine of the right bank, from about 11.5 ha on the highest part of the Pomerol plateau, where a lens of blue-grey clay rises to the surface. The clay swells in wet weather and shrinks in drought, feeding the vines slowly. The wine is almost pure Merlot. Madame Loubat, who owned it from 1925 to 1961, made it a luxury name; the Moueix family took over, and Jean-François Moueix's family owns it today. Petrus spells its name without an accent and without 'Château'.

sites.name: Château Le Pin
sites.text: The original Bordeaux micro-cuvée: Jacques Thienpont bought just over 1 ha with a lone pine tree in 1979 and made wine in a cellar under a farmhouse. Le Pin is now about 2.8 ha, Merlot on gravel over clay, and costs more than Petrus at auction. A new cellar designed by Paul Robbrecht opened in 2011.

sites.name: Château Lafleur
sites.text: A small estate of about 4.5 ha next to Petrus with a higher share of Cabernet Franc, giving a fragrant, intense, long-lived wine. The Guinaudeau family has run it since 1985, when Jacques and Sylvie Guinaudeau took over from the Robin family; their son Baptiste and his wife Julie now manage it.

sites.name: Vieux Château Certan
sites.text: One of the oldest estates in Pomerol, with records going back to the sixteenth century. The Belgian Thienpont family bought it in 1924; Alexandre Thienpont and his son Guillaume make a wine with a high proportion of Cabernet Franc and some Cabernet Sauvignon. It is the most Médoc-like and perfumed of the great Pomerols.

sites.name: Château L'Église-Clinet
sites.text: A small estate around Pomerol's church on gravel and clay. Denis Durantou, who ran it from 1983 until his death in 2020, made it one of the best Pomerols with old vines, including a plot of ungrafted pre-phylloxera Merlot and Cabernet Franc. His daughters now run it.

sites.name: Château La Conseillante
sites.text: Owned by the Nicolas family since 1871, on the border with Saint-Émilion and Cheval Blanc. Its silver and violet capsule echoes the violet perfume of its wine, among the most silky and elegant in Pomerol.

sites.name: Château L'Évangile
sites.text: Next to Petrus and Cheval Blanc, on gravel and clay. The Rothschilds of Lafite have owned it since 1990 and built a new winery in 2004. Rich, dense and long-lived Pomerol.

sites.name: Château Trotanoy
sites.text: Owned by the Moueix family since 1953, on a slope of dense clay and gravel west of Pomerol church. The name comes from 'trop ennuie', too troublesome, because its clay was so hard to plough. It is one of the most powerful Pomerols.

sites.name: Château La Fleur-Pétrus
sites.text: Owned by the Moueix family since 1950, between Petrus and Lafleur on gravel and clay. It added parcels from Le Gay and has grown in quality, with a fresh, floral style.

sites.name: Château Clinet
sites.text: On the high gravel of the Pomerol plateau. Michel Rolland's early work here in the 1980s made it a model of ripe, opulent Merlot. The Laborde family has owned it since 1998.

sites.name: Château de la Dauphine
sites.text: An eighteenth-century château on the Fronsac hillside above the Dordogne, said to be named after the Dauphine Marie-Josèphe de Saxe, who visited. Moueix once owned it; the Labrune family has run it since 2015 with organic farming. It shows Fronsac's fresh, mineral side.

sites.name: Château La Cardonne
sites.text: In Blaignan-Prignac, once owned by the Rothschilds of Lafite (1973 to 1990). Its clay-limestone and gravel hill gives fresh, structured Médoc. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: Château Castéra
sites.text: A medieval castle in Saint-Germain-d'Esteuil which, according to local tradition, was burnt by the Black Prince's troops in the fourteenth century and later rebuilt. Its gravel and clay-limestone soils make firm, fresh Médoc. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: Château Laujac
sites.text: A large estate in Bégadan in the northern Médoc, owned by the Cruse négociant family for more than a century. Its gravel ridge gives a classic, firm Médoc. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: Château Paloumey
sites.text: In Ludon, close to La Lagune. Martine Cazeneuve revived the estate from 1989, replanting the gravel vineyard and building new cellars. The wine is ripe and supple, with the soft texture typical of the sandy gravels of the southern Haut-Médoc. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: Château Reysson
sites.text: In Vertheuil, north-west of Saint-Estèphe, owned by the Dourthe group. A Merlot-dominant Haut-Médoc from clay-limestone, polished and generous rather than austere, and one of the Haut-Médoc estates ranked Exceptionnel in the 2025 classification.

sites.name: Château Malescasse
sites.text: In Lamarque, between Margaux and Saint-Julien, on gravel ridges near the estuary ferry to Blaye. Owned since 2012 by businessman Philippe Austruy, who invested heavily in the cellar and vineyard. It was ranked Exceptionnel in both 2020 and 2025.

sites.name: Château de Malleret
sites.text: A historic estate in Le Pian-Médoc on the edge of the city, with gravel soils close to La Lagune and a large wooded park. The wine is supple, Cabernet-led southern Haut-Médoc. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: Château du Taillan
sites.text: A seventeenth-century château in Le Taillan-Médoc, owned by the Cruse family since 1896. Its white wine, La Dame Blanche, is sold as Bordeaux. Exceptionnel in 2020 and 2025.

sites.name: Château Reverdi
sites.text: A family estate in Listrac, on the clay-limestone and gravel of the Médoc's highest commune, at the edge of the pine forest. Its fresh, firm reds show the cooler side of the Médoc. It is the only Listrac estate among the fourteen Exceptionnels of 2025.

sites.name: Château d'Arsac
sites.text: A large estate in Arsac on the western edge of the Margaux appellation, owned by Philippe Raoux, known for contemporary art in its vineyards, including a giant blue sculpture. Exceptionnel in 2020 and 2025.

sites.name: Château Mongravey
sites.text: A small family estate in Arsac, on the western edge of the Margaux appellation, run by Régis Bernaleau and his family. It makes ripe, structured Margaux from gravel soils, at a fraction of classed-growth prices. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: Château Paveil de Luze
sites.text: Owned by the de Luze family, Bordeaux négociants, since 1862, in Soussans in the north of the Margaux appellation. Its gravel and clay soils give elegant, fresh, fairly priced Margaux. Ranked Exceptionnel in both 2020 and 2025.

sites.name: Château Le Crock
sites.text: An early-nineteenth-century château in Saint-Estèphe, owned by the Cuvelier family (also of Léoville Poyferré) since 1903. It makes firm, savoury, long-lived Saint-Estèphe. Ranked Exceptionnel in both 2020 and 2025.

sites.name: Château Lafitte Carcasset
sites.text: A Saint-Estèphe estate north of the village, unrelated to Lafite Rothschild despite the name, which comes from an older owner. Its gravel and clay soils give a firm, classic Saint-Estèphe that ages well. Ranked Exceptionnel in 2025.

sites.name: La Cité du Vin
sites.text: A curving, glass-and-aluminium wine museum on the Garonne quays at Bacalan, opened in 2016 and designed by XTU architects (Anouk Legendre and Nicolas Desmazières) to evoke wine swirling in a glass. Its permanent exhibition covers wine cultures from Georgia to China, and its top-floor bar looks across the Port of the Moon, the crescent-shaped river front listed by UNESCO in 2007.

sites.name: Musée du Vin et du Négoce, Chartrons
sites.text: The Chartrons district, just outside the old city walls, was where foreign merchants (Irish, English, Dutch, German) built their cellars from the seventeenth century, free from the city's rules. This small museum occupies vaulted cellars built in 1720 for the Irish merchant Francis Burke and tells the story of the négoce, the trade that sold Bordeaux to the world.

sites.name: Battle of Castillon Monument
sites.class: Site of the battle of 17 July 1453
sites.text: A monument marks the field where the French army defeated John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, on 17 July 1453, in one of the first battles won by field artillery. It ended the Hundred Years War and three centuries of English rule in Bordeaux, and with it the privileged trade that had sent claret to England. The site lies on the Dordogne just east of Castillon-la-Bataille.

sites.name: Citadelle de Blaye
sites.text: Built by Vauban in the 1680s to guard the Gironde estuary with Fort Pâté and Fort Médoc on the other side, the citadel is part of the UNESCO-listed Fortifications of Vauban. Its walls overlook the vineyards of the Blayais and the passage of ships to Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château des Ducs d'Épernon
sites.text: Built from 1599 for Jean-Louis de Nogaret de La Valette, Duc d'Épernon, the favourite of Henri III, it was one of the grandest palaces in France. Later it became a women's prison. Today it is a monument in the centre of Cadillac, the sweet-wine town on the Garonne.

sites.name: Abbaye de la Sauve-Majeure
sites.class: UNESCO World Heritage (Routes of Santiago de Compostela, 1998)
sites.text: Founded in 1079 by Gérard de Corbie, this Benedictine abbey ruled a large part of the Entre-Deux-Mers in the Middle Ages and planted vines across it. Its Romanesque ruins, with carved capitals, are on the pilgrim route to Santiago and are listed by UNESCO.

sites.name: Château de Fargues
sites.text: The Lur-Saluces family's home since 1472, a ruined fortress in Fargues. When Alexandre de Lur-Saluces left Yquem, he continued here, making Sauternes in the same way. Vines were replanted only in the 1930s; the first vintage was 1943. The wine is often compared to Yquem in style and quality.

sites.name: Château Sociando-Mallet
sites.text: Jean Gautreau bought this run-down estate in Saint-Seurin-de-Cadourne in 1969 and, on gravel overlooking the estuary, made one of the best unclassified wines of the Médoc, and chose to stay outside the Crus Bourgeois system. The wine is dense and long-lived.

sites.name: Château Poujeaux
sites.text: On the Grand Poujeaux gravel ridge, Poujeaux was one of the Médoc's 'exceptional' Crus Bourgeois before it left the system. The Cuvelier family (Clos Fourtet) bought it in 2008. Its wines regularly compete with classed growths in blind tastings.

sites.name: Château Chasse-Spleen
sites.text: The name, 'chase away melancholy', is often linked to Byron or Baudelaire, though the story is not proven. The estate makes one of the richest wines of Moulis and hosts a contemporary art centre.

sites.name: Château Loupiac-Gaudiet
sites.text: A family estate on the clay-limestone slopes facing Barsac across the Garonne, a reference for the Loupiac style: lighter and fresher than Sauternes, but with genuine botrytis in good years, and old vintages that keep remarkably well.

sites.name: Château Roc de Cambes
sites.text: A natural amphitheatre facing the Gironde, bought in 1988 by François Mitjavile of Tertre Rôteboeuf. Its success showed that Bourg could make wines of great depth.

sites.name: Ambonnay
sites.text: A south-facing grand cru on the Montagne de Reims, famous for ripe, powerful Pinot Noir. Krug's Clos d'Ambonnay, a walled plot of 0.68 ha, is one of the most expensive Champagnes in the world. Egly-Ouriet, Marguet and Paul Déthune make grower Champagnes here, and the village also produces still red Coteaux Champenois.

sites.name: Avize
sites.text: The heart of the Côte des Blancs, home of the Lycée Viticole de la Champagne and of Anselme Selosse, the grower who changed Champagne by vinifying in barrels and treating it as a wine of terroir. Its Chardonnay is rich, saline and deep, from chalk with a little more clay than Le Mesnil.

sites.name: Aÿ
sites.text: Aÿ is the historic capital of Pinot Noir in Champagne, part of the UNESCO-listed hillsides. Bollinger, Deutz, Gosset and Ayala are based here, and Henri IV is said to have called himself 'Sire d'Aÿ'. In April 1911 rioting growers burned houses here suspected of using grapes from outside the region. Since 2016 it has formed the commune of Aÿ-Champagne with Mareuil-sur-Aÿ and Bisseuil.

sites.name: Beaumont-sur-Vesle
sites.text: A small grand cru on the flat land at the north-eastern edge of the Montagne de Reims, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. It is the least known grand cru and its grapes go mostly to the houses.

sites.name: Bouzy
sites.text: A south-facing grand cru on the Montagne de Reims, famous for full, ripe Pinot Noir and for Bouzy Rouge, the still red Coteaux Champenois. Paul Bara, Benoit Lahaye and Barnaut are local growers.

sites.name: Chouilly
sites.text: At the northern end of the Côte des Blancs, just east of Épernay. Its Chardonnay is a little rounder and earlier than Cramant's; under the old échelle only its white grapes were rated 100%, its Pinot Noir 95%. Many houses own vines here, and Champagne Legras & Haas and Vazart-Coquart are local growers.

sites.name: Cramant
sites.text: A Chardonnay grand cru known for creamy, floral blanc de blancs. Mumm's famous lower-pressure 'Crémant de Cramant' was renamed Mumm de Cramant when the word crémant was reserved for sparkling wines from other French regions. Diebolt-Vallois, Lilbert-Fils and Suenen are notable growers.

sites.name: Louvois
sites.text: A Pinot Noir grand cru at the south of the Montagne de Reims, near a seventeenth-century château built for Louis XIV's minister, the Marquis de Louvois. Its vines face south on the plateau's edge, near Bouzy.

sites.name: Mailly-Champagne
sites.text: A north-facing Pinot Noir grand cru on the Montagne de Reims, famous for its cooperative, Mailly Grand Cru, founded in 1929 by growers during the Depression and now one of the best cooperatives in Champagne, with deep chalk cellars.

sites.name: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger
sites.text: The most austere and long-lived of the Chardonnay grand crus, on pure chalk at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs. Salon, the original blanc de blancs, is made only from Le Mesnil grapes and only in exceptional years, and Krug's Clos du Mesnil is here. Pierre Péters, Jacques Selosse and Robert Moncuit also make wines from it.

sites.name: Oger
sites.text: Between Avize and Le Mesnil, a Chardonnay grand cru with a rich, full style. Jean Milan and Claude Cazals are local growers. The village's vines were long a major supply for the big houses.

sites.name: Oiry
sites.text: A small grand cru on flat land at the northern tip of the Côte des Blancs, near Chouilly. Its Chardonnay is lighter and more delicate.

sites.name: Puisieulx
sites.text: The smallest grand cru, a few dozen hectares on the gentle north-eastern slopes of the Montagne de Reims, close to Sillery. Its vineyards, mostly Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, are almost all sold to the big Reims houses, so a village-named bottle is a rarity.

sites.name: Sillery
sites.text: In the eighteenth century, 'Sillery' was the most famous name in Champagne, used for the still and sparkling wines of the Marquis de Sillery. Today it is a small grand cru with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Tours-sur-Marne
sites.text: A grand cru for Pinot Noir on the Marne river, and the home of Laurent-Perrier. Its Chardonnay was rated premier cru only, a reminder that the old échelle could rate grapes by variety.

sites.name: Verzenay
sites.text: A north-facing Pinot Noir grand cru on the Montagne de Reims, known for structured, nervy wines. Its lighthouse, built in 1909 by Joseph Goulden as advertising, is now a museum of the vine.

sites.name: Verzy
sites.text: A north-facing grand cru on the Montagne de Reims next to the forest of the Faux de Verzy. Its Pinot Noir is firm and fresh, with Chardonnay also planted.

sites.name: Hautvillers
sites.class: Premier Cru village; UNESCO World Heritage (2015)
sites.text: The hilltop village of the Benedictine abbey where Dom Pérignon worked from 1668 until his death in 1715, part of the UNESCO-listed Champagne hillsides. Wrought-iron signs on the houses show trades and wine scenes.

sites.name: Mareuil-sur-Aÿ
sites.class: Premier Cru village; UNESCO World Heritage (2015)
sites.text: A Pinot Noir premier cru (rated 99% on the old échelle) along the Marne, home of Billecart-Salmon and of Philipponnat's Clos des Goisses, a steep 5.5-ha walled slope facing south over the canal, one of the most famous single vineyards in Champagne.

sites.name: Cumières
sites.text: A Marne premier cru with south-facing slopes that ripen early; it is often the first village to harvest in Champagne and is known for still red Coteaux Champenois as well as Champagne.

sites.name: Dizy
sites.text: A premier cru between Aÿ and Hautvillers on the south-facing slopes of the Grande Vallée de la Marne, and the home of Jacquesson, a house whose numbered 700-series cuvées and single-vineyard wines influenced modern Champagne.

sites.name: Vertus
sites.text: The largest premier cru, at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs, with Chardonnay and some Pinot Noir. Larmandier-Bernier, a biodynamic pioneer, and Duval-Leroy are based here.

sites.name: Chigny-les-Roses
sites.text: A premier cru on the northern slopes of the Montagne de Reims, named for its rose gardens, home of Champagne Cattier and its Armand de Brignac brand.

sites.name: Rilly-la-Montagne
sites.text: A premier cru on the northern slopes of the Montagne de Reims, known for its old cellars and for Vilmart et Cie, a grower who ages wines in large oak casks.

sites.name: Avenay-Val-d'Or
sites.text: A premier cru in the Val d'Or, a side valley that opens onto the Marne near Aÿ, planted mainly with Pinot Noir and Meunier. Its sheltered, south-facing slopes give rounder, riper fruit than the exposed northern face of the Montagne de Reims.

sites.name: Trépail
sites.text: A premier cru on the eastern edge of the Montagne de Reims, unusual for growing mostly Chardonnay on a Pinot Noir hill. Its cool, east-facing slopes give lean, high-acid white grapes that keep blends fresh.

sites.name: Cuis
sites.text: A premier cru at the northern end of the Côte des Blancs, mostly Chardonnay, on slopes higher and cooler than the grand crus nearby. Its wines have sharper acidity and lighter body, useful for freshness in blends.

sites.name: Villers-Marmery
sites.text: A premier cru on the eastern edge of the Montagne de Reims, almost entirely Chardonnay, giving fresh, citrusy blanc de blancs. Along with Trépail it forms a small white-grape enclave on a hill otherwise known for Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Bisseuil
sites.text: A premier cru on the Marne east of Mareuil, since 2016 part of the merged commune of Aÿ-Champagne, with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on gentle slopes and flatter land along the river toward Tours-sur-Marne.

sites.name: Les Riceys
sites.text: The largest wine commune in Champagne, in the Aube on the Burgundian border, made up of three hamlets. It is the only commune in France with three AOCs: Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys. Its Kimmeridgian slopes are planted with Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Urville
sites.text: A small village of the Côte des Bar, home of Drappier, whose cellars were built by Cistercian monks of Clairvaux in the twelfth century. Charles de Gaulle drank Drappier at his home in nearby Colombey-les-Deux-Églises.

sites.name: Celles-sur-Ource
sites.text: A Côte des Bar village in the Ource valley with one of the highest concentrations of grower-producers in Champagne. Nearby Courteron is home to Champagne Fleury, which converted to biodynamics in 1989, the first in the region.

sites.name: Sézanne
sites.text: The main town of the Côte de Sézanne, where east-facing slopes of chalk mixed with clay give ripe, round Chardonnay that many houses use to soften the austerity of Côte des Blancs fruit in their blends.

sites.name: Damery
sites.text: A Marne village whose growers stormed and wrecked the cellars of a négociant suspected of using outside grapes in April 1911, during the Champagne riots.

sites.name: Montgueux
sites.text: An isolated chalk hill west of Troyes, sometimes called the 'Montrachet of Champagne' for its ripe, intense Chardonnay. Its south-facing slope stands alone in the Aube plain. Grower Emmanuel Lassaigne (Jacques Lassaigne) made it famous.

sites.name: Moët & Chandon
sites.text: Founded by Claude Moët in 1743 and now part of LVMH, the largest Champagne house, with about 28 km of cellars under the Avenue de Champagne. Its prestige cuvée Dom Pérignon, first released with the 1921 vintage in 1936, is named after the monk of Hautvillers, whose abbey Moët owns. Napoleon was a friend of Jean-Rémy Moët and visited often.

sites.name: Pol Roger
sites.text: Founded by Pol Roger in 1849 and still family-owned, in Épernay. Its prestige cuvée Sir Winston Churchill honours the British prime minister, a loyal customer who called the house's address, then 44 Avenue de Champagne, 'the world's most drinkable address'. When he died in 1965, the house put a black border on its labels for the British market.

sites.name: Perrier-Jouët
sites.text: Founded by Pierre-Nicolas Perrier and Rose-Adélaïde Jouët in 1811 on the Avenue de Champagne. Its Belle Époque cuvée is known for the Japanese anemone bottle designed by Émile Gallé in 1902, rediscovered in 1964. Perrier-Jouët is famous for Chardonnay-led wines.

sites.name: Mercier
sites.text: Eugène Mercier founded this house in 1858 to make Champagne for the many rather than the few. He commissioned a giant barrel holding the equivalent of 200,000 bottles for the 1889 Paris Exhibition, pulled by oxen to Paris. Visitors tour the 18 km of cellars by small train.

sites.name: De Castellane
sites.text: Founded by Viscount Florens de Castellane in 1895, its 66-m tower, built in 1904, is the landmark of Épernay. The label uses the red cross of Saint Andrew.

sites.name: Gosset
sites.text: Gosset claims to be the oldest wine house in Champagne, founded in Aÿ in 1584 by Pierre Gosset, when it made still wines. It moved its headquarters to Épernay in 2009. Its wines often avoid malolactic fermentation, keeping high acidity.

sites.name: Veuve Clicquot
sites.text: Founded by Philippe Clicquot in 1772, the house was run from 1805 by his widow, Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin, one of the first women to lead an international business. Her team developed the riddling table around 1816 and made the first known blended rosé in 1818. Now part of LVMH, it is known for its yellow label and its chalk cellars (crayères) in Reims.

sites.name: Ruinart
sites.text: The oldest established Champagne house, founded in 1729 by Nicolas Ruinart, nephew of the Benedictine monk Dom Thierry Ruinart. Its Gallo-Roman chalk pits (crayères) in Reims, listed as a historic monument, are part of the UNESCO site. Ruinart is known for Chardonnay-led blanc de blancs.

sites.name: Taittinger
sites.text: Pierre Taittinger bought the house of Forest-Fourneaux, founded in 1734, in 1932. Its cellars in Reims are carved out of Gallo-Roman chalk pits under the ruins of the Saint-Nicaise abbey. The Comtes de Champagne is a famous Chardonnay prestige cuvée. In 2017 the house began planting vines in Kent, England, for its English sparkling wine Domaine Evremond.

sites.name: Pommery
sites.text: Louise Pommery, a widow from 1858, made the first commercial brut Champagne, the Pommery Nature 1874, for the British market. She converted 120 Gallo-Roman chalk pits into 18 km of cellars and built an Elizabethan-style estate on the Saint-Nicaise hill. The cellars now host contemporary art exhibitions.

sites.name: Krug
sites.text: Founded in Reims in 1843 by Joseph Krug, a German from Mainz, Krug ferments all its wines in small oak casks and blends Grande Cuvée from more than 120 wines across 10 or more years. Its single-vineyard Clos du Mesnil and Clos d'Ambonnay are among the most expensive Champagnes. LVMH has owned it since 1999.

sites.name: Louis Roederer
sites.class: Champagne house (founded 1776 as Dubois Père et Fils)
sites.text: Still family-owned, Roederer is famous for Cristal, created in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia in a clear glass bottle (so no bomb could be hidden in it, according to legend). Roederer owns most of its vines, a rarity among the large houses, and has farmed a large part biodynamically.

sites.name: Charles Heidsieck
sites.text: Founded in 1851 by Charles-Camille Heidsieck, 'Champagne Charlie', who sold his wine across the United States in the 1850s and was briefly imprisoned as a spy during the Civil War. Its 47 Gallo-Roman crayères in Reims are part of the UNESCO site. It is known for long ageing and high reserve wine content.

sites.name: G.H. Mumm
sites.text: Founded in Reims in 1827 by the German Mumm brothers, it was seized by the French state during the First World War. Its red ribbon Cordon Rouge, first used in 1876, recalls the Légion d'honneur. It is now owned by Pernod Ricard.

sites.name: Lanson
sites.text: Founded in 1760, Lanson was long known for blocking malolactic fermentation, which gave its wines a crisp, sharp acidity; recent cellarmasters have relaxed the rule for some cuvées. Its Clos Lanson is a walled vineyard in Reims.

sites.name: Henriot
sites.text: Founded in Reims in 1808 by Apolline Henriot, a widow who inherited vineyards in the Côte des Blancs. It is known for Chardonnay-rich blends and its prestige cuvée Hemera. In 1995 the Henriot family bought Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune; the whole group passed to François Pinault's Artémis Domaines in 2022.

sites.name: Bollinger
sites.text: Founded in Aÿ in 1829 and still family-owned. Lily Bollinger ran it from 1941 to 1971 and toured its vineyards by bicycle. It ferments most base wines in oak, keeps its reserve wines in magnums under cork, and owns 'Vieilles Vignes Françaises', two tiny plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir in Aÿ. James Bond drinks it.

sites.name: Deutz
sites.text: Founded in Aÿ in 1838 by William Deutz and Pierre-Hubert Geldermann from Aachen. The house was sacked during the 1911 riots. Now owned by Roederer, it is known for its Amour de Deutz blanc de blancs.

sites.name: Billecart-Salmon
sites.text: Founded in 1818 in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ by Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon, and still family-run. It makes one of the best-known rosés and the Clos Saint-Hilaire, a single plot of Pinot Noir in Mareuil.

sites.name: Philipponnat
sites.text: The Philipponnat family has been in Aÿ since 1522. In 1935 it bought Clos des Goisses, a 5.5-ha walled vineyard on a steep slope above the Marne canal, now one of the most famous single-vineyard Champagnes.

sites.name: Salon
sites.text: Eugène-Aimé Salon, a fur merchant, created the first blanc de blancs Champagne from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger grapes, first released in 1905 (commercially from 1921). Salon is made only in the best years, about 40 vintages in a century, from a single grand cru and a single grape, aged about ten years before release.

sites.name: Clos du Mesnil
sites.text: A walled vineyard of 1.85 ha in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, first walled in 1698 and bought by Krug in 1971. The first Clos du Mesnil vintage, 1979, was released in 1986. It is pure Chardonnay, intense and long-lived.

sites.name: Jacques Selosse
sites.text: Anselme Selosse, who took over his father's estate in Avize in the 1970s, changed Champagne by vinifying like a Burgundian, in barrels with indigenous yeasts, and treating Champagne as a wine of place. His single-site cuvées and his solera-style Substance became legends, and his inn, Les Avisés, is a pilgrimage site.

sites.name: Laurent-Perrier
sites.text: In Tours-sur-Marne. Bernard de Nonancourt, who rebuilt it after the Second World War, was a pioneer of stainless-steel fermentation and launched the macerated Cuvée Rosé in 1968. Its Grand Siècle is a multi-vintage blend.

sites.name: Jacquesson
sites.text: Founded in 1798 in Châlons, now in Dizy, Jacquesson won Napoleon's praise. The Chiquet brothers numbered their non-vintage cuvées (700 series) from 2000 and made single-vineyard Champagnes such as Dizy Corne Bautray.

sites.name: Egly-Ouriet
sites.text: Francis Egly's estate in Ambonnay makes some of Champagne's most sought-after grower wines, rich and vinous Pinot Noir from old vines with long lees ageing, and still red Ambonnay Rouge.

sites.name: Pierre Péters
sites.text: A family estate in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger making pure Chardonnay. Its Les Chétillons cuvée, from a single parcel in Le Mesnil, is a reference blanc de blancs, and Rodolphe Péters uses a perpetual reserve.

sites.name: Larmandier-Bernier
sites.text: Pierre and Sophie Larmandier converted to biodynamics around 2000 in Vertus and make low-dosage, terroir-focused Champagnes such as Terre de Vertus and Vieille Vigne du Levant from Cramant.

sites.name: Drappier
sites.text: A family house in Urville in the Aube since 1808, with twelfth-century cellars built by the monks of Clairvaux. Michel Drappier makes low-sulphur wines and keeps old varieties such as Arbane and Petit Meslier.

sites.name: Abbaye Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers
sites.text: The Benedictine abbey where Dom Pierre Pérignon was cellarmaster from 1668 to 1715. He worked to stop bubbles rather than create them, but he improved blending and pressing. His tomb lies in the church, and Moët & Chandon owns the abbey.

sites.name: Reims Cathedral
sites.text: The coronation church of the kings of France, where most kings from the eleventh century to Charles X in 1825 were crowned, which gave the wines of Reims prestige at court. Damaged by German shelling in 1914, it was restored with funds partly from the Rockefeller family. Windows by Marc Chagall and a set given by Champagne winegrowers showing vineyard work were installed in the twentieth century.

sites.name: Phare de Verzenay
sites.text: A lighthouse in the vineyards, built in 1909 by Joseph Goulden as an advertisement for his Champagne house. It now houses a museum of the vine and offers views over the grand cru slopes of the Montagne de Reims.

sites.name: Faux de Verzy
sites.text: A forest of about 1,000 dwarf beech trees with twisted branches on the Montagne de Reims, a genetic curiosity on land that belonged for centuries to the abbey of Saint-Basle. It is a reminder of the wild plateau above the grand crus.

sites.name: Aÿ (1911 riots)
sites.text: On 12 April 1911, thousands of growers from the Marne rioted in Aÿ and Damery, burning the cellars and homes of houses accused of buying grapes from outside Champagne. Troops occupied the region. The riots led to the delimitation laws that still protect the appellation.

sites.name: Avenue de Champagne
sites.text: Épernay's grand boulevard, lined with the mansions of Moët & Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger and others, built over more than 100 km of chalk cellars. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the 'Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars'.

sites.name: Colline Saint-Nicaise
sites.text: The hill of Saint-Nicaise in Reims is riddled with Gallo-Roman chalk quarries (crayères), now the cellars of Ruinart, Veuve Clicquot, Taittinger, Charles Heidsieck and Pommery. Part of the UNESCO listing since 2015.

sites.name: Mas de Daumas Gassac
sites.text: In 1970 Aimé and Véronique Guibert bought a farm in the Gassac valley near Aniane. Geographer Henri Enjalbert found glacial soils similar to the Côte d'Or, and the Guiberts planted Cabernet Sauvignon. Their first vintage, 1978, made with advice from Émile Peynaud, was hailed as the 'Lafite of the Languedoc', proving the region could make great wine. Guibert fought Robert Mondavi's plan to buy land in Aniane in 2001.

sites.name: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
sites.text: Laurent Vaillé's estate near Aniane, created in 1989 after he worked with Gérard Chave, Jean-François Coche-Dury and Eloi Dürrbach. Its red (Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cabernet Sauvignon) and white (Roussanne, Marsanne, Chardonnay) are among France's most sought-after wines. Vaillé gives few interviews and sells little.

sites.name: Mas Jullien
sites.text: Olivier Jullien founded his estate in Jonquières in 1985 at the age of 20 and became the inspiration for the Languedoc's quality revolution, making wines that express the terroirs of the Larzac foothills.

sites.name: Domaine d'Aupilhac
sites.text: Sylvain Fadat's estate in Montpeyroux, created in 1989, champions old Carignan and Cinsault and planted the high, cool Cocalières amphitheatre. A key figure in Montpeyroux's campaign for its own AOC, finally won in 2026.

sites.name: Domaine de l'Hortus
sites.text: Jean and Marie-Thérèse Orliac planted vines below the cliffs of the Montagne de l'Hortus, facing the Pic Saint-Loup, in the late 1970s and helped make Pic Saint-Loup's name with Syrah-led reds.

sites.name: Pic Saint-Loup
sites.text: A 658-m limestone peak north of Montpellier that gives its name to the appellation. It faces the Montagne de l'Hortus across a valley, and the vineyards lie between them in a cool, sheltered combe.

sites.name: Château de la Négly
sites.text: Jean Paux-Rosset's estate on the La Clape massif near Fleury, between the garrigue and the sea, known for dense Syrah and Mourvèdre reds such as La Porte du Ciel and for saline whites from Bourboulenc.

sites.name: Château l'Hospitalet
sites.text: Gérard Bertrand, a former rugby player, bought this estate on the La Clape massif in 2002 and made it his flagship, with a hotel, restaurant and summer jazz festival. His group is one of the largest owners of biodynamic vineyards in France.

sites.name: Abbaye de Fontfroide
sites.text: A Cistercian abbey in a valley of the Corbières near Narbonne, founded in 1093. It was a centre of the fight against the Cathars; Pierre de Castelnau, the papal legate whose murder in 1208 triggered the Albigensian Crusade, was a monk here. The abbey still makes wine.

sites.name: Abbaye de Saint-Hilaire
sites.text: A Benedictine abbey near Limoux whose monks, according to local claims, made the world's first sparkling wine. A 1531 document records the abbey buying flasks of 'blanquette', but it is not proof that the wine was sparkling.

sites.name: Abbaye de Valmagne
sites.text: A Cistercian abbey founded in 1138 near Villeveyrac, whose Gothic church has served as a wine cellar since the Revolution, with giant oak casks in the chapels. It still produces wine.

sites.name: Clos Centeilles
sites.text: Patricia Boyer-Domergue's estate in Siran saved forgotten local grapes such as Piquepoul Noir, Riveyrenc and Œillade, and was a pioneer of Minervois-La Livinière, making elegant reds with little or no new oak.

sites.name: Château de Pennautier
sites.text: Owned by the Lorgeril family since 1620, this château near Carcassonne is nicknamed the 'Little Versailles of the Languedoc'. It is the leading estate of Cabardès.

sites.name: Argeliers
sites.text: The village where Marcellin Albert, a café owner, launched the revolt of the winegrowers of the Midi in 1907 against fraud and falling prices. He led rallies of hundreds of thousands, then lost his followers after a meeting with Clemenceau.

sites.name: Narbonne Town Hall
sites.text: In June 1907, Narbonne's mayor, Dr Ernest Ferroul, resigned in protest and became a leader of the winegrowers' revolt. On 19 and 20 June, troops fired on demonstrators in Narbonne, killing several people. The 17th Infantry Regiment mutinied in Béziers in sympathy.

sites.name: Place de la Comédie
sites.text: On 9 June 1907 the Place de la Comédie in Montpellier hosted the largest of the winegrowers' rallies, with estimates of 500,000 to 800,000 people, one of the biggest demonstrations in French history.

sites.name: Allées Paul Riquet, Béziers
sites.text: Where soldiers of the 17th Infantry Regiment, many of them local, sat down and refused to fire on the crowd in June 1907, after mutinying from Agde. The song 'Gloire au 17e' celebrated them.

sites.name: Faculté de Médecine de Montpellier
sites.text: One of the oldest medical schools in the world, where Arnau de Vilanova taught in the late thirteenth century. He described stopping fermentation with spirit, the basis of the vins doux naturels of Roussillon and Languedoc.

sites.name: Pinet
sites.text: The village on the Étang de Thau that gives its name to Picpoul de Pinet. Oyster beds stretch across the lagoon, and the crisp white wine is their natural partner.

sites.name: Roquebrun
sites.text: A village on the Orb with steep schist terraces and a Mediterranean garden, known for one of the best cooperatives in France. Saint-Chinian Roquebrun has been a cru since 2005.

sites.name: Berlou
sites.text: A schist village in the hills north of Saint-Chinian, which gives its name to the cru Saint-Chinian Berlou, known for old Carignan and a strong cooperative, the Vignerons de Berlou.

sites.name: Boutenac
sites.text: The village at the heart of Corbières-Boutenac, the first cru of Corbières (2005), where old Carignan must make up a large share of the blend.

sites.name: La Livinière
sites.text: The village that gave its name to the Languedoc's first communal cru in 1999, on the limestone Petit Causse below the Montagne Noire, where south-facing terraces give some of the Minervois's deepest reds.

sites.name: Frontignan
sites.text: A coastal town between Sète and the Étang de Thau whose sweet Muscat was praised by Voltaire and bought by Thomas Jefferson. The cooperative's twisted bottle is iconic.

sites.name: Faugères
sites.text: A schist village north of Béziers with three restored windmills overlooking vineyards on the Cévennes foothills. It gives its name to the appellation, built entirely on hard, fractured schist.

sites.name: Fitou
sites.text: A village between the Étang de Leucate and the Corbières hills, giving its name to the Languedoc's oldest red AOC (1948), with a medieval castle above the vines.

sites.name: Domaine Gauby
sites.text: Gérard Gauby, in Calce, transformed Roussillon in the 1990s with old-vine Grenache, Carignan and white wines from limestone and schist, farmed biodynamically. His son Lionel continues. Calce has become a hub of young winemakers.

sites.name: Mas Amiel
sites.text: Founded in 1816 in Maury, this estate is famous for its field of thousands of glass bonbonnes, in which young Maury ages outdoors in the sun for a year before going into barrels. It makes Maury VDN from fresh to very old, and dry Maury Sec.

sites.name: Cellier des Templiers
sites.text: The cooperative that makes most Banyuls and Collioure, founded in 1921. Its cellar holds thousands of old oak barrels and casks, some containing wines decades old used in blending.

sites.name: Domaine de la Rectorie
sites.text: Marc and Thierry Parcé's estate in Banyuls-sur-Mer, founded in 1984 on terraces their family had farmed for generations. They make Banyuls in a fresh, reductive style and Collioure dry wines.

sites.name: Domaine du Mas Blanc
sites.text: The family estate of Dr André Parcé, who campaigned for the Banyuls and Collioure appellations. His son Jean-Michel continued. Its old Banyuls Hors d'Âge are among the greatest examples.

sites.name: Château Royal de Collioure
sites.text: A royal castle at the harbour of Collioure, built by the Templars and then the kings of Majorca, fortified by Vauban. The town was painted by Matisse and Derain in 1905, the birth of Fauvism.

sites.name: Domaine Cazes
sites.text: Founded in 1895 in Rivesaltes, Cazes became one of Roussillon's largest biodynamic estates. It keeps old stocks of Rivesaltes Ambré and Tuilé, some decades old.

sites.name: Château de Jau
sites.text: A former Cistercian property in Cases-de-Pène in the Agly valley, owned by the Dauré family since the 1970s, who make Côtes du Roussillon Villages and Muscat de Rivesaltes and run a contemporary art centre at the estate.

sites.name: Domaine du Clos des Fées
sites.text: Hervé Bizeul, a former sommelier and journalist, founded this estate in Vingrau in 1998. His Petite Sibérie, from old Grenache on limestone, was one of France's most expensive wines when released.

sites.name: Tautavel
sites.text: A village on limestone in the Agly valley, famous for Tautavel Man, human fossils about 450,000 years old found in the Caune de l'Arago cave. Its wines can add 'Tautavel' to the Côtes du Roussillon Villages name.

sites.name: Caramany
sites.text: A hilltop village on granite and gneiss above the Agly reservoir. Its rules have long required Carignan to be vinified by carbonic maceration, which softens the grape's rustic edges.

sites.name: Latour-de-France
sites.text: A village on schist in the Agly valley whose name recalls a border tower from the time when the Agly marked the frontier between France and the Crown of Aragon, before the 1659 annexation.

sites.name: Lesquerde
sites.text: A village on decomposed granite in the upper Agly valley, one of the coolest parts of Roussillon, which gives fresh, elegant reds and has its own village name under Côtes du Roussillon Villages.

sites.name: Clos de la Coulée de Serrant
sites.text: A 7-ha slope above the Loire, planted by Cistercian monks in 1130 and owned by Nicolas Joly's family since 1962. Joly, a former banker, converted it to biodynamics in 1981 and became biodynamics' most famous voice. The appellation belongs to his estate alone. Horses work the steep schist and volcanic slope, and the wine, rich and powerful dry Chenin, can age for decades.

sites.name: La Roche aux Moines
sites.text: Steep schist slopes above the Loire, once owned by the monks of Saint-Nicolas of Angers. In July 1214 Prince Louis of France defeated King John of England here, a battle that ended Plantagenet rule in Anjou. The wines are dense, powerful dry Chenin.

sites.name: Domaine des Baumard
sites.text: Founded in 1634, the Baumard family estate in Rochefort-sur-Loire makes Savennières, Quarts de Chaume and Coteaux du Layon. Florent Baumard pioneered screwcaps for top Loire wines and was at the centre of the cryoextraction dispute over Quarts de Chaume.

sites.name: Quarts de Chaume
sites.text: A south-facing amphitheatre of schist above the Layon at Rochefort-sur-Loire. The medieval lord of the area took a quarter (quart) of the harvest from these best plots, hence the name. Since 2011 it has been the Loire's only appellation with 'Grand Cru' on the label, with must of at least 298 g/l of sugar and hand-picked tries.

sites.name: Château de Fesles
sites.text: The leading estate of Bonnezeaux on the slopes above the Layon at Thouarcé, famous for long-lived, honeyed sweet Chenin. It was owned in the 1990s by the pastry chef Gaston Lenôtre and then by the Germain family of Bordeaux.

sites.name: Clos Rougeard
sites.text: The Foucault family's estate in Chacé made Saumur-Champigny a cult wine. Charly and Nady Foucault farmed organically, aged their Cabernet Franc in old barrels in tuffeau caves, and sold their Le Bourg and Les Poyeux to the world's best restaurants.
