After Charly's death the estate was sold to Martin and Olivier Bouygues in 2017.

sites.name: Château de Brézé
sites.text: A Renaissance château built over a fortress with an extensive network of underground tuffeau tunnels and a dry moat 18 m deep. The Brézé hill produced one of eighteenth-century France's most famous white wines.

sites.name: Bouvet-Ladubay
sites.text: Étienne Bouvet founded this Saumur sparkling house in 1851 and married Célestine Ladubay. Its kilometres of tuffeau caves in Saint-Hilaire-Saint-Florent hold millions of bottles, and the Monmousseau family, who ran it for decades, made it a centre for contemporary art.

sites.name: Abbaye Royale de Fontevraud
sites.text: Founded in 1101, this abbey was the burial place of Henry II of England, Eleanor of Aquitaine and Richard the Lionheart, the Plantagenet dynasty that ruled Anjou, England and Aquitaine and spread the wines of both Bordeaux and the Loire to English tables.

sites.name: Domaine Huet
sites.text: Founded by Victor Huet in 1928, made famous by his son Gaston, mayor of Vouvray, the estate owns three great vineyards: Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and Clos du Bourg. Under Noël Pinguet, Gaston's son-in-law, it converted to biodynamics in 1990. Its sweet and dry Chenins age for decades.

sites.name: Domaine du Clos Naudin
sites.text: The Foreau family's Clos Naudin is one of Vouvray's most respected estates. Philippe Foreau makes dry, demi-sec, moelleux and sparkling Chenin according to the vintage and ages bottles for years in tuffeau caves.

sites.name: Domaine François Chidaine
sites.text: François Chidaine, who took over his family vines in 1989 and later turned to biodynamic farming, led Montlouis's revival with precise, mineral dry Chenins such as Clos du Breuil and Les Bournais. He also farms vines across the river in Vouvray.

sites.name: Abbaye de Marmoutier
sites.text: Founded by Saint Martin of Tours around 372, Marmoutier was among the great monasteries of the West and spread viticulture along the Loire. Legend says Saint Martin's donkey nibbled the vines, and the monks noticed that the pruned vines yielded better grapes.

sites.name: Domaine Charles Joguet
sites.text: Charles Joguet, painter and sculptor, took over his family estate in Sazilly in 1957 and began bottling single-site Chinons, notably Clos de la Dioterie from old vines on clay-limestone, which showed that Chinon could be serious and long-lived.

sites.name: Domaine Bernard Baudry
sites.text: Bernard Baudry and his son Matthieu in Cravant-les-Coteaux make site-specific Chinons on sand, gravel, clay and limestone, organic for many years, showing the range of Cabernet Franc from soft to structured.

sites.name: Forteresse royale de Chinon
sites.text: The royal fortress above the Vienne where Joan of Arc met the future Charles VII in March 1429. Henry II of England died here in 1189. Below, the town's cellars run into the tuffeau.

sites.name: Abbaye de Bourgueil
sites.text: Founded in 990, the abbey of Saint-Pierre de Bourgueil is said to have planted the area's first Cabernet Franc. The tradition gives the grape its local name, Breton, after the monks' supposed source.

sites.name: Domaine Didier Dagueneau
sites.text: Didier Dagueneau, the wild-haired 'enfant terrible' of Pouilly-Fumé, cut yields, ploughed by horse, fermented in barrels and made single-terroir wines (Silex, Pur Sang, Buisson Renard) that redefined Sauvignon Blanc. He died in a plane crash in 2008; his son Louis-Benjamin continues.

sites.name: Château du Nozet
sites.text: The nineteenth-century château of the de Ladoucette family, the largest producer of Pouilly-Fumé, set in a park above the Loire. Its prestige cuvée Baron de L, from selected parcels, was first made in the 1970s and helped make Pouilly-Fumé a luxury name.

sites.name: Château de Tracy
sites.text: A castle above the Loire, parts of it medieval, owned by the same family for centuries. Its Sauvignon on flint and limestone is among the most refined in Pouilly-Fumé.

sites.name: Chavignol
sites.text: A hamlet of Sancerre known for steep Kimmeridgian slopes (the Monts Damnés, the Côte des Monts Damnés, Les Culs de Beaujeu) and for the Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese, Sancerre's classic partner.

sites.name: Les Monts Damnés
sites.text: A very steep slope of Kimmeridgian marl above Chavignol, so hard to work that it was said to be 'damned'. It gives powerful, long-lived Sancerre. Producers include François Cotat, Pascal Cotat, Gérard Boulay and Henri Bourgeois.

sites.name: Bué
sites.text: A Sancerre village surrounded by vineyards on caillottes and terres blanches, home of Lucien Crochet and a dense cluster of family estates. Its Le Chêne Marchand slope is a famous lieu-dit.

sites.name: Domaine Edmond Vatan
sites.text: A tiny Chavignol estate whose Clos la Néore, from old vines on terres blanches, is one of the rarest and most profound Sancerres. Edmond Vatan's daughter Anne continues the work.

sites.name: Domaine de Bellivière
sites.text: Éric and Christine Nicolas, from 1995, revived the Loir valley with intense, mineral Chenin from Jasnières and spicy Pineau d'Aunis reds, farming biodynamically. Their success drew a new generation of growers to this cold northern outpost.

sites.name: Château de Chambord
sites.text: François I's great Renaissance château in the Sologne, with a double-helix staircase possibly designed by Leonardo da Vinci. In 2015 the estate replanted a vineyard with Romorantin, the grape François I is said to have brought from Burgundy.

sites.name: Clos du Tue-Boeuf
sites.text: The Puzelat brothers' family estate in Les Montils, a pioneer of natural wine in the Loire from the 1990s, with Pineau d'Aunis, Romorantin, Menu Pineau and Gamay.

sites.name: Domaine de l'Écu
sites.text: Guy Bossard, organic from 1975 and biodynamic from the 1980s, bottled wines by bedrock (Granite, Gneiss, Orthogneiss), the idea behind today's crus communaux. Fred Niger Van Herck has run it since 2012.

sites.name: Domaine de la Pépière
sites.text: Marc Ollivier's estate in Maisdon-sur-Sèvre showed Muscadet's potential with old vines, long lees ageing and cru wines from Clisson and Gorges, sold at modest prices. Rémi Branger now co-runs it.

sites.name: Château de Goulaine
sites.text: A fifteenth-century château owned by the Goulaine family for a thousand years, which gives its name to one of the crus communaux recognised in 2019. It also houses a butterfly greenhouse and a museum of the LU biscuit company.

sites.name: Le Puy-Notre-Dame
sites.text: A hilltop village south of Saumur whose collegiate church holds a relic said to be the Virgin's girdle. It gives its name to Saumur Puy-Notre-Dame, a red-wine sub-zone with stricter Cabernet Franc rules.

sites.name: Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule
sites.text: The centre of the Saint-Pourçain appellation, a medieval wine town on the Sioule whose wines reached the courts of Saint Louis and the Avignon popes.

sites.name: Clisson
sites.text: A medieval town with Italianate architecture at the meeting of the Sèvre and the Moine, rebuilt after the Vendée wars. The cru communal Clisson, on coarse granite, gives broad, powerful Muscadet with long ageing on the lees.

sites.name: Gorges
sites.text: Gorges sits on gabbro, a dark igneous rock rich in iron and magnesium, and its wines are tight, smoky and long-lived. It is one of the three original crus communaux of 2011.

sites.name: Le Pallet
sites.text: The birthplace of the philosopher Peter Abelard (1079), now one of the original crus communaux, on gneiss and gabbro. Its wines are fine and supple with a smoky note.

sites.name: Château-Thébaud
sites.text: A cru communal on the steep slopes of the Maine river, recognised in 2019. Its granite gives taut, saline wines with a firm, almost tannic grip after long lees ageing.

sites.name: Monnières-Saint-Fiacre
sites.text: A cru communal recognised in 2019 on the slopes of the Sèvre, on gneiss and schist, making elegant, mineral wines that need several years to open.

sites.name: Mouzillon-Tillières
sites.text: A cru communal recognised in 2019 on the eastern side of the appellation, around the villages of Mouzillon and Tillières, mostly on gabbro, making full-bodied, structured Muscadet that ages well.

sites.name: Vallet
sites.text: The self-styled capital of Muscadet, at the centre of the Sèvre et Maine vineyard. Vallet was one of three crus communaux put to INAO public consultation in 2025 and still awaiting final approval in 2026.

sites.name: La Haie-Fouassière
sites.text: A village on the Sèvre, home of the Maison des Vins de Nantes, proposed as a cru communal in 2025 and still under INAO review in 2026.

sites.name: Champtoceaux
sites.text: A clifftop village above the Loire on the border of Anjou, proposed as the first cru communal of Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire in 2025, still under INAO review in 2026.

sites.name: Domaine Tempier
sites.text: The Peyraud family estate in Le Plan-du-Castellet, the reference for Bandol. Lucien Peyraud, who married Lucie (Lulu) Tempier in 1936, led the creation of the appellation in 1941. Lulu's cooking, celebrated by Richard Olney and Alice Waters, made the estate a legend. Its single-vineyard reds La Tourtine, La Migoua and Cabassaou are deep Mourvèdre.

sites.name: Château de Pibarnon
sites.text: Bought by Henri de Saint-Victor in 1977, Pibarnon sits on one of the highest points of Bandol, about 300 m, in an amphitheatre of terraces on Triassic limestone and blue marl. Its Mourvèdre reds are among the most elegant in Bandol.

sites.name: Château Pradeaux
sites.text: An estate near the sea at Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer, owned by the descendants of Jean-Marie-Étienne Portalis, one of the authors of the Napoleonic Civil Code, famous for traditional, uncompromising Bandol: pure Mourvèdre, whole bunches, years in old foudres.

sites.name: Château Simone
sites.text: The Rougier family has owned Château Simone since 1830; its cellars were dug by Carmelite monks in the sixteenth century. Its north-facing vineyard on the outskirts of Aix makes most of the Palette appellation, with old vines of dozens of varieties.

sites.name: Domaine de Trévallon
sites.text: Eloi Dürrbach, son of a painter friend of Picasso, planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in 1973 on the north side of the Alpilles. His wine became Provence's most famous red, but in 1995 the Baux appellation limited Cabernet, so Trévallon is sold as IGP. Labels carry drawings by his father, René Dürrbach.

sites.name: Château Miraval
sites.text: A large estate in Correns whose recording studio, Studio Miraval, hosted Pink Floyd during the making of *The Wall* in 1979. Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie rented it from 2008 and bought it in 2011, and its rosé, made with the Perrin family of Beaucastel, became one of the world's best-known; the couple's legal dispute over the estate later made headlines.

sites.name: Château d'Esclans
sites.text: Sacha Lichine bought this estate in La Motte in 2006 and launched Whispering Angel, a pale rosé that became a global phenomenon and changed Provence's economy. LVMH took a majority stake in 2019. Its top rosé, Garrus, is fermented and aged in large barrels.

sites.name: Clos Mireille
sites.text: Domaines Ott's estate on the coast at La Londe-les-Maures, on schist facing the sea. A 1955 cru classé, it is known for whites and rosés. The Ott family, from Alsace, came to Provence in 1896; Champagne Louis Roederer took control of the company in 2004.

sites.name: Château Sainte-Roseline
sites.text: A former abbey in Les Arcs where Saint Roseline, a fourteenth-century prioress, is buried in a chapel with a mosaic by Marc Chagall. It is one of the 18 surviving crus classés of 1955.

sites.name: Château Minuty
sites.text: A Second Empire château at Gassin, near Saint-Tropez, owned by the Matton-Farnet family since 1936 and a 1955 cru classé. Its pale rosés became fashionable on the Riviera, and in 2023 LVMH took a majority stake.

sites.name: Château de Bellet
sites.text: The historic estate that gave its name to the Bellet appellation in the hills above Nice, held for centuries by the de Charnacé family. It grows Rolle, Braquet and Folle Noire on steep terraces.

sites.name: Château de Crémat
sites.text: A château above Nice, one of the main Bellet producers, with vines on terraces of poudingue facing the Var valley and old cellars dug into the hillside.

sites.name: Clos Sainte-Magdeleine
sites.text: An estate on a promontory between the port of Cassis and the cliffs of Cap Canaille, with vines that run down to the sea. Its Marsanne and Clairette whites are the reference for Cassis.

sites.name: Château La Coste
sites.text: Irish businessman Paddy McKillen bought this estate in Le Puy-Sainte-Réparade in 2002 and turned it into an art and architecture park with works by Tadao Ando, Frank Gehry, Renzo Piano and Louise Bourgeois among the biodynamic vines.

sites.name: Château Vignelaure
sites.text: Georges Brunet, former owner of Château La Lagune in Bordeaux, planted Cabernet Sauvignon here in Rians in the 1960s, at 350 to 480 m, and showed that Provence could make serious red wine.

sites.name: Abbaye du Thoronet
sites.text: One of three great Cistercian abbeys of Provence, built in the late twelfth century in the forest of the Var. Its pure, austere architecture influenced Le Corbusier. The monks planted vines in the surrounding valley.

sites.name: Château Romanin
sites.text: A biodynamic estate in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence with a cathedral-like cellar carved into the rock of the Alpilles. Its reds are among the reference wines of Les Baux.

sites.name: Montagne Sainte-Victoire
sites.text: The limestone ridge east of Aix that Paul Cézanne painted more than 80 times. Its southern slopes carry the vineyards of Côtes de Provence Sainte-Victoire, recognised in 2005, where cool nights and limestone give fresh rosés.

sites.name: Domaine Antoine Arena
sites.text: Antoine Arena, a former law student, returned to his family's vines in 1975 and became the leader of Patrimonio's quality revolution, with organic farming and wines from Nielluccio, Vermentinu and the rare Biancu Gentile, which he helped rescue. His sons Antoine-Marie and Jean-Baptiste continue.

sites.name: Domaine Leccia
sites.text: A family estate in Poggio-d'Oletta, one of the best in Patrimonio, making firm, dark Nielluccio reds on clay-limestone, saline Vermentinu and Muscat du Cap Corse. Annette Leccia runs it; her brother Yves Leccia has his own estate nearby.

sites.name: Domaine Gentile
sites.text: Dominique Gentile's family estate near Saint-Florent, a pioneer of quality in Patrimonio since the 1970s, known for structured Nielluccio reds, Vermentinu whites and rich Muscat du Cap Corse.

sites.name: Clos Nicrosi
sites.class: Estate (Coteaux du Cap Corse, Muscat du Cap Corse)
sites.text: A tiny estate in Rogliano at the northern tip of Cap Corse, on schist terraces above the sea. Its Vermentinu and Muscat du Cap Corse are among the island's most sought-after wines.

sites.name: Domaine Comte Abbatucci
sites.text: Jean-Charles Abbatucci, descendant of a Corsican general of the Revolutionary era, farms biodynamically on granite in the Taravo valley. His father Antoine collected dozens of nearly extinct Corsican grapes from old vineyards, and the estate keeps them in a conservatory vineyard.

sites.name: Clos Capitoro
sites.text: The Bianchetti family's estate south-east of Ajaccio, a reference for Sciaccarellu on granite: pale, fragrant reds with red fruit, pepper and maquis notes. The family also makes a traditional, oxidative-style dessert wine, a rarity on the island.

sites.name: Clos Canarelli
sites.text: Yves Canarelli's biodynamic estate in Figari, in the windswept far south, revived Carcajolu Neru and Biancu Gentile and makes some of Corsica's most refined wines.

sites.name: Domaine de Torraccia
sites.text: Christian Imbert, a former adventurer, founded this estate near Porto-Vecchio in 1964, replanting Corsican grapes on granite at a time when much of the island was planting French varieties. His son Marc now runs it.

sites.name: Calvi
sites.text: A citadel town in the Balagne, north-west Corsica, which gives its name to the Calvi sub-area of Vin de Corse, with granite soils and elegant wines.

sites.name: Sartène
sites.text: A granite town in the south-west, called 'the most Corsican of Corsican towns' by Prosper Mérimée, which gives its name to a Vin de Corse sub-area.

sites.name: Château de Monbazillac
sites.text: A sixteenth-century castle with round towers overlooking the Dordogne and Bergerac, owned by the Monbazillac cooperative since 1960. It houses a museum of the wine and the Protestant history of the region, whose growers sold their sweet wines to Holland.

sites.name: Château Tirecul la Gravière
sites.text: Claudie and Bruno Bilancini bought this estate in 1992 and made Monbazillac wines of Sauternes quality, including Cuvée Madame from botrytised Muscadelle and Sémillon, picked berry by berry.

sites.name: Château Tour des Gendres
sites.text: Luc de Conti's family estate in Ribagnac, a pioneer of organic farming and of serious Bergerac. His La Gloire de Mon Père red and Moulin des Dames white showed what Bergerac could do.

sites.name: Château de Tiregand
sites.text: The largest estate of Pécharmant, a château overlooking the Dordogne, owned for generations by the family of the Comte de Saint-Exupéry. Its long-lived reds come from sand and gravel over the iron-rich 'tran'.

sites.name: Pont Valentré
sites.class: UNESCO World Heritage (Routes of Santiago de Compostela, 1998)
sites.text: A fortified fourteenth-century bridge over the Lot at Cahors, with three towers. Legend says the builder made a pact with the devil to finish it. It is the symbol of the city whose black wines travelled downstream to Bordeaux and on to England.

sites.name: Château Lagrézette
sites.text: A fifteenth-century château in Caillac bought by Alain-Dominique Perrin, former head of Cartier, in 1980. He invested heavily and made rich, oaky Cahors with consultant Michel Rolland.

sites.name: Château du Cèdre
sites.text: The Verhaeghe family's organic estate in Vire-sur-Lot, run by brothers Pascal and Jean-Marc. Their Le Cèdre and GC cuvées are among the best pure Malbec in Cahors.

sites.name: Clos Triguedina
sites.text: The Baldès family has made wine at Puy-l'Évêque since 1830. Jean-Luc Baldès revived the historic 'black wine' with The New Black Wine, made from grapes briefly heated in an oven as Cahors producers once did.

sites.name: Château Montus
sites.text: Alain Brumont bought Montus in 1980 and showed that 100% Tannat aged in new oak could make great wine. Its Montus Prestige, from a hill of rolled pebbles, made Madiran's name in the 1980s and 1990s.

sites.name: Château Bouscassé
sites.text: The Brumont family's original estate in Maumusson-Laguian, on clay-limestone slopes. Alain Brumont took over in the late 1970s and makes Madiran and Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh here, including late-harvest sweet whites from Petit Manseng.

sites.name: Vigne de Sarragachies
sites.text: A pre-phylloxera vineyard of under a hectare planted 'en foule' with about 20 grape varieties, some found nowhere else. In 2012 it became the first vineyard in France to be classified as a historic monument, protected by the Plaimont cooperative.

sites.name: Plaimont
sites.text: The Plaimont cooperative, created in 1979 by André Dubosc, unites hundreds of growers in the Gers. It campaigned for the Saint-Mont appellation, saved local grapes like Arrufiac and Manseng Noir, and protects old vineyards.

sites.name: Château de Pau
sites.text: Where the future Henri IV was born in 1553. According to legend, his grandfather Henri d'Albret rubbed his lips with garlic and Jurançon wine at his baptism, a story that has served Jurançon's marketing for centuries.

sites.name: Domaine Cauhapé
sites.text: Henri Ramonteu's estate in Monein, one of the largest private estates in Jurançon. His Quintessence and Noblesse du Temps, from Petit Manseng picked into December, are among the most famous Jurançons.

sites.name: Clos Uroulat
sites.text: Charles Hours's small estate in Monein, now run by his daughter Marie. Its Jurançon sweet and Cuvée Marie dry whites set the benchmark for elegance.

sites.name: Domaine Arretxea
sites.text: Thérèse and Michel Riouspeyrous's biodynamic estate on steep terraces of red sandstone and ophite. They showed that Irouléguy can make refined, mineral Tannat and Manseng.

sites.name: Domaine Ilarria
sites.text: Peio Espil's organic estate in the village of Irouléguy, one of the first independent producers in an appellation long dominated by the cooperative. His Tannat-based reds come from terraced red sandstone slopes.

sites.name: Abbaye Saint-Michel de Gaillac
sites.text: Founded in 972 on the banks of the Tarn, the abbey organised Gaillac's medieval vineyard and wine trade. It now houses a wine museum and the Maison des Vins de Gaillac.

sites.name: Domaine Plageoles
sites.text: Robert Plageoles and his son Bernard, in Cahuzac-sur-Vère, revived Gaillac's forgotten grapes (Ondenc, Prunelard, Verdanel, Mauzac Noir) and its traditional vin de voile and ancestral sparkling wine.

sites.name: Château Bellevue la Forêt
sites.text: The estate that put Fronton on the map from the 1970s with Négrette blends, created by Patrick Germain. Its large vineyard sits on the gravel terraces near the town of Fronton.

sites.name: Domaine du Cros
sites.text: Philippe Teulier's family estate in Goutrens, one of the largest independent estates in Marcillac, makes pure Mansois (Fer Servadou) from the red, iron-rich rougier soils, peppery and bright, from old vines on steep slopes.

sites.name: Vignerons de Buzet
sites.text: The cooperative, founded in 1953, makes most of the Buzet appellation's wine, ages its best reds in barrels from its own cooperage (a rarity for a cooperative) and has led environmental projects such as hedges and biodiversity corridors.

sites.name: Château de Duras
sites.text: A twelfth-century fortress rebuilt as a château by the Durfort family, overlooking the vineyards of the Côtes de Duras. It now houses a museum and is open to visitors.

sites.name: Saussignac
sites.text: A village with a Renaissance château, at the centre of the small Saussignac sweet-wine appellation, known for strict rules such as hand-picked tries and no chaptalisation, which give intense, botrytised wines.

sites.name: Château de Montaigne
sites.text: The home of philosopher Michel de Montaigne, who wrote the *Essais* in a tower whose beams are still carved with his favourite maxims; the tower survived the fire that destroyed the main house in 1885. The estate still produces Montravel wines.
